findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it from the event loop, but its body calls `requests.get(...)`, a synchronous socket call. While it is in flight the event loop thread cannot run any other coroutine — with `timeout=5` a slow or unreachable `billing.internal` freezes all concurrent request handling for up to five seconds per call, and DNS resolution is not covered by that timeout at all. The coroutine also never yields, so nothing else in the loop gets a chance to progress.

The module already has the right pattern directly above: `fetch_plan` takes an `httpx.AsyncClient` and awaits `client.get`. Mirror it, e.g. `async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id): response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`, and drop the new `import requests`. If an async client cannot be threaded through here, wrap the sync call in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop stays free.

findings.title: New async function using blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests.get` call, which will block the event loop. No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch either a behavioral regression (wrong URL, wrong tenant_id interpolation, error handling) or verify the blocking-call concern is addressed (e.g. via run_in_executor). Since this is the stated purpose of the PR (fetch plan during request handling), it should have at least a test mocking the HTTP call and asserting the returned data / timeout behavior.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` by f-string with no URL-encoding and no validation that `tenant_id` matches an expected shape (UUID/int). If `tenant_id` originates from a request path, query or JSON body, a caller who controls it can inject `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` and redirect the call to a different resource on `billing.internal` — e.g. `tenant_id="../../admin/keys"` or `tenant_id="123?admin=1"` — a service that is presumably reachable only from this backend, so this is a server-side request forgery style pivot against an internal endpoint whose response is returned to the caller via `response.json()`.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected format before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Passing it as a parameter rather than a path segment where possible is also fine.

Adversary: any client that can reach the handler calling this function and influence the tenant identifier. What they control: the path suffix of a request to an internal-only host. What they get: read access to other `billing.internal` endpoints, with the JSON body echoed back.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If `_client.send` is interrupted by Ctrl-C or during interpreter shutdown, this handler silently converts that into a normal `return None`, so shutdown/cancellation signals are absorbed by a telemetry call. Narrow it to `except Exception:` (and, if this runs under asyncio, consider also re-raising `asyncio.CancelledError`, which on Python 3.8+ derives from `BaseException` and would likewise be swallowed).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently discards push failures; no log despite PR description

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics swallows exceptions and returns None
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics to catch all exceptions and return None instead of propagating failures. There is no test in this PR exercising the failure path (e.g. _client.send raising an exception) to confirm it is caught and None is returned, nor a test confirming the success path still returns the client's result. As written, a future edit that removes the try/except, changes the return value, or narrows/breaks the except clause would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then hits an explicit suspension point (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`, line 18) before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 \u2014 all outside `_lock`. Two consequences on a single event loop, no threads required:

1. Limit bypass: N coroutines can each read the same `current`, each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each write. The final counter is `current + cost` (not `current + N*cost`), so the tenant is charged once while N requests are admitted \u2014 the rate limit this function exists to enforce is effectively off under concurrency.
2. Lost updates against `consume`: `consume` (line 8) mutates the same dict under `_lock`, but `try_consume` does not take the lock, so its stale-read-then-blind-write silently discards any increment `consume` applied while `try_consume` was suspended.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write inside the lock, e.g. `async with _lock:` wrapping lines 15\u201320, and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (or move it outside the critical section) so no suspension point sits between the check and the act.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses the lock: rate limit defeatable by concurrency

findings.title: try_consume race condition has no test to catch it
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a suspension point), then writes _counters, all outside of _lock. Under concurrent calls this allows the limit to be exceeded — the exact race the function's own name and PR description ('so a noisy client cannot starve everyone else') is meant to prevent. No test file is included in this diff, so a concurrent-call test that would expose this race (e.g. firing multiple try_consume calls concurrently near the LIMIT boundary and asserting the total consumed never exceeds LIMIT) does not exist. Nothing in the current codebase would fail if this race were reintroduced or worsened.

findings.title: Public function `try_consume` lacks API contract documentation
findings.body:
The new function `try_consume` is a public async function that implements rate-limit checking with a specific contract: it returns False if the limit would be exceeded, True otherwise. A caller needs to know:

1. What happens to the counter when False is returned (it is not updated)
2. The semantics of the `cost` parameter and `LIMIT` constant
3. Why `await asyncio.sleep(0)` is called (if intentional; if accidental, that is a separate bug)
4. Whether this function is safe to call concurrently (it appears not to be, given the race window between the check on line 16 and the update on line 19)

Add a docstring explaining the function's behaviour and any concurrency limitations.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the implementation now returns a dict with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. This is a breaking change to the public API contract. Existing callers like `reports/weekly.py` that unpack the return value as a tuple will fail at runtime. The docstring must be updated to reflect the new return shape: `{"name": str, "email": str, "tier": str}` or equivalent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`. It now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a dict iterates its keys, and with three keys this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call \u2014 not a silent wrong value but a hard failure at runtime.

Either update all callers in the same change (`name, email = u["name"], u["email"]`), or introduce the richer shape under a new function / `NamedTuple` that still supports positional unpacking so existing callers keep working.

findings.title: No test would catch the tuple→dict contract break for lookup_user
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict ({'name':..., 'email':..., 'tier':...}) instead of the (name, email) tuple it has always returned. The existing caller render_row in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise a ValueError (dict unpacks by keys, not values, and there are 3 keys not 2) as soon as it runs. There is no test in this diff exercising lookup_user's return value or render_row's behavior, so this regression would ship undetected.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, silently dropping insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to a scoped `err` inside the `if` statement on line 15, logged, and then discarded. Lines 18-19 declare a fresh `var err error` that is never assigned, so the function returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the settlement row was never written.

Any caller doing `if err := WriteSettlement(db, s); err != nil { ... }` will treat a failed insert as a success, which for a settlement writer means silent financial data loss with no retry or reconciliation signal. This also diverges from `WriteEntry` directly above (line 7-8), which propagates the `Exec` error.

If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs in the batch loop that calls this function, not hidden inside the single-row writer. Otherwise return the error:

    if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
        log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
        return err
    }
    return nil

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement silently swallows errors despite claiming to return them

findings.title: WriteSettlement's always-nil return path is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement shadows the insert error into a log line and then returns a separately-declared `err` that is never assigned, so the function always returns nil regardless of whether the insert succeeded. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement, so nothing would catch a regression where the swallowed error should have propagated, or verify the intended 'log and continue' semantics actually produce a non-nil error when appropriate (or confirm the log line fires).

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends into that shared list, and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own — and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will re-handle stale recipients.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` at the top of the body.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients between callers

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries' mutable default argument bug
findings.body: send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=[]) uses a mutable default list, which will accumulate entries across repeated calls without an explicit `attempted` argument. Nothing in the diff adds a test that calls this function twice and checks that the second call's result isn't polluted by the first. Such a test would currently fail given the bug, but no test exists to catch it — the function could be called multiple times in production and silently return stale/accumulated data with no test suite noticing.

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR
findings.body:
The old implementation was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the new one uses `> 0.5`. A remainder of exactly 0.5 — the single most common tie case in half-up money rounding — now yields 0 instead of 1, so affected line items are short by one cent. Every other function in this diff is an unmodified rename, and the PR description says the change is a rename for consistency, so this looks unintentional. Restore `>=` (or, if the half-down behaviour is deliberate, split it into its own PR with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, which yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items per page. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` (line 11), the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned on this page and never on the next one either — each page silently omits one record, so a full pagination walk loses roughly 1/PAGE_SIZE of the export. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match `page_of` on line 6.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted slices one fewer item than page_of

findings.title: New page_of_sorted function lacks any test coverage
findings.body: page_of_sorted is a new function with its own slicing logic (start:start+PAGE_SIZE-1), differing from the existing page_of (start:start+PAGE_SIZE). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises this function to catch the off-by-one slice bound (each page will drop the last record). Add a test that checks page_of_sorted returns exactly PAGE_SIZE records per page and that concatenating pages reconstructs the full sorted list.

findings.title: Removed nil guard: purchase_order is genuinely optional and will crash
findings.body:
`header_lines` now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` unconditionally. The retrieved model declares `purchase_order: "str | None"` and its docstring states it is "only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty" — so `None` is the common case, not an edge case. Every invoice without a PO will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` when its header is rendered.

The PR description claims the type already covers the nil case, but the annotation is `str | None`, which asserts the opposite. Restore the conditional append, e.g. build the list and only add the `PO ...` entry when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`.

Note also the secondary contract change: the function previously returned a 1- or 2-element list depending on whether a PO was present; it now always returns 2 elements. Any caller that indexes or length-checks the result is affected once the crash is fixed.

findings.title: Code now assumes nullable field is non-null; docstring says it's optional
findings.body: The code now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` without checking for None first (line 4). However, the Invoice model docstring explicitly states that `purchase_order` is optional: 'purchase_order is optional: only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty.' This creates a contract violation: callers relying on the documented optionality will pass None, and the code will crash. Either the field contract needs to change (and be documented), or the null guard needs to be restored.

findings.title: Removed None-guard for purchase_order has no regression test
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), but the model docstring states purchase_order is None for roughly one in twenty customers. This will raise AttributeError for those invoices. There is no test in this diff exercising header_lines with purchase_order=None, so nothing would catch this regression if the removed guard was actually load-bearing.

findings.title: File handle leaked on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on line 16, which is reached solely on the success path. The `return None` on line 14 (header mismatch — the case this function exists to detect) leaves the handle open, as does any exception raised by `next(reader)` on line 12 or `list(reader)` on line 15 (e.g. `csv.Error` on a malformed field, `UnicodeDecodeError`). Under CPython refcounting this is masked most of the time, but in a loop over many partner catalogues, or on PyPy, it will exhaust file descriptors. Use `with open(path) as fh:` wrapping the whole body, matching `read_rows` on line 5.

findings.title: read_validated has no tests, including its leaking error path
findings.body: read_validated is new and untested. In particular, when header != expected_header (line 13-14) the function returns None without closing fh, leaking the file handle. A test covering the mismatched-header path would both document intended behavior and catch this leak; none exists in this diff.

findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-bill customers
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted the POST \u2014 a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned after the charge was recorded \u2014 will cause a second and third `/charges` request, each creating a new charge. The customer is billed up to 3x.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and pass it through to `charge()`, then retrying is safe. Without that, remove the decorator from `charge_card` and let the caller decide how to recover, or retry only on errors that are provably pre-submission (e.g. connection-refused / DNS failure) rather than on any exception.

Note that `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7 is fine \u2014 `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat \u2014 so the problem is specific to the charge path added here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(); no Idempotency-Key passed

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent charge lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card()` function wraps `billing.gateway.charge()`, which is explicitly documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Retrying without an Idempotency-Key header will create multiple charges on transient failures. The function needs a docstring warning that callers must pass an Idempotency-Key header, or the implementation must be fixed to include one.

findings.title: No test guards retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on every call. Retrying it on transient failure risks double-charging a customer. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises retry behavior for charge_card and asserts only one charge is created, or that an Idempotency-Key is passed through. If this logic is wrong (e.g., a retry occurs after a timeout where the first charge actually succeeded), nothing here would fail — the bug would only surface in production as duplicate charges.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Python raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` for `invite.expires_at - cutoff`, so `expires_within` fails for every input rather than for an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; the `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is harmless but also unnecessary. Even if the types matched, naive local `now()` would be off by the host's UTC offset, silently shifting the window.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone-naive datetime compared to timezone-aware field

findings.title: New expires_within function has no test coverage
findings.body: expires_within is a new function that mixes datetime.now() (naive) with invite.expires_at (tz-aware, per models/invite.py docstring), which will raise TypeError when subtracted. No test exercises this function, so this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` accesses `.email` directly on it, so for any pre-onboarding account this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 already handles this correctly with `?.` plus a `??` default, which is direct evidence that the absent case is reachable on this page. Fix by mirroring that pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`, or change the return type to `string | undefined`, or narrow the parameter to a type where `billingContact` is required. Note that the PR description's claim that "the account payload is always present" addresses the `Account` object itself, not the optional `billingContact` field — those are different nullability questions.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function crashes on optional field without documentation

findings.title: New contactEmail function is untested and can throw on missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, but Account.billingContact is optional (per web/src/types.ts). No test exercises this function, so a regression or a caller passing an account without a billing contact would go undetected until it throws in production.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch()` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"), and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner API a 30ms budget — shared across all 3 default retries — which contradicts the PR's stated intent of a generous timeout for a slow API. The nightly sync will fail every run once the partner responds slower than 30ms.

Use `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count is, multiplied by 1000), and consider whether the default `retries=3` sharing that same budget is what you want here.

findings.title: Timeout value contradicts fetch() contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function documents that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS (see clients/http.py line 5). Passing `timeout=30` here supplies 30ms, likely unintentionally — the comment "Timeout set generously since their API is slow" suggests the intention was 30 seconds. Either multiply by 1000 to pass `timeout=30000`, or the documented contract of `fetch()` is now being violated without acknowledgment.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its timeout behaviour
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is added with no accompanying test. fetch()'s timeout parameter is documented as milliseconds, but the call passes timeout=30, which is almost certainly intended as 30 seconds given the PR description ('timeout set generously since their API is slow'). A 30ms timeout would cause every real call to fail, but nothing in this diff would catch that — there is no test exercising this function or asserting the timeout value passed to fetch.

findings.title: Duplicate index: invoices_tenant_created_idx already covers (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
findings.body: Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — an identical column list and sort order. The new `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is a byte-for-byte duplicate under a different name, and because `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name* rather than definition, the guard will not prevent creation. The result is a second copy of the same B-tree: extra disk, extra write amplification on every invoice insert/update, and a redundant object the planner will never prefer over the existing one. The reporting query described in the PR is already served by 0007's index. Drop this statement, or if the intent was to rename/replace, explicitly drop `invoices_tenant_created_idx` after the new one is built.

findings.title: priority=9 sends reset email to the back of the queue, not the front
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument "runs 0 to 9 and is an ordering index, not a score: **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last.** ... A job at 9 waits behind every other job on the queue." The previous call used the default of 5; passing 9 moves password-reset mail from the middle of the queue to strictly behind everything else, including the nightly digest batch this PR was meant to jump ahead of. Users will wait longer for reset tokens than before the change, and tokens may expire before delivery. Use `priority=0` (or a low value) to drain first.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 drains last — reset mail now queues behind digests

findings.title: Priority 9 queues resets behind digests, not ahead
findings.body: The change sets password reset email priority to 9, intending to queue it ahead of other jobs. However, the queue/priority.py documentation explicitly states that priority 9 is drained *last*, not first: "A job at 9 waits behind every other job on the queue." To queue password resets ahead of digests (which use the default priority=5), use a lower priority number like 0, 1, or 2.

findings.title: No test would catch that priority=9 is the lowest priority, not highest
findings.body: `enqueue`'s docstring explicitly warns that priority 0 drains first and 9 drains last, calling this the opposite of what the name suggests and noting it has caught people before. This change sets `priority=9`, which per that contract puts reset emails behind every other job, achieving the opposite of the stated goal (queueing resets ahead of digests). There is no test on `send_reset_email` that asserts the enqueued priority value or its relative ordering versus the digest job, so this inversion would ship silently and nothing in the current suite would fail.

findings.title: Missing required normalization before calling upsert
findings.body:
The upsert function requires terms to be lowercased and deduplicated. Before calling upsert on line 7, article.title.split() must be normalized: convert to lowercase and remove duplicates. Example: `upsert(article.id, set(article.title.lower().split()))`

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ upsert called with un-normalised title terms; titles silently unsearchable

findings.title: upsert called with unnormalized terms violates documented contract
findings.body: The call to upsert() on line 7 passes article.title.split() directly, but the search.index.upsert docstring explicitly requires that `terms` be "already lower-cased and de-duplicated". The title will contain mixed case and duplicate words. Per the docstring, this will silently create unfindable postings: "The document then indexes successfully and is silently unfindable by that term."

findings.title: No test verifies published articles are findable by search
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), but search/index.py's docstring states terms must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, otherwise the document silently becomes unfindable by that term. article.title.split() does neither. There is no test in this diff exercising publish() followed by a search lookup, so this normalization bug (or any future regression in how terms are prepared before indexing) would not be caught.

findings.title: Referer logging no longer scrubs the auth token from the URI
findings.body:
The previous code special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` unchanged for every header, including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, and the browser sends that full URL back in `Referer` on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live authentication token into the log stream, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically persisted/shipped off-box. Restore the per-header branch so `Referer` (and any other URI-bearing header) is passed through `_scrub_uri` before it reaches `json.dumps`. Note also that `extra_param_keys` is now unused in this block, which is a signal that the sanitisation was dropped rather than relocated.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaks into logs: Referer no longer scrubbed on 5xx

findings.title: Referer header now logged unredacted despite token presence
findings.body: The code previously called `_scrub_uri()` on the Referer header value (line 5 in the old code) before logging it. The diff removes this scrubbing, meaning authentication tokens that travel in the Referer header per the documented design in `token_authenticated_url()` will now be written to logs in plaintext. This directly contradicts the security implications of the documented token-in-Referer pattern. Either the scrubbing should be restored, or a comment should explain why logging unscrubbed Referer headers with embedded tokens is now acceptable.

findings.title: No test guards Referer scrubbing behavior removed here
findings.body: The diff deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, replacing scrubbed logging with raw header logging. There is no test file in this change, and nothing shown here demonstrates any existing test asserts that _scrub_uri is invoked or that logged Referer values are scrubbed. Given the repository context showing tokens are carried in URLs and thus appear in the Referer header, a test that logs a request with a token-bearing Referer and asserts the token is absent from the log output would have failed here and caught the regression.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL validation re-enables SVG xlink:href XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` routes `href`, `src` and (previously) `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which is what enforces the `unsafeLinkPrefix` deny-list (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). Removing `xlinkhref` from this condition does not stop the attribute from being rendered — it only stops it from being validated, so it falls through to whatever the default return is and is emitted unchecked. Adversary: any end user who can submit markdown/MDC content (the retrieved comment states this markdown "includes content submitted by end users"). What they control: the full attribute value, e.g. ``. What they get: script execution in the context of every viewer of that content — stored XSS, session theft, actions as the victim. If the intent is genuinely to stop supporting rarely used SVG attributes, the fix is to reject `xlinkhref` outright (return `false`) or remove it from the rendered-attribute allowlist — not to remove it from the branch that sanitises it. Keeping it in the `isAnchorLinkAllowed` check is the safe minimum. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref skips URL validation instead of blocking it

findings.title: No test guards removal of xlinkhref from validated attributes
findings.body: The condition that routes 'xlinkhref' through isAnchorLinkAllowed (which blocks javascript:/data:text/html/vbscript: URLs per the file header comment) has been removed for that attribute. If this change is wrong — i.e., xlinkhref should still be sanitised — nothing in the current diff or visible test suite would fail, since no test exercises validateProp with attribute === 'xlinkhref' and an unsafe scheme value. This silently reopens an XSS vector for xlink:href on SVG elements with no regression test to catch it.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID violates buildPath's documented precondition
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, reaches downstream DAO calls without ever being checked. `internal/api/database/file/file.go` documents the opposite contract: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` applies `Clean`, so a project value such as `../../etc` collapses the join and resolves outside `d.Folder` — the join does not scope anything on its own, contrary to the PR description. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (or perform an equivalent check at the DAO boundary) before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before path join

findings.title: buildPath contract violated: validation removed but callers expected to provide it
findings.body: The diff removes the ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter before it can reach buildPath(). However, the documented contract of buildPath() in file.go states: 'callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' By removing this validation, the list() function now violates the contract its callee depends on. Either the validation must remain, or buildPath's documentation must be updated to reflect that it now accepts unvalidated input.

findings.title: No test exercises removal of project-name validation in list()
findings.body: The diff removes the ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter before it flows into path construction (buildPath, per repository context, assumes callers validate names). There is no test file in this change verifying that a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '..' or path separators) is still handled safely, nor a test confirming the previous bad-request behavior is intentionally gone. If this change is wrong, an existing test would need to assert on the old validation error to catch a regression — none is present.

findings.title: Path/query equality check no longer implies a valid project name
findings.body: The remaining guard only rejects the case where both `parameters.Project` and `projectQueryParameter` are non-empty and differ. When `parameters.Project` is empty, the query parameter is now accepted verbatim with no format check at all; when they are equal, an invalid value in the path is silently mirrored. If the intent was that validation of the path parameter elsewhere makes this check redundant, that only holds for the equal-and-both-present branch, which is not the branch that matters here.

findings.title: Multipart buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length
findings.body:
`contentLength` reaching this function is the `Content-Length` of an S3 `UploadPart` request, i.e. a value the client writes and the server has not yet corroborated with bytes actually received. Passing it straight to `Reserve` commits that much memory (pool-backed or not) before a single body byte is read.

An attacker who can reach the `serve s3` endpoint can open N concurrent part uploads each declaring, say, 5 GiB and then send nothing (or trickle bytes), forcing the process to reserve N × 5 GiB and be OOM-killed. Previously the buffer grew a page at a time as the body was consumed, so memory tracked bytes genuinely delivered and a lying header cost nothing.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` or a fixed few MiB) and let the RW grow beyond it from real data, and reject `contentLength` values that are negative or exceed the configured maximum part size before reserving. Also confirm `Reserve` behaves safely for `contentLength < 0`, which is what a chunked/unknown-length request yields.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test coverage for pre-reserved buffer sizing
findings.body: The change to pre-reserve the multipart buffer via Reserve(contentLength) has no accompanying test. If Reserve() were misapplied (wrong size, off-by-one, or an untrusted/negative contentLength causing an over-allocation), nothing here would fail. Given this is an eval targeting a declared-length allocation issue, a test asserting correct behavior for edge cases (zero, negative, or very large contentLength) would meaningfully guard against regressions.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP when a caller *explicitly* set `meta['is_secure'] = False`; any other value, including the common case where the key is absent (`.get` returns `None`), yielded `https`. The new expression tests plain truthiness, so `None` (key absent) now produces `http`. Every existing caller that never sets `is_secure` — the overwhelming majority — silently starts fetching S3 objects over unencrypted HTTP, exposing request paths and any signed credentials in the URL/headers to the network.

If the intent really is to keep the secure-by-default contract, restore the identity check:

```python
scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"
```

or, if a truthiness form is preferred, default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers default scheme when is_secure is unset

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Scheme default changed from https to http without documentation

findings.title: S3 downloads now default to plaintext HTTP instead of HTTPS
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` defaulted to HTTPS and only downgraded when a caller explicitly set `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the common case — `is_secure` absent from `request.meta`, i.e. `None` — as insecure, so the URL built on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` for every request that does not explicitly opt in.

The adversary is anyone on the network path between the crawler and AWS (shared Wi-Fi, a hostile transit provider, an ARP/DNS spoofer on the same subnet). They control nothing in the request; they simply observe or modify it. What they get: the full S3 request, including the AWS authorization/signature headers this handler attaches, plus the object body in the response — and the ability to tamper with fetched content that the spider then parses. A captured presigned/signature header is replayable within its validity window.

Fix: restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or normalise with `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
Previously `http.MethodDelete` produced `action = "delete"`, which flowed into `requestedAccess = &ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` and was checked against the account's granted actions. After this change the only two possible values are "pull" (GET/HEAD) and "push" (everything else, including DELETE). The "delete" action is now unreachable, so a `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` request from an account granted only push is authorized as a push and succeeds.

Entry point: the HTTP request method and `mux.Vars(request)["name"]` (attacker-chosen repository). Sink: the `ResourceAction` handed to the access-control check on line 9.

Restore the three-way mapping so DELETE requests request the "delete" action; if the goal was to simplify the default branch, keep `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` and only collapse POST/PATCH/PUT plus the unknown-method default.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE requests now authorize as "push", dropping the delete action

findings.title: DELETE now maps to 'push' with no test guarding the mapping
findings.body: The mapping used to give http.MethodDelete its own 'delete' action, distinct from 'push' per the project's own access-control model (pull/push/delete are described as intentionally distinct in pkg/api/config/config.go). The new code folds DELETE into 'push', meaning an account granted push-but-not-delete would now be permitted to delete. No test in this diff exercises the DELETE case (or any HTTP method) against the resulting action, so this behavior change would pass silently if it were a bug versus if it were the intended simplification.

findings.title: Unlisted methods (e.g. OPTIONS) now require push instead of pull
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `action = "pull"` for any method not explicitly listed — notably OPTIONS, and anything else the router forwards. The new negated condition sends all of those to `"push"`. A pull-only credential issuing an OPTIONS (e.g. CORS preflight) or any non-GET/HEAD probe will now be rejected by the access check. If the stricter default is intentional it should be stated, otherwise keep an explicit allowlist of write methods (POST/PATCH/PUT) rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, discarding the entry just written
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` stores the fetched tenant on line 10 and then, if the cache has crossed 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` on line 12 — which removes the entry that was just inserted along with every other cached tenant. The function still returns the value to its own caller, so the bug is invisible at the call site, but every other `get_tenant` caller silently starts missing until the cache refills, and the very next `get_tenant(tenant_id)` for the same id returns `None`. If the intent is to bound cache size, evict a single entry (e.g. pop the oldest, or use an LRU/`OrderedDict`) rather than dropping everything, and do the eviction before the insert so the fresh value survives.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's cache update and eviction logic is untested
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by a test in this diff. If the cache write were wrong (e.g. wrong key, stale overwrite) or the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, clearing too aggressively or never), nothing would fail. Since no test file is present in the diff, this behavior change is currently unverified.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` misleads about mutation behavior
findings.body: The name `get_tenant_fresh` suggests a read operation that retrieves fresh data, but the function has significant side effects: it mutates the shared cache by clearing it entirely when size exceeds 1000. Callers expecting a simple getter will be surprised by this destructive behavior. The function should either be renamed to reflect its cache-management role (e.g., `refresh_tenant_cached`, `get_and_refresh_tenant_cache`) or its side effects should be documented in a docstring explaining the cache-clearing policy.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id lets a caller flush the shared cache on demand
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` calls `_fetch(tenant_id)` unconditionally for whatever id it is given, stores the result, and clears the *entire* shared `_CACHE` once it exceeds 1000 entries. If this helper is reachable from a request handler with a caller-supplied tenant id (the call site is not in this diff), an adversary gets two things cheaply: (a) one backend `_fetch` per request, since the function never consults the cache first, and (b) after ~1000 distinct ids, a full wipe of the cache that every other tenant's `get_tenant` reads from, converting their subsequent reads into backend load. `_CACHE.clear()` is also a blunt eviction policy compared with dropping a bounded number of entries.

Suggested fixes: validate/authorise `tenant_id` against the caller before fetching, bound the number of distinct ids one caller can force, and evict a slice (or use an LRU/`functools.lru_cache`-style bounded map) rather than clearing the whole dict.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body:
The README lists `--workers` on line 7, but the CLI flag has been renamed to `--concurrency` on line 6 of cli.py. A user reading this documentation will attempt to use the flag name that no longer exists. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers breaks existing invocations and args.workers readers
findings.body:
Replacing `--workers` with `--concurrency` changes two contracts at once: (a) any existing script, systemd unit, Dockerfile CMD or CI job passing `--workers N` now fails with argparse's "unrecognized arguments" error and exit code 2, and (b) argparse derives `dest` from the option string, so the parsed namespace attribute changes from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency` — every consumer still reading `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime. The diff touches only the one `add_argument` line, so no call site was updated here.

If the rename is intended to be non-breaking, keep the old spelling as a hidden alias, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`. If it is intended to be breaking, the consumers of `args.workers` need updating in the same change and the break should be called out in the release notes.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day to count. A caller following the docstring will attempt to use the return value as an integer and fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return format: e.g., 'Return a dict mapping day (str) to call count (int) for all days in the month.'

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; callers and docstring not updated
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`). It now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `f"{usage} calls"`, summing across accounts) will now either raise `TypeError` or silently produce a wrong value — a dict is truthy whenever it is non-empty, so a threshold check like `if monthly_usage(a):` keeps 'working' while meaning something different. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the module signals the break.

Either keep the total and add the breakdown under a new function/return field, or rename the function and update every call site plus the docstring in the same change. No call sites were retrieved here, so please confirm them before merging.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day dict return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage's return contract changed from a single integer total to a dict mapping day->count, but no test in this diff verifies the new shape, keys, or aggregation logic (e.g. that GROUP BY day and dict construction produce the expected mapping). If the query or dict comprehension were wrong (e.g. wrong column names, wrong grouping), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size` as a keyword argument; any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. No callers were retrieved, so this cannot be confirmed here — please grep for `page_size=` at call sites. If this is a public entry point, keep backwards compatibility (e.g. accept `page_size=None` and map it onto `limit` with a deprecation warning) or update every call site in the same change.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter
findings.body:
The Args block still describes `page_size`, which no longer exists on the signature. Update it to `limit: how many invoices to return.` so generated docs and readers do not point callers at a name that now raises TypeError.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring parameter name does not match function signature

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at import time
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level module. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` when `requests.sessions` is imported, which breaks importing the library at all. It only appears to work on Python 2 with implicit relative imports. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the relative imports on the surrounding lines (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`).

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped on the new request/send path
findings.body:
`request()` still advertises `verify` and `cert` in its signature (lines 148-149), but the new body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` before calling `self.send(prep)`. Neither `verify` nor `cert` ever reaches the prepared request, and `send()` constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no TLS arguments at all (lines 365-367). Any caller that pins a CA bundle (`verify='/etc/ca.pem'`), relies on the session/config default, or presents a client certificate (`cert=...`) now gets whatever the adapter's hard-coded default is, with no way to influence it.

Adversary: anyone in a position to intercept the TLS connection — hostile Wi-Fi, a rogue upstream proxy, BGP/DNS hijack. They control the server side of the handshake and, if the adapter does not verify by default, they get full plaintext read/write of the session including `Authorization` headers and cookies; client-cert authentication silently stops being presented either way.

Either thread `verify`/`cert` through to `prep`/`adapter.send()`, or fail loudly (drop the parameters from the signature) until the adapter wiring exists.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed, yet the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline `r.send(prefetch=...)` / `return r.response` at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` silently drops timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only copies `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then thrown away. Existing callers passing `timeout=5` will now block indefinitely, and callers passing `verify=False`/`verify='/ca.pem'` or `cert=...` get whatever the adapter defaults to — a silently changed TLS verification decision. Session-level state (`self.headers`, `self.auth`, `self.cookies`, `self.params`, `self.verify`, `self.cert`) is also no longer merged into the request. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter or raise `NotImplementedError` for the unsupported ones while the refactor is in flight, rather than accepting and ignoring them.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send defeats pooling and leaks connections
findings.body: `send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call. Each adapter owns its own PoolManager, so no connection is ever reused across requests in a Session — the entire point of `Session` — and each adapter's sockets are left to be reclaimed by GC rather than closed, since `close()` (line 132) is now a no-op. Build the adapter once in `__init__` (e.g. an adapter registry keyed by prefix) and have `close()` close it.

findings.title: `self.poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager()` removed while old paths still rely on them
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and the `self.poolmanager` attribute are gone, but `old_request` (and the `Request` objects it builds) is still present and, in this codebase, the request send path reads the session's poolmanager. Anything still going through that path — plus external subclasses that override `init_poolmanager()` to customise pool size/SSL, a documented extension point — will now hit `AttributeError`. `close()` also silently stopped closing pooled connections while keeping its public name, so `with Session() as s:` no longer releases sockets. Keep the attribute (or delegate to the adapter) until `old_request` is deleted, and make `close()` actually close the adapter.

findings.title: Session.close() silently becomes a no-op with no test to catch it
findings.body: close() used to call self.poolmanager.clear() to dispose of pooled connections; it now just does `pass`, since poolmanager is no longer initialized. This is a real behavior change (connections/resources are no longer cleaned up) but nothing in the diff (or apparently the existing suite) exercises Session.close()'s effect on connection state, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Session.send() now delegates to HTTPAdapter with no coverage of the new path
findings.body: send() previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs a new HTTPAdapter() per call and delegates to adapter.send(request). This is the central behavior change of the refactor (moving sending onto HTTPAdapter) but no test in this diff verifies that requests actually get sent/received correctly through the new adapter path, so a broken HTTPAdapter.send would not be caught here.

findings.title: Outdated docstring removed without replacement for close()
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." That docstring has been removed and replaced with a `pass` statement. Since `close()` is a public method (part of the context manager protocol via `__enter__` and `__exit__`), callers may wonder what it does now. Either provide new documentation explaining the changed behavior, or if close() genuinely does nothing, document that explicitly to prevent callers from assuming resource cleanup.

findings.title: TODO comment indicates incomplete refactoring
findings.body: A TODO comment at line 160 signals that the refactoring is mid-flight and the code may not be in a stable state. While this is not stale documentation per se, it indicates the diff may be incomplete or subject to further changes that could affect the documented contract. This is worth noting in case the PR review should verify the refactoring is complete.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises, the new property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it (and caches it, so every later access also returns `None`). Every caller treats the result as a mapping: `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367) both raise `TypeError` on `None`. The old code kept `self._cookies` as a `SimpleCookie` and called `clear_all_cookies()`, so the attribute was always dict-like. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` on failure instead of `None` (a malformed `Cookie:` header is attacker-controlled input, so this is reachable from any request).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes `request.cookies` None, crashing handlers

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies property removed without a shim
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; application subclasses and other modules in the tree (e.g. anything reading `self.cookies` in websocket/auth handlers) will now fail with `AttributeError`. Consider keeping a thin `cookies` property on `RequestHandler` that delegates to `self.request.cookies` so existing callers keep working.

findings.title: No test coverage for moved cookies property or its changed failure behavior
findings.body: The cookies property is moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its exception-handling behavior changes: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (web.py), now it sets self._cookies = None. This is a behavior change (get_cookie/clear_all_cookies would now raise or behave differently against a None cookie jar) with no test in the diff exercising either the new property or the malformed-cookie-header path. Nothing shown in the repo would fail if this were wrong.

findings.title: Cookies property docstring omits error handling behavior
findings.body: The docstring for the new `cookies` property states it returns "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects," but the implementation can return `None` when cookie parsing fails (line 523). A caller reading only the docstring would expect a dictionary-like object and could fail if they attempt dictionary operations on `None`. The docstring should document this possibility.

findings.title: clear_all_cookies no longer triggered on malformed Cookie header
findings.body: Previously a malformed `Cookie` header caused `clear_all_cookies()` to run, so the client was instructed to drop the bad cookies. With the parsing moved to `HTTPRequest`, the failure is now swallowed silently and the client keeps re-sending the unparsable header on every request. If the clearing behaviour was intentional, it needs to be re-established at the handler level; if not, it should be noted as a deliberate behaviour change.

findings.title: Missing .strip() makes boundary lookup fail for standard headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with their leading whitespace intact. For the overwhelmingly common header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ`, the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"`, so `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`. The loop completes without `break`, the `for ... else` fires, and the body is discarded with `logging.warning("Invalid multipart/form-data")` — all multipart form posts from real browsers/clients silently lose their arguments and files. The previous code (`if 'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression introduced by this change. Fix by partitioning the stripped token: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: per-field whitespace not stripped
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz`), so `field` is `" boundary=----..."` and `k` becomes `" boundary"`. The `k == "boundary"` comparison then fails for well-formed requests, the `for` loop completes without `break`, and the `else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" while the body is dropped and `self._request.arguments` stays empty. Fix by partitioning the stripped field, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

Two related robustness gaps in the same loop, worth handling while you are here: the parameter name comparison is case-sensitive though Content-Type parameter names are case-insensitive per RFC 2045, and a quoted value (`boundary="abc"`) is passed to `_parse_mime_body` with the quotes intact, so consider `v.strip('"')`.

Security note, stated plainly: I could not establish an adversary who gains anything here. The entry point is the attacker-controlled `Content-Type` request header; the sink is `_parse_mime_body`, which uses the value only as a literal delimiter for splitting the body, not as input to any interpreter, and the failure mode is fail-closed (multipart data is discarded, not mis-attributed). The only residual risk is an application that treats "no arguments parsed" as "nothing was uploaded" and therefore skips validation it would otherwise run — that depends on code not in this diff.

findings.title: No test covers new multipart boundary-scanning logic
findings.body: The change alters how the boundary parameter is extracted from a multipart Content-Type header, moving from a naive split to scanning all ';'-separated fields via partition. No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type header where 'boundary' is not the last parameter (the exact scenario this PR claims to fix), nor one with surrounding whitespace (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz') which the partition-based split would not strip. Without such a test, a regression in field parsing (e.g. reordering, whitespace handling, or accidental removal of the `break`) would not be caught by the existing suite.

findings.title: No tests accompany newly added parsing/header logic
findings.body: make_headers and get_host contain non-trivial branching logic (encoding normalization, URL parsing with scheme/port/auth splitting and error raising) but no test file is included in this diff. A regression in port parsing, scheme defaulting, or header construction would not be caught by anything shown here.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing diverges from urlsplit (host-confusion / SSRF bypass)
findings.body:
`get_host` strips the path only on `/` (line 92-93) and then treats everything before the last `@` as userinfo (line 94-95). Per RFC 3986 the authority also ends at `?` or `#`, so the two parsers disagree:

    get_host('http://trusted.example?x=@evil.example/')  ->  ('http', 'evil.example', None)
    urlsplit('http://trusted.example?x=@evil.example/').hostname  ->  'trusted.example'

The same holds for `#`. Any application that validates a user-supplied URL against a host allowlist with `urlparse`/`urlsplit` and then hands the *original string* to urllib3 will connect to a host the allowlist never approved — the standard SSRF-filter-bypass shape.

Separately, the returned host is never checked for control characters: `get_host('http://evil.example\r\nX-Injected: 1/')` returns a host containing CRLF, which flows into the connection's `Host` header on Python versions without header sanitisation.

Suggested fix: delegate authority parsing to `urlsplit` (or at minimum split the authority on the first occurrence of any of `/?#`, and reject hosts containing characters outside the RFC 3986 `reg-name` set) before returning.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: The exception is raised with the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — the `%s` is never interpolated, so callers and logs see a placeholder instead of the offending URL. This is the only diagnostic a caller gets for an unparseable authority. Change it to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (note that `url` has already been split down to the host portion at this point, so consider capturing the original argument first if the full URL is wanted).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns a list / None, not the documented boolean
findings.body: The docstring promises "Returns True if the connection is dropped". Three different return shapes actually occur: the no-poll branch (line 117) returns the readable-socket *list* from `select`, the poll branch returns `True` (line 125), and when `p.poll(0.0)` yields nothing — or yields only fds that do not match `conn.sock.fileno()` — the function falls off the end and returns `None`. Callers that use the result truthily are fine, but anything doing `is is_connection_dropped(c) is False` or serialising/logging the result gets a surprise. Wrap the select branch in `bool(...)` and add an explicit `return False` after the loop.

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode string is silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The type dispatch tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. Under Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. from a config file or a `from __future__ import unicode_literals` module) matches neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls into the `else` branch and the caller's explicitly requested encoding is silently discarded and replaced with `'gzip,deflate'`. Since `six` is already imported on line 16, use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)`.

findings.title: No test exercises sort="status"
findings.body: SORTABLE defines three columns (created_at, amount, status) but only created_at (default) and amount are covered by tests/test_invoices.py. If the status column mapping were wrong (e.g. mismatched column name or missing DB column), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Removed casts assume a two-member discriminated union that isn't shown
findings.body:
Both casts are removed on the assumption that `kind === "click"` narrows `Event` to the click variant and that the fall-through is necessarily the key variant. That only type-checks if (a) `kind` is declared with literal types (`kind: "click"` / `kind: "key"`, not `kind: string`) and (b) the union has exactly two members — a third variant would make the fall-through on line 9 a union that has no `code` property, and `event.code` would not compile.

The fact that the original author wrote `event as { x: number; y: number }` — a cast to a shape that doesn't even carry `kind` — is a strong signal that plain narrowing did not work here. Please confirm the declaration at the top of the file is a literal-discriminated two-member union, and if there are more variants, replace the bare fall-through with an explicit `if (event.kind === "key")` plus an exhaustiveness check rather than casts.

findings.title: Location attribute type now contradicts documentation
findings.body: The `HTTPMove.location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object on line 8 rather than a string. The documentation explicitly states it should be 'the string it was constructed with'. This breaks the documented contract that application code relies on when comparing it against configured strings and passing it to `str.startswith`. Callers expecting a string will now receive a URL object and may fail.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument (a string when callers pass one); now it is assigned `URL(location)`. The documented contract states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so existing callers doing `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` will raise `AttributeError`, and `exc.location == "/foo"` will now be `False` for every configured string. Additionally `URL(...)` normalises/quotes the input, so even `str(exc.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip the original value.

If the intent is only to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the constructed value and use a local variable for the header:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `.location` becomes a URL, breaking string-based redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: No test guards HTTPMove.location's documented string type
findings.body: The change makes `self.location` a `URL` instance instead of the plain string it was constructed with, which contradicts docs stating callers rely on `str.startswith` and string comparisons against `location`. No test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched) asserts `type(exc.location) is str` or exercises `location.startswith(...)`; such a test would have caught this regression immediately.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after loop is downgraded to `if`
findings.body:
`_wait` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer; its docstring explicitly instructs callers to re-check their condition after waking. Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes that re-check: after a spurious wake the code falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF, returning `b''`. Callers of `readany()` universally treat `b''` as end-of-stream, so a consumer will silently truncate the body mid-message. Restore the `while` loop (re-checking `not self._buffer and not self._eof` after each wake).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany can return b'' early, letting a peer truncate a body

findings.title: No test guards the while->if change in readany wait loop
findings.body: The change replaces a `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` loop with a single `if` check before `await self._wait('readany')`. The docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns that the waiter can resolve with no new data in the buffer, meaning a single wait is not guaranteed to leave the buffer non-empty or eof set afterward. If this assumption is wrong (e.g., a spurious wake with still-empty buffer and not eof), `_read_nowait(-1)` would return empty bytes prematurely, but no test in the diff exercises this scenario — nothing would fail if the change were wrong.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module loading on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so on any Python 3 interpreter this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` and `import requests` fails entirely. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: it silently resolves to a top-level `adapters` module if one exists on `sys.path`, importing the wrong `HTTPAdapter`. The neighbouring import on line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`) uses the explicit relative form, confirming the package-relative intent. Restore the leading dot: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Implicit import lets a top-level `adapters` module shadow the package one
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolved unambiguously to `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead (and under Python 3, where implicit relative imports were removed, it resolves *only* through `sys.path`).

Adversary: any principal who can place a file named `adapters.py` in a directory that appears on `sys.path` ahead of the intended one — most commonly the current working directory or the invoking script's directory, but also a world-writable entry in a shared deployment. They control the entire contents of that file. What they get: arbitrary code execution at import time inside any process that imports `requests.sessions`, plus full control over the `HTTPAdapter` used for every outbound request (certificate verification, proxying, request/response interception, credential capture).

This is an unnecessary loss of a guarantee the original line provided for free. Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`), or use the fully-qualified absolute form (`from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`) if the intent was to drop relative imports.

findings.title: Import change is untested; no test would catch breakage under Python 3
findings.body: Changing `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` relies on implicit relative imports, which only work in Python 2. If this module is ever imported under Python 3 (or with absolute_import semantics), this line will raise ImportError. There is no test in this diff, and if there is no existing test that imports `requests.sessions` and exercises `HTTPAdapter` usage, this regression would go undetected until a user hits the ImportError at runtime.

findings.title: Removed None guard: get_cookie raises TypeError on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which returns `None` if `self._cookies is None` and states "every consumer has to allow for that"). The premise in the PR description — that `cookies` is always a mapping after construction — does not hold.

With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed Cookie header. That turns a client-controlled malformed header into a 500 on every handler that calls `get_cookie` (including secure-cookie/XSRF paths that build on it), where previously it correctly returned `default`.

Restore the guard, or alternatively change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping and audit every consumer that currently branches on `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError

findings.title: Code contradicts documented API: cookies can be None
findings.body: The change removes the `is not None` guard from `get_cookie`, but `request.cookies` is explicitly documented in the repository as potentially `None`: 'Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that.' This means calling `get_cookie` when cookies cannot be parsed will now raise a `TypeError` (attempting `in` on None) instead of returning the default value, violating the contract implied by the docstring 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default.' Either restore the guard or update the cookies property documentation to guarantee it is never None.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The retrieved httpserver.py docstring states cookies is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. The diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard, so `name in self.request.cookies` would raise TypeError in that case. There is no test in this PR (or apparently in the existing suite, since this diff was accepted) that sends a malformed Cookie header and calls get_cookie, so this regression would go undetected until it hits production.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for normal Content-Type headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the OWS that RFC 7231 permits around parameters, so for the ubiquitous header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"`. Previously `field.strip()` removed that leading space before `partition("=")`; now `k` is `" boundary"`, the test `k == "boundary"` on line 5 is false, `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached, and the multipart body is silently discarded — form fields and file uploads vanish with no error. Only senders that omit the space after `;` would still work.

If the intent was merely to stop stripping the value, keep the key normalisation, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (unchanged), or at minimum `k, sep, v = field.partition("="); k = k.strip()`.

findings.title: Unstripped Content-Type parameter creates multipart parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the request's `Content-Type` header, i.e. it is entirely attacker-controlled. After `split(";")`, every parameter except the first retains its leading whitespace, and the last retains any trailing whitespace. Two consequences follow from dropping `.strip()`:

1. For the ordinary, RFC-conformant form `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`, `k` is now `" boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`. The loop falls through, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the body is silently discarded — handlers see no arguments and no error. A client can toggle this at will by adding or removing one space.
2. When the parameter is written without the space (`...;boundary=abc `), `v` now includes trailing whitespace/CR, so Tornado delimits parts on `abc ` while an upstream proxy, WAF or upload scanner that normalises per RFC 2045 delimits on `abc`. The two see different part boundaries, which is the standard shape of a multipart smuggling / filter-bypass bug: content the scanner reads as one inert part, Tornado reads as a different set of fields (or vice versa).

Restore the normalisation: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and ideally strip `v` and remove surrounding quotes as well before using it as the boundary.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace after semicolon
findings.body: The change drops field.strip() before partition, so a Content-Type like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=abc' (with a space after the semicolon, which is the common real-world format) would now produce k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary check `k == "boundary"` to fail and multipart parsing to silently skip. No test in this diff exercises this whitespace case, so a regression here would not be caught.

findings.title: Error message contains unsubstituted format placeholder
findings.body: The LocationParseError is raised with the message 'Failed to parse: %s', but no argument is provided to substitute the placeholder. This results in the literal string 'Failed to parse: %s' being shown to users instead of 'Failed to parse: <url>', making the error message unhelpful. The commit message indicates the intent was to shorten the message by removing the URL detail, but the implementation accidentally removed only the format argument while leaving the placeholder itself. Either remove the placeholder from the string or provide the url argument.

findings.title: No test verifies LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The diff changes `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`, dropping the `% url` interpolation entirely. This means the exception message will now literally contain the string '%s' instead of the invalid URL. If there is no test asserting on the exception message text (e.g. `str(exc)` or `exc.args[0]`) for this parse-failure path, this regression would go undetected — a test that only checks that `LocationParseError` is raised (without checking the message) would still pass despite the message being broken.

findings.title: Dangling %s placeholder left in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The interpolation argument `% url` was dropped but the `%s` conversion specifier was left in the literal, so the exception message is the uninterpreted string `Failed to parse: %s`. That is neither the shortened message the change intends nor the original diagnostic — callers logging `str(exc)` will surface a raw format placeholder and lose the offending URL entirely. Either drop the placeholder (`"Failed to parse URL"`) or keep the interpolation (`"Failed to parse: %s" % url`).

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
