`contentLength` is the declared length of an S3 UploadPart request body — it arrives from the `Content-Length` header of a request handled by `cmd/serve/s3` and is not the number of bytes actually received. Passing it straight to `Reserve()` makes the server commit memory up front, before `io.Copy` on line 8 reads a single byte. A client that sends `Content-Length: 5000000000` with an empty or one-byte body causes a multi-gigabyte allocation per in-flight request; a handful of concurrent requests OOM-kills the process, and the attacker pays nothing for it.

The previous code grew the pooled RW page-by-page as bytes actually arrived, so allocation was bounded by real traffic. That property is what this change removes.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to a sane bound before using it, e.g. `reserve := contentLength; if reserve < 0 || reserve > maxPartSize { reserve = 0 /* or maxPartSize */ }`, where `maxPartSize` is the configured/S3 part ceiling — and additionally reject the part if the copied byte count `n` does not match `contentLength`. Reserving is only safe once the value is validated against a limit rather than trusted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Reserve called with possibly negative/unknown contentLength

findings.title: No test coverage for new Reserve(contentLength) behaviour
findings.body: The change adds `.Reserve(contentLength)` to pre-allocate the multipart buffer based on a caller-supplied Content-Length. This is exactly the kind of change (CVE-related, per the branch name) where contentLength could be attacker-controlled, negative, zero, or mismatched with actual body size. There is no test in this diff exercising Reserve with edge-case values (e.g. contentLength=0, negative, or larger than actual body) to confirm the buffer behaves correctly and that io.Copy still produces the correct byte count/hash regardless of the pre-reservation size. If Reserve's behavior is wrong for any of these cases, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected HTTP when a caller explicitly set `is_secure=False`; a missing key (`.get` returns `None`) fell through to HTTPS. The new expression tests truthiness, so a missing `is_secure` key — the common case for any request that does not set the meta flag — now yields `"http"`, and the URL built on line 6 sends the AWS-signed request over plaintext. Any caller relying on the secure-by-default behaviour is silently downgraded, exposing the signed request (and response body) in transit.

Restore the explicit-false check, or invert the default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

Secondary note: the truthiness test also treats falsy-but-not-False values (`0`, `""`) as insecure, which the previous identity comparison did not.

findings.title: S3 requests now default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP when a caller *explicitly* set `request.meta["is_secure"] = False`; every other case (key absent, `None`, any truthy value) got HTTPS. The replacement `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the common case — the key not being present at all, which `.get()` returns `None` for — as "not secure" and builds an `http://` URL on line 6.

Consequence: unless every caller remembers to set `is_secure`, all S3 downloads are performed over unencrypted HTTP. The S3 download handler signs requests with AWS credentials (an `Authorization` / signature header derived from the access key), so the signed request and the returned object body travel in cleartext.

Adversary: anyone in a position to observe or modify traffic between the crawler and `s3.amazonaws.com` — shared/hostile Wi‑Fi, a compromised upstream router, an on-path ISP or cloud middlebox, or an attacker who can poison DNS/ARP. They control nothing about the request and still get: the AWS signature and request metadata (replayable within the signature's validity window for the exact signed request), the full contents of any private S3 object fetched, and the ability to tamper with the response body that is then parsed by the spider.

Fix: restore fail-closed behaviour, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make the default explicit: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) is False else "https"`. The security-relevant property is that the *absence* of the key must mean HTTPS, not HTTP.

findings.title: S3 scheme default changed from HTTPS to HTTP without doc update
findings.body: The logic change inverts the default S3 connection scheme: the old code defaulted to HTTPS (secure), while the new code defaults to HTTP (plaintext). This is a breaking behavioral change that contradicts standard security practices and any documentation that assumes S3 connections are encrypted by default. Either the change is incorrect, or documentation/docstrings describing this function's behavior must be updated to reflect that S3 connections now default to plaintext HTTP when `is_secure` is not set.

findings.title: No test guards the new default-scheme behavior
findings.body: The old code defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new code defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy (including when the key is absent). This is a meaningful behavior change (default scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset), but no test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this line were wrong or reverted incorrectly.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete privilege
findings.body:
The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action. The new two-branch form only distinguishes GET/HEAD from everything else, so a DELETE request produces `action = "push"` and the `ResourceAction` handed to the authorizer on line 9 asks for push permission on a destructive operation.

Entry point: `request.Method` (and `vars["name"]`, the target repository) on an authenticated registry request. Sink: the `ResourceAction` at line 9 that the access-control layer evaluates. An account provisioned with push-only access on a repository — exactly the case `pkg/api/config/config.go` documents as intentional ("an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones") — can now issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and have it authorized, destroying tags it was never granted rights over. Accounts holding `delete` but not `push` are simultaneously locked out.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch. If the goal was to simplify, keep three arms rather than two; the action set is three-valued by design, not two-valued.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now requires "push", so the "delete" action is never checked

findings.title: No test covers DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the distinct ActionDelete mapping for http.MethodDelete, folding it into 'push'. This is a authorization-relevant behavior change (per the repo's own docs, delete and push are intentionally distinct permissions), but no test in this diff exercises a DELETE request and asserts the resulting action. If this mapping is wrong, no test would fail.

findings.title: Size-cap eviction wipes the whole cache, discarding the just-fetched value
findings.body:
When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` removes every entry, including `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` written two lines earlier. The function still returns `tenant` to its own caller, but the write it was asked to perform is silently undone: an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None`. It also drops every other tenant, so one call past the threshold forces a full re-fetch storm for all callers rather than evicting a single entry. Use a bounded structure (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/an LRU dict) so the freshly fetched entry survives and only the oldest entry is evicted.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Full cache flush on overflow lets one caller evict all tenants

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage
findings.body: The new function performs three distinct behaviors: fetching fresh data via _fetch, writing it into the shared _CACHE, and clearing the cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of these are exercised by any test in this diff. If the cache-write were skipped, the eviction threshold were off-by-one, or _fetch's result were not returned correctly, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` misleads about cache mutation
findings.body: The function name suggests a straightforward read operation ("get") that returns fresh data. A caller using only the function name and signature would not expect this function to mutate the shared `_CACHE` dictionary, nor to clear it when it exceeds 1000 entries. The `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` assignment on line 10 and the `_CACHE.clear()` call on line 12 are side effects that should be visible in the name or documented in a docstring, since the function's contract cannot be inferred from its public interface alone.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag with old name
findings.body: The README on line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the code on line 6 of cli.py has renamed it to `--concurrency`. A user reading the README will try to use `--workers` and the flag will not be recognized. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Renaming --workers breaks existing callers with no alias
findings.body:
`--workers` is removed outright and replaced by `--concurrency`. Two classes of caller break:

1. Any existing invocation (scripts, CI jobs, systemd units, docs-following users) passing `--workers 8` will now fail with `unrecognized arguments`.
2. Any code downstream of `parser()` that reads `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError`, because argparse now populates `args.concurrency` instead.

If the rename is intended, keep backwards compatibility for at least one release, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4)` so the old spelling keeps working while the attribute becomes `concurrency`, and grep the repo for `args.workers` / `.workers` to update the consumers. The README on line 7 still advertises `--workers`, which is direct evidence that at least one documented consumer contract was not updated with the rename.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary with days as keys and counts as values. Any caller relying on the docstring will expect an integer and will receive a dict, causing their code to break. Update the docstring to reflect the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without updating callers/docstring
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer; it now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic (`monthly_usage(a) + 1`), comparison (`> limit`), or formatting will now either raise `TypeError` or silently produce wrong output (e.g. `bool({})` vs `bool(0)` still agree, but `sum` / `>` do not). The docstring on line 2 still states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so the breakage is not even visible to someone reading the signature. Either keep the total and add a separate `monthly_usage_by_day` function, or update every caller and the docstring in this PR. No callers were retrieved for this review, so the blast radius should be confirmed before merge.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict of day->count instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. Any caller relying on the old integer-return contract (and the docstring itself, which still says 'total number of API calls' as an integer) would silently break with no test catching the change in return type or the grouping logic.

findings.title: Docstring documents renamed parameter incorrectly
findings.body:
The function parameter on line 1 has been renamed from `page_size` to `limit`, but the docstring on lines 6 still documents it as `page_size`. A caller reading the docstring will look for a `page_size` parameter that no longer exists, and may assume `limit` is something else entirely.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `page_size` is a public positional-or-keyword parameter of `list_invoices`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime, with no deprecation path. If this rename is intended, either search and update all call sites in the same change, or keep a compatibility shim (e.g. accept `page_size=None` and map it to `limit` with a deprecation warning). No callers were retrieved here, so this needs a human to confirm the blast radius.

findings.title: PR description does not match the change
findings.body: The PR says it renames the pagination parameter "from page to offset", but the code renames `page_size` to `limit`. Either the description is stale or the wrong rename was applied; worth confirming which before merge, since `limit` and `offset` mean different things to a pagination API.

findings.title: Non-relative import of adapters will break `import requests`
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on `sys.path`. Every other import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). On Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` at import time, making the whole package unimportable. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped — TLS validation no longer enforced per request
findings.body:
The new `request()` still declares `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but neither value is ever stored on `req`, merged with session config, or forwarded through `self.send(prep)` / `adapter.send(request)`. The old path (now `old_request`) carried these through to the send call. As written, whatever the caller (or session config) asks for regarding certificate verification and client certificates is discarded, and the actual TLS behaviour is decided by whatever `HTTPAdapter.send()` defaults to.

Adversary: anyone in a position to intercept the connection (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream proxy, DNS/BGP tamperer). They control the network path and the presented certificate; if the adapter's default is not to verify, they get full read/write access to the plaintext of every request made through this Session, including `auth` credentials and cookies. Even if the adapter defaults to verifying, callers pinning a CA bundle or supplying a client cert via `cert=` silently lose that control.

Fix: thread `verify` and `cert` (merged with session defaults) onto the prepared request or through `send()` into the adapter before this path is used, or raise if they are supplied while unsupported.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call through `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline `r.send(prefetch=...)` / `return r.response` at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts timeout/verify/cert/prefetch/config and silently ignores them
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only copies `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor. That is worse than removing them: callers passing `timeout=5` or `verify=False` get silently unbounded/unverified requests rather than a `TypeError`. It also no longer merges the session-level defaults (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.proxies`) that `old_request` merged, so configured Sessions stop applying their configuration. At minimum thread these through to `prepare()`/`send()`, or raise `NotImplementedError` for the ones not yet wired up.

findings.title: `send()` builds a fresh HTTPAdapter per request, defeating pooling
findings.body: A new `HTTPAdapter()` is instantiated on every `send()` call, so every request gets a brand-new connection pool: no connection reuse across requests in a Session (the entire point of Session), and the per-call pools are never closed, so their sockets are only reclaimed when GC runs. The adapter should be created once in `__init__` (and closed from `close()`), not per call. This also means the `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize` config values that `init_poolmanager` used to honour are now unreachable.

findings.title: `poolmanager`/`init_poolmanager` removed while consumers may still use them
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and the `self.poolmanager` attribute are gone, and `close()` is now a no-op. Anything that reaches for `session.poolmanager` (the legacy `Request.send` path that `old_request` still funnels into, plus user subclasses that override `init_poolmanager` — a documented extension point) will now fail with `AttributeError`, and `close()`/`__exit__` no longer release pooled connections, so sockets leak for the lifetime of the process. If the adapter now owns the pool, `close()` should delegate to it rather than being `pass`.

findings.title: No test covers the new send()/HTTPAdapter delegation or close() no-op
findings.body: Session.close() was changed from closing the poolmanager to `pass` (line 132), and Session.send() now constructs a brand-new HTTPAdapter per call instead of reusing a pooled connection manager (lines 365-367). Both are significant behavioral changes to connection lifecycle and resource management, and no test in this diff exercises either path. If close() silently stops releasing connections, or if creating a new HTTPAdapter per send() request defeats connection pooling entirely, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Stale documentation removed but docstring claims persist
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring explaining it disposes of internal state by closing the PoolManager and pooled connections. This implementation has been removed (the method now just passes), but if a similar docstring existed elsewhere or in version control history, callers might still believe close() performs cleanup. The removal is correct, but ensure no documentation elsewhere still describes the old behavior.

findings.title: `import adapters` is a top-level import hijackable via sys.path
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a generically-named top-level module rather than the package-relative `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves against `sys.path`, whose first entry is the script's directory or the CWD. Any `adapters.py` sitting there — dropped by a local user, unpacked from an archive, or left in a shared working directory — is imported and executed in-process the moment `requests.sessions` is loaded.

Adversary: any local user or process that can write a file into the directory an application is launched from. What they control: the contents of `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code execution inside every process that imports `requests`, plus control over `HTTPAdapter.send()`, i.e. all outbound traffic.

Use the relative import `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to bind it to the package.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
The old implementation kept `self._cookies` as a `SimpleCookie` and called `clear_all_cookies()` when parsing raised; the property always returned a mapping. The new version assigns `self._cookies = None` in the `except` block, so `HTTPRequest.cookies` can return `None` for any request with a malformed `Cookie` header — a value an attacker or a buggy client controls. Every caller then fails: `get_cookie` (`name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`), `clear_all_cookies` (`None.iterkeys()` → AttributeError), and `get_secure_cookie` via `get_cookie`. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the handler instead of `None` so the return shape is invariant.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes cookies None, crashing every consumer

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies property removed without a shim
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; application subclasses and templates that call `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` will now raise AttributeError. If the intent is only to expose the data on the request, keep a thin delegating property on `RequestHandler` (`return self.request.cookies`) for backwards compatibility rather than deleting it outright.

findings.title: No test covers cookies property or its changed error-fallback behavior
findings.body: The `cookies` property was moved from `RequestHandler` to `HTTPRequest`, and its exception-handling fallback changed from calling `self.clear_all_cookies()` (web.py, old behavior) to `self._cookies = None` (httpserver.py, new behavior). If a malformed 'Cookie' header is sent, `self.request.cookies` will now be `None`, and downstream callers such as `get_cookie` (`name in self.request.cookies`) and `clear_all_cookies` (`self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`) will raise a TypeError instead of behaving as before. No test in this diff exercises a malformed Cookie header, valid cookie parsing, `get_cookie`, or `clear_all_cookies` against the new `HTTPRequest.cookies` property, so this behavioral change (and any future regression in it) would not be caught.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring: cookies property can return None
findings.body: The docstring states 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects' but the implementation can return `None` when a Cookie header parse fails (line 523). A caller reading only the docstring would expect a dict-like object, not a nullable value. This is a breaking change from the RequestHandler.cookies property, which called `clear_all_cookies()` instead of returning None on error. The docstring should document the None case and the conditions under which it occurs.

findings.title: Docstring stale: clear_all_cookies no longer describes its behavior
findings.body: The `clear_all_cookies` docstring says 'Deletes all the cookies the user sent with this request' but the implementation now calls `.iterkeys()` on `self.request.cookies`, which may be `None` (from the HTTPRequest.cookies property). The docstring does not reflect this behavioral change or the new failure mode. If parse errors occur, this method will crash with AttributeError rather than silently handling it.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: missing strip() on split fields
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with their leading OWS intact. For the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"`, so `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`. The loop then completes without `break`, the `for ... else` fires, and every multipart request is rejected with "Invalid multipart/form-data" while `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The previous code used `'boundary=' in content_type` and was immune to the space, so this is a regression that disables all file/multipart form uploads.

Fix by normalising each field before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider `v.strip('"')` since RFC 2045 allows a quoted boundary value).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Content-Type parameters not stripped; boundary never matches

findings.title: No test covers boundary-not-last-field parsing behavior
findings.body: The change fixes a real bug (assuming 'boundary=' is the last parameter in Content-Type), but no test is added to verify parsing when boundary appears before other parameters (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'). Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the original bug and nothing would catch it.

findings.title: get_host() ignores '?' and '#', allowing host-parsing confusion
findings.body:
`get_host()` only terminates the authority on `/`, then strips everything before the last-seen `@`. It never treats `?` or `#` as authority terminators, so it disagrees with RFC 3986 / `urllib.parse`.

Example: for `http://legit.com#@attacker.com/x` the stdlib returns netloc `legit.com` (the rest is a fragment), but this function computes `url = 'legit.com#@attacker.com'` at line 93, then splits on `@` at line 95 and returns host `attacker.com`. The same holds for `http://legit.com?@attacker.com/`.

Adversary: anyone who can supply or influence a URL that an application feeds to urllib3 — a user-submitted fetch target, or a redirect `Location:` header from an upstream server. What they control: the URL string. What they get: the connection is opened to a host of their choosing even though the calling application's allowlist check (typically done with `urlparse().netloc`) saw a permitted host — i.e. SSRF past a host allowlist, and requests/credentials sent to the wrong origin.

Fix: split off the fragment and query before parsing the authority (e.g. cut at the first of `/`, `?`, `#`), or delegate to `urllib.parse.urlsplit` and only special-case the scheme-less form.

Note: I do not have the callers (`connectionpool.py`, `poolmanager.py`) in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm here that `get_host` is the function used for redirect targets — hence the reduced confidence.

findings.title: New header/URL parsing helpers have no accompanying tests in this diff
findings.body: make_headers() and get_host() contain non-trivial branching logic (accept_encoding type dispatch, basic auth encoding, URL scheme/host/port/path/auth splitting including error raising on a malformed port). This diff adds these functions with no test file, so a regression in any branch (e.g. get_host mishandling an '@' in a path, or a non-digit port silently passing) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: The raised message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — there is no `% url` (or `% (url,)`) interpolation, so every parse failure reports the placeholder instead of the offending URL. Since `url` has already been reassigned by the splits above, you probably want to capture the original argument at the top of the function and format with that, e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % original_url)`.

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode value is silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: On Python 2 a `unicode` argument is not an instance of `str`, so `make_headers(accept_encoding=u'identity')` falls through to the `else` branch and the caller's value is silently replaced with `'gzip,deflate'` — a wrong header rather than an error. The module already imports `six` (line 16) for `six.b`; use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` so both byte and text strings are passed through unchanged.

findings.title: No test exercises describe() for both event kinds
findings.body: The diff changes describe() to rely on type narrowing instead of casts. If the narrowing were subtly wrong (e.g. Event union redefined without discriminant, or a typo in the branch), nothing in this PR would catch it. No test file is included and no repository context shows existing tests for this function.

findings.title: `self.location` type changed from str to URL, breaking documented contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument (a string when callers pass one), and only the header was normalised via `str(URL(location))`. The new code assigns `self.location = URL(location)`, so the public attribute is now a `yarl.URL`. The documented behaviour is that `.location` is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code calls `str.startswith` on it and compares it to configured strings. `URL` has no `startswith`, so such callers raise `AttributeError`, and `url == "/foo"` comparisons against plain strings become `False`. Additionally `URL(location)` normalises the value (encoding, path handling), so even `str(self.location)` may not equal the original argument.

Keep the original value on the attribute and use a local for the header, e.g. `self.location = location; self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type changed from str to URL, breaking documented contract

findings.title: Location attribute now stores URL object, not string
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object instead of the original string. The documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states that `.location` is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that "Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`". Code relying on this documented contract—treating `.location` as a string for comparisons or method calls—will now break.

findings.title: No test guards the type of self.location after this change
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object instead of the original string. Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `location` being 'the string it was constructed with' and calls things like str.startswith on it. Nothing in this diff (or apparently the existing suite) asserts on the type or string-compatibility of HTTPMove.location, so this behavior change (str -> URL) could break downstream consumers silently while all existing tests keep passing.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after single wait
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve at the end of a chunk even when no new data landed in the buffer, and its docstring instructs callers to re-check their condition after waking. Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake with an empty buffer and `self._eof` still false, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns empty bytes. For a stream reader, empty bytes is the end-of-stream sentinel, so consumers looping `while True: chunk = await readany(); if not chunk: break` will truncate the body silently mid-response. Restore the loop (`while not self._buffer and not self._eof`) so the wait is retried until data is buffered or EOF is observed.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single-wait readany() can return empty bytes, read as premature EOF

findings.title: No test covers the loop→if change for spurious wakeups
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can resolve at the end of a chunk with no new data, requiring callers to re-check their condition. Changing `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to a single `if` removes the retry loop, so a spurious wakeup with an empty buffer and no eof will now return from readany() with an empty/incorrect result instead of waiting again. There's no test in this change (or evident in the referenced context) that simulates a feed_data()-triggered wakeup with an empty buffer to verify readany() still waits correctly; such a test would fail under the old assumption but nothing here would catch a regression.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `requests.sessions` on Python 3
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` and `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` are not the same module reference. The dotted form resolves `requests.adapters` explicitly; the dotless form is an implicit relative import, which was removed in Python 3 (PEP 328). Under Python 3 — or under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import` — importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'`, taking down `import requests` entirely since `sessions` is on the main import path. On Python 2 it still works only by accident, and will silently bind to an unrelated top-level `adapters` module if one happens to be on `sys.path`, yielding a wrong `HTTPAdapter`.

Restore the leading dot: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` does not: under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) it is an absolute import resolved by walking `sys.path` in order. `sys.path[0]` is the invoking script's directory — and the empty-string CWD entry for `-c`/REPL/some embedding contexts — so any `adapters.py` sitting there is imported instead of the packaged one.

Adversary: any local principal who can write a file into the directory an application is launched from, or into any earlier `sys.path` entry (a shared deploy dir, a world-writable job working directory, an unpacked archive the app `chdir`s into). What they control: a file named `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code executed at import time inside the process that imports `requests`, plus the ability to return a malicious `HTTPAdapter` that sees every request/response, credential and TLS decision the session makes.

Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or the fully-qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`). The relative form is not merely stylistic here — it is what pins the import to this package.

findings.title: No test would catch a broken import from this change
findings.body: Changing `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` alters import resolution from package-relative to top-level absolute, which can fail at import time depending on Python version and how the package is invoked (e.g. Python 3 requires explicit relative imports; this would raise ImportError). No test in the diff exercises importing `requests.sessions` or instantiating a `Session`, so if this change breaks module loading, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when Cookie header is unparseable
findings.body: The PR description claims `cookies` is always a mapping after construction, but `HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and it explicitly short-circuits `if self._cookies is None: return None`. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed Cookie header \u2014 a fully attacker-controllable input that turns a returned default into a 500. Restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` guard, or change the property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` (and update every other consumer accordingly).

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash get_cookie
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote client. What they control: the raw `Cookie` request header (e.g. a deliberately malformed value). What they get: an unhandled exception in every handler that calls `get_cookie` — a 500 on each such request, and in Tornado this also affects `check_xsrf_cookie` and secure-cookie paths, so a trivially cheap request turns normal endpoints into error responses (and, with `debug=True`, into stack-trace pages).

Either restore the `self.request.cookies is not None` check here, or fix the invariant at the source by having `HTTPRequest.cookies` return an empty mapping instead of `None` on parse failure — but do not remove the guard while the property can still return `None`.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The removed guard `self.request.cookies is not None` suggests cookies can be None (per httpserver.py docstring: 'Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed'). The new code `name in self.request.cookies` will raise TypeError if cookies is None. No test in this diff exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading whitespace that virtually every client emits after the semicolon, e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` yields the field `" boundary=----abc"`. The old `field.strip().partition("=")` removed that space; with the strip gone, `k` is `" boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The multipart body is silently discarded — no exception, just missing form arguments and files on every normal upload.

The strip being removed is on the whole *field*, not on the parameter value, so it is not redundant. Restore it (or strip `k` before comparing, and keep stripping `v`, which may also carry trailing whitespace before a subsequent parameter).

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes boundary parsing whitespace-sensitive
findings.body:
`field.partition("=")` is now applied to the raw segment produced by `content_type.split(";")`. For the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----X` the second segment is `" boundary=----X"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails: `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the request body is silently discarded (no arguments, no files) instead of being parsed.

The security-relevant consequence is that an attacker who controls the `Content-Type` header now controls *which* parameter Tornado treats as the boundary purely via whitespace. With `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B`, an RFC-conformant parser in front of Tornado (reverse proxy, WAF, upload scanner) strips OWS and selects `A`, while this code skips `" boundary=A"` and selects `B`. The two components then split the same body into different parts, which is the classic setup for slipping a part past an inspecting intermediary. Trailing whitespace in the value is also no longer removed, so `boundary=X ` yields a delimiter that will not match the body.

Restore the strip (or strip `k` and `v` individually) so parameter names and values are compared after whitespace removal.

findings.title: No test guards the whitespace-stripping behavior change
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` before partitioning on '=', which changes behavior when a Content-Type header has spaces around fields, e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (leading space before 'boundary'). With strip() removed, `k` would be ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary check `k == "boundary"` to fail and multipart parsing to silently not trigger. No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type header with whitespace after the semicolon to confirm boundary parsing still works.

findings.title: No test verifies the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` interpolation, so the raised error will literally contain the string "%s" instead of the offending URL. There is no test file in this diff exercising this error path or asserting on the exception message, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or new test.

findings.title: Dangling %s placeholder in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The interpolation argument `% url` was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the format string. The exception message becomes the literal `"Failed to parse: %s"`, which both loses the offending URL and looks like a formatting bug to anyone reading the traceback. If the intent is to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or `LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should still be reported, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string into shell=True mis-parses and executes injected input
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by interpolating `name` and `directory` directly into a string that is then run with `shell=True`. Two concrete failures for reachable inputs:

- Correctness: a `directory` of `my docs` becomes `tar -czf /exports/x.tar.gz my docs`, which tars two nonexistent paths and raises `CalledProcessError` instead of archiving the directory. Any space, glob character, or quote in either argument silently changes the command.
- Security: a `name` or `directory` containing `;`, `&&`, backticks or `$(...)` runs arbitrary commands as the service user — e.g. `directory="/tmp; rm -rf /exports"`.

Both go away with an argument list and no shell:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

This matches `list_exports` on line 5, which already passes a list and no `shell=True`. If `name` is caller-supplied, also reject path separators so it cannot escape `/exports` via `../`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection: unescaped params into shell=True tar command

findings.title: create_archive has no test exercising its behavior
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression in argument handling, quoting, or unexpected shell interpretation of name/directory. Given the existing list_exports function uses an argument list (safer pattern) while create_archive switches to shell=True, a test verifying the constructed command or its safe behavior would catch both correctness and safety regressions.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in a file whose existing middleware (line 6) restricts origins to an `ALLOWED` list. This removes origin-based access control for any route it is mounted on.

Adversary: anyone who can get a logged-in user to load a page they control. What they control: the `Origin` header of a cross-site `fetch`/`XHR` with `credentials: "include"`. What they get: the browser attaches the victim's session cookie and, if the response carries a permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, the attacker's script can read the authenticated response body — a full cross-origin data read, and a CSRF read-and-act primitive.

One nuance worth stating honestly: with the standard `cors` npm package, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `*`, which browsers refuse to honour alongside credentials, so the immediate effect may be a *broken* dashboard rather than a live leak. That is exactly how this bug usually escalates — the next commit "fixes" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which is fully exploitable. Either way the intended control is off.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin, e.g. `origin: [DASHBOARD_ORIGIN]` (or add it to `ALLOWED`) and keep `credentials: true`. Never pair a wildcard or a reflected origin with credentials.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the Fetch/CORS spec requires user agents to fail a credentialed request whenever the allow-origin header is the literal `*`. The result is that the dashboard's cookie-bearing calls will be blocked by the browser, which is the exact scenario the PR description says it is enabling — the change cannot work as written.

Reflect the actual dashboard origin instead, e.g. add it to the existing `ALLOWED` list used by the middleware on line 6, or pass a function/array origin so the middleware echoes a concrete origin back. That also avoids opening the credentialed API to every site on the internet.

findings.title: New CORS config with wildcard+credentials has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers reject this combination) and is also a common security misconfiguration. There is no test verifying the actual behavior of this middleware (e.g. what Access-Control-Allow-Origin header value is produced, whether credentialed requests are actually accepted). If this configuration is wrong or behaves unexpectedly at runtime, nothing in the current diff would catch it.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal `acme_live_...` value and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is removed in the same hunk). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one.

Adversary: anyone with read access to the repository or its history — internal contributors beyond the payments team, CI log/artifact readers, forks, mirrors, or anyone who later obtains a clone or backup. They control nothing and still get a production payments credential, i.e. the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer/transaction data.

Remediation: revoke and rotate this key at AcmePay immediately (it must be treated as compromised the moment it lands in git history — removing the line in a follow-up commit is not sufficient), restore the `os.environ` lookup or a secrets-manager read, and purge the value from history if feasible. Consider adding a secret scanner to CI to prevent recurrence.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env-var configuration

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test asserting the api_key value
findings.body: The diff changes client() to hardcode ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY instead of reading os.environ. Only a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) was added, which defines fake_client() but is not itself a test and contains no assertions. There is no test in the diff that calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value, so this behavioral change (and any future regression, e.g. reverting to env-based config or misconfiguring the key) would not be caught by anything shown here.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module (callers presumably do `client().Charge.create(...)`), but `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`. Any test that substitutes this fixture for `client()` will fail on attribute access rather than exercising the code under test. If the fixture is meant to stand in for `client()`, return an object exposing the same surface (e.g. a `Mock` or a stub module); if it is only meant to expose the test key, that intent is worth making explicit.

findings.title: tenant_of() returns a tenant id from an unverified token
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload whose signature was never checked. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can mint an unsigned (or arbitrarily signed) token with any `tenant_id` and be treated as that tenant. Note also that skipping verification skips `exp`/`aud` checks, so expired and misaudienced tokens are accepted too.

The module already has the correct primitive one line above: `claims_for(token)` decodes against `public_key()` with `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement `tenant_of` on top of it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and let the caching of `public_key()` (not the dropping of verification) be what avoids the key-store round trip.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: New tenant_of() has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token with verify_signature=False and trusts the tenant_id claim. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would catch a regression such as accidentally verifying (or failing to extract) the claim, a KeyError on missing tenant_id, or a future change that silently alters trust behavior. Given this reads a security-sensitive claim without verification, at minimum a test asserting the returned tenant_id for a crafted unverified token, and behavior on a token missing the claim, should exist.

findings.title: Unguarded subscript raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` raises `KeyError` for any otherwise well-formed token that lacks the claim — which, with verification disabled, includes tokens an unauthenticated caller can craft. That surfaces as an unhandled 500 rather than a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then saves — with no `require_owner(user, pm)` call. The `user` returned on line 11 is fetched and then never used, which is the tell: authentication happened, authorisation did not.

Adversary: any signed-in user of the service. What they control: the `pm_id` path/route parameter and the `billing_name` field in the request body. What they get: the ability to enumerate or guess another account's payment-method ID and rewrite the billing name on that saved card — a cross-tenant write to payment data, plausibly a step in a social-engineering or chargeback-dispute path.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, matching the read handler on line 6. `api/auth.py` documents this explicitly: "Every object mutation must call this."

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method never calls require_owner on the fetched object

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked `body["billing_name"]` and unvalidated `PaymentMethod.get` result

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Update payment method lacks authorization check

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and entirely untested. Nothing would fail if it let a user update another user's payment method (it never calls require_owner, unlike get_payment_method above), and nothing would fail if billing_name were silently dropped or save() failed. Add a test that asserts a non-owner is rejected and one that asserts the update persists.

findings.title: Public function `update_payment_method` lacks a docstring
findings.body: This new public API endpoint has no docstring explaining what it does, what parameters it accepts, or what it returns. Callers cannot determine the function contract from the signature alone.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` no longer carries `@rate_limit("5/hour")`, so an unauthenticated caller can invoke it in a loop with any `email` value and drive `send_reset_email` without bound. Concretely this enables (a) mail-bombing an arbitrary victim's inbox with reset messages, (b) high-volume account enumeration if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, and (c) burning the sending domain's reputation / provider quota, which is a denial of service against every other transactional email the product sends.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider throttling is global and per-sender, not per-caller or per-target-address: it will not stop 10,000 requests aimed at one victim, and when it does trip it degrades delivery for all users rather than the abuser. If the goal is a looser policy, raise the limit (e.g. keyed on source IP *and* target email) rather than deleting the decorator.

If reset tokens are short or predictable, unlimited issuance also widens the window for token guessing; that depends on `send_reset_email`, which is not in this diff.

findings.title: Password reset loses its only per-caller throttle
findings.body:
`@rate_limit("5/hour")` was the only thing bounding how often `request_reset` could be driven for a single address. After this change the handler calls `send_reset_email(email)` on every request with no bound at all, so an unauthenticated caller can loop on one victim's address (mailbox flooding, reset-token grinding) or enumerate addresses at full request rate.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — is about a different limit: providers cap outbound volume per sending account, which protects the provider and your sending reputation, not a specific recipient and not the cost of the unbounded `send_reset_email` calls themselves. Those two limits are not substitutes.

If the decorator genuinely must go, replace it with an equivalent bound at the layer that now owns it (per-email cooldown before enqueueing the send, or a gateway-level limit on this route) and say so, rather than leaving the handler with none.

findings.title: No test guards password reset endpoint's (removed) rate limiting behavior
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, a security-relevant control. No test file is included in this change. If this removal is wrong (e.g. the email provider's throttling assumption is incorrect or absent), nothing in the visible change would fail — there is no test asserting rate-limiting behavior on this endpoint, before or after.

findings.title: Preview path bypasses _confined(), allowing traversal outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The download path on line 14 resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead calls `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the service process are then returned to the caller.

The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download" 

u2014 make that literal: `path = _confined(name)` here too, and keep the `open`/`read(limit)` body as-is.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal reads

findings.title: Public function read_export_preview lacks path confinement documentation
findings.body: The new function `read_export_preview` does not document its path handling behaviour. The preceding function `read_export` documents its safety through the name `_confined`, but `read_export_preview` calls `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly without any confinement call, creating a semantic contradiction: callers familiar with `read_export` would reasonably expect similar protection, but the code provides none. This undocumented difference in safety is a public contract defect.

findings.title: No test exercises read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike read_export (line 14) which calls _confined(name). No test in this diff exists for this new function, so a regression where 'name' contains '../' traversal would go undetected. Add a test that calls read_export_preview with a traversal-style name and asserts it is rejected or confined, mirroring whatever coverage _confined has for read_export.

findings.title: Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (cross-tenant IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; that loop and the `require_owner` import were deleted. The handler now loads `Report.get(rid)` for every caller-supplied id and serialises it with `to_dict()` without ever comparing `report.tenant_id` to `user.tenant_id`.

Adversary: any authenticated user (any tenant, including a self-service signup). What they control: the `report_ids` list in the request. What they get: full serialised contents of arbitrary reports belonging to other tenants, in bulk, by enumerating or guessing ids.

Authentication is not authorisation — `current_user(request)` only establishes who is calling, not what they may read. Restore the check, and prefer pushing it into the query (e.g. fetch reports filtered by `user.tenant_id`) so the fast path is also the safe path rather than an N-call loop. If the loop was the performance problem, a single tenant-scoped bulk fetch gives the speedup without dropping the control.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export returns other tenants' reports after ownership check removal

findings.title: No test guards the removed per-report ownership check
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report before returning data; that call is deleted in this diff with no accompanying test change. If a caller passes report_ids belonging to another tenant, the function will now silently return that data instead of raising Forbidden, and no test in this PR would fail to reveal that. This is exactly the kind of behavior change that needs a test asserting cross-tenant access is denied (or, if intentional per the stated rationale, a test documenting the new authenticated-only contract) — otherwise a future revert or refactor could reintroduce the check or break it further without anyone noticing.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params.

Besides the obvious injection exposure, this is broken for ordinary input: a customer name containing an apostrophe (`O'Brien`) terminates the quoted literal and the statement fails with a syntax error, and `None` for `status` renders the literal string `'None'` rather than a NULL comparison. Any `%` or `_` a user types is also silently treated as a LIKE wildcard.

Rewrite as a parameterised query, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers is a new public function with no accompanying test in this diff. It builds its SQL via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into the query text rather than using the `execute(sql, params)` parameterised pattern documented in billing/db.py and used by get_customer. A test exercising this function with a value like `' OR '1'='1` or a value containing a quote would fail today (or reveal the injection), but nothing here would catch it since no test exists.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS destination check
findings.body:
The existing delivery path in this module validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` before issuing a request (lines 8-9). `verify_endpoint` performs a request to a caller-supplied `url` with no such check, so the invariant "this module only talks to allowed hosts" no longer holds. Since the feature description says tenants register the URL, the input is attacker-controlled and this reaches internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, loopback admin ports, private RFC1918 ranges) that the guarded path deliberately refuses. Route the URL through the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used above before calling `requests.get`, and consider `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot redirect the request onward past the check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that makes an outbound GET request to an arbitrary URL, unlike the sibling function above which validates the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS first. There is no test file in this diff, and nothing shown exercises verify_endpoint's behavior (e.g. that it returns the status code, or that it should/shouldn't validate the host). If this function's logic changes or regresses, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Invoices bucket created with all public-access protections disabled
findings.body:
This hunk adds a second bucket, `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`), plus an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`. Since S3's account/bucket defaults now block public access, explicitly setting these to `false` actively removes protection: any public-read ACL or bucket policy applied later to `acme-customer-invoices` will take effect, and existing public ACLs will no longer be ignored.

The PR description says this change adds "the public assets bucket for the marketing site" — it says nothing about invoices. The invoices block is character-for-character the assets block with the name swapped (including the same unaligned `bucket =` line), which strongly suggests a copy-paste that carried the permissive settings onto data that must not be public.

If the invoices bucket is genuinely needed, drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` override entirely (or set all four flags to `true`) so customer invoices stay private, and split it into its own change so it gets reviewed on its own merits.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same kind of HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte. The function three lines above already does this correctly. Replace line 12 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match `verify_stripe`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new security-relevant function (webhook signature verification) added with no test in this diff. Nothing exercises it to confirm it correctly accepts valid signatures and rejects invalid ones, so a regression or logic error here (including the non-constant-time comparison) would go undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: 500 handler returns exception text and full traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response. Any client who can reach an endpoint that raises — including an unauthenticated one, since a malformed request is often enough — receives absolute filesystem paths, module and package layout, framework/library versions inferable from frame paths, and the exception message itself. Exception messages routinely carry sensitive fragments: DB driver errors echo the failing SQL and sometimes the DSN, `KeyError`/`ValueError` echo the attacker-supplied value alongside internal key names, and connection errors echo internal hostnames and ports. That is a free map of the internals for anyone probing the service, and it is exactly the reconnaissance step that turns a blind injection or SSRF attempt into a targeted one.

The operational goal is already met by the line above: `log.exception("request failed")` puts the full trace in the logs. Keep the client body opaque and give on-call a correlation handle instead, e.g. generate a UUID, log it with the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500`. If you genuinely need the trace in the body for local work, gate it on an explicit debug setting that is off by default in production rather than on unconditionally.

Separately, `traceback.format_exc()` reads the *current* exception being handled, not `exc`. If `handle()` is ever called outside an `except` block it returns the string `"NoneType: None"`, so this does not reliably do what the description claims either.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores the `exc` argument it is meant to describe

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and `error` value are no longer stable

findings.title: No test verifies the new error response contract
findings.body: The `handle` function's return value changed from a fixed error message to including `str(exc)` and a full traceback. There is no test file in this diff exercising `handle()` to confirm the response shape, status code, or content. If this change were reverted or altered (e.g., traceback field renamed, or exception message formatting broken), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` returns `hashlib.md5(raw.encode()).hexdigest()` — a single round of an unsalted, GPU-fast hash — for what the name and the module both indicate is a user password chosen during a reset flow. The adversary is anyone who obtains a copy of the credential table (SQL injection, a backup leak, a compromised replica, an insider). They supply no input at all and still recover plaintext: unsalted MD5 of human-chosen passwords falls to rainbow tables and to multi-billion-guess-per-second cracking rigs. What they get is the victim's plaintext password, which is typically reused on other services.

Because the same module already defines `hash_password` using `bcrypt.hashpw(..., bcrypt.gensalt())`, this also means a password's resistance to offline cracking silently depends on whether it was last set through registration or through reset — and the reset path is the weak one, so it downgrades existing accounts.

Fix: make the reset path call the same bcrypt routine, e.g. `return hash_password(raw)`, and delete `hash_reset_password` (or keep it as a thin alias). If the value is genuinely not a password but a single-use reset token, it should be generated with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, stored hashed with SHA-256, given an expiry, and the function should not be named `hash_reset_password`.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), but `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same stored column and are checked by a common verifier, `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` on an MD5 digest raises `ValueError: invalid salt` rather than returning `False` \u2014 so the reset flow fails with a 500 instead of a clean auth rejection. If instead the verifier is format-sniffing, an attacker-supplied MD5 of a guessed password becomes trivially reversible via rainbow tables, since the digest is also unsalted (identical passwords yield identical digests). Either way the two functions should produce the same format: use `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` here too, or drop the separate helper and call `hash_password`.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password introduces a new, security-relevant code path (used for password reset) but no test exists in this diff to verify its behavior or catch a regression/incorrect algorithm choice. Since no test file is included, nothing would fail if this function's output format, algorithm, or behavior changed unexpectedly.

findings.title: checksum() reads the entire file into memory
findings.body: `fh.read()` materialises the whole file before hashing, so checksumming a large upload or backup allocates a buffer the size of the file and can OOM the process. Stream it instead: iterate with `for block in iter(lambda: fh.read(65536), b""): h.update(block)`. The `with` block correctly closes the handle, so only the buffering is at issue.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted fork code with repo secrets
findings.body:
This change makes the workflow trigger on `pull_request_target` (line 4), which runs in the context of the base repository with access to secrets and a writable `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and then explicitly checks out the attacker's commit via `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (lines 11-12) and executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` in its environment (lines 13-15).

Attacker: any person on the internet who can open a pull request from a fork — no prior access required. What they control: the entire contents of the checked-out tree, including `scripts/measure.sh` itself (and anything it sources, e.g. package manifests / lifecycle scripts). What they get: arbitrary code execution inside a job that holds `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` and the base-repo `GITHUB_TOKEN`; both can be printed/exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled host, and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` in `pull_request_target` defaults to write access (no `permissions:` block is set here), allowing repository and release tampering. Merging the PR is not required — opening it is enough.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. Forked PRs do run under `pull_request`; they simply get a read-only token and no secrets — which is the correct signal for a size check.
2. If a token is genuinely required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a privileged `workflow_run` job that never checks out fork code.
3. At minimum, if `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out `head.sha`, do not execute any script from the PR tree, drop `NPM_TOKEN`, and add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out and executes untrusted fork code with secrets

findings.title: Workflow edits in a PR no longer take effect until merged
findings.body: `pull_request_target` always evaluates the workflow definition from the base branch, not from the PR. After this change, edits to `.github/workflows/size.yml` (or to the `measure` job wiring) can no longer be validated in the PR that makes them — the old base-branch version runs instead. Expect a confusing loop when iterating on this file; note it for whoever maintains the workflow.

findings.title: Size now measured on head SHA, not the merge result
findings.body: Under `on: pull_request`, `actions/checkout` defaults to `refs/pull/N/merge` — the result of merging the PR into the base branch — so the reported size reflected what the base branch would look like after merge. Pinning `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the PR branch in isolation, which will diverge whenever the base branch has moved (e.g. another PR changed a shared bundle). If any downstream check or comparison assumes the number describes the post-merge tree, it will now report stale or misleading sizes on long-lived branches.

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted
findings.body:
The previous key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any hashable value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, enums, frozen dataclasses, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` accepts only str/int/float/bool/None/list/dict, so any existing caller passing such a value now gets an uncaught `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from `cached_render`, before rendering is even attempted. If `_render` itself tolerates those values (templates commonly format dates and decimals), this turns a working call into a hard failure.

Either pass `default=repr`/a custom encoder to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails. The new tests only exercise int values, so this path is untested.

findings.title: Behavior change (JSON-serializability requirement) is untested
findings.body: The old key = (template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items()))) worked for any hashable context value. The new key relies on json.dumps(context), which raises TypeError for values that aren't JSON-serializable (sets, tuples-as-values, datetimes, custom objects). This is a real behavior regression introduced by the diff, and none of the added tests exercise a context with such a value, so nothing would catch it if the encoding were wrong or a caller passed a previously-valid context.

findings.title: Test only checks mock kwarg, not the actual argv content
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` only asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects `spy.last_call.args` to confirm the command was actually built as a list (`["tar", "-czf", ..., directory]`) rather than a formatted string. If someone regressed the code to build a shell string but still passed `shell=False` (which subprocess would then treat as a single non-existent executable, or silently misbehave), or reintroduced string interpolation while leaving `shell=False`, this test would still pass. It's asserting on a mock's kwarg, not on what the code produced.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test depends on an undefined `spy` fixture and would otherwise run real tar

findings.title: Allowlist rejects names that previously worked (dots, spaces, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters, so any existing caller that passes a timestamped or dotted name (`nightly.2025-01-01`, `tenant 42`, a long tenant slug) now gets a `ValueError` where it previously got a completed archive. `create_archive` also had no declared exceptions before this change, so callers have no `except ValueError` around it. Either widen the class to include `.` (and raise the length bound), or sanitise/slugify the name instead of rejecting, and confirm the allowlist against the names real callers pass. Note also that a non-str `name` (e.g. `None`) reaches `fullmatch` and raises `TypeError`, not the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: No test verifies argv is a proper list preventing shell injection via directory
findings.body: The whole point of this change is that `directory` and `name` are passed as separate argv elements instead of being interpolated into a shell string. No test constructs the actual subprocess.run call and asserts that `directory` appears as its own list element (e.g., with a directory value containing spaces or shell metacharacters like `; rm -rf /`) and is not otherwise mangled. The `name` allowlist is tested, but the core safety property of the argv list — that `directory` is never subject to shell parsing — is unverified.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly constrained, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` with no validation. Because of the `--` separator it cannot be interpreted as a tar option, so this is not argument or command injection. The remaining exposure is content selection: whoever supplies `directory` chooses which part of the filesystem gets packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, a predictable path the same caller can name. If `directory` originates from a request parameter, a caller could pass `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, or an application config directory and then retrieve the resulting archive, reading files the process can read but the caller should not.

If `directory` is only ever built server-side from trusted state, this is a non-issue and worth a comment saying so. If it can be caller-influenced, resolve it with `os.path.realpath` and assert it stays under an allowed root before invoking tar.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer shell-expanded; globs/tilde/multi-path callers break
findings.body: Under the old `shell=True` string the shell split `directory` on whitespace and expanded globs and `~`, so a caller passing `"/srv/data/*"`, `"~/data"`, or `"/srv/a /srv/b"` archived several paths. With the list form the whole value is one literal filename, so tar will fail with "no such file or directory" (and `check=True` turns that into a `CalledProcessError`) rather than archiving anything. If any caller relies on that, accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv, or expand with `glob`/`os.path.expanduser` explicitly before the call.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result without any assertion. The only failure it can ever detect is an uncaught exception — if `render` starts returning `None`, an empty string, a stray header, or the wrong currency formatting for the zero-line case, this test still passes green. Since the blank-invoice case is exactly the boundary this test exists to pin down, assert on the return value, e.g. that it equals the expected empty-invoice rendering or that it contains the zero total. If the intent really is only "does not raise", say so explicitly in the test name/body so a future reader does not mistake it for coverage of the output.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts only mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never checks what render() actually produced, so it would pass even if the formatted output were dropped, mis-ordered, or concatenated incorrectly.
