_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing half-to-even test deleted, but no rounding fix is in the diff
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` is removed rather than updated, and this is the only file in the change set — there is no accompanying edit to the implementation of `round_cents`. If the rounding behaviour really was fixed, the test should have been amended to assert the new expected value (e.g. `Decimal("2.35")` if the intent is half-up), which would keep the boundary case covered. As written, the exact-half input `Decimal("2.345")` — the single most error-prone input for a money-rounding helper — now has no assertion at all, so a regression in either direction will pass CI silently. Please restore the test with the corrected expectation, and include the implementation change the description refers to.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding fix for the 2.345 case has no test coverage

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, binding `deliver` into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. This test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times \u2014 it may hit real I/O, be slow/flaky, and it asserts `False` only by accident of whatever the real transport returns. Change the target to `"notify.sender.deliver"`, matching the existing test on line 2.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches notify.transport.deliver, not notify.sender.deliver

findings.title: Test patches wrong target, contradicting module documentation
findings.body: The docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly states that patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect the `deliver` function used in `send_with_retry`, because `deliver` is bound into the module's namespace at import time. This new test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, which means it does not actually test the retry logic—it tests nothing, since the patched function is never called. The test should patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, as demonstrated by the existing test on line 2.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each cell with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,` with no quoting, while `csv_escape` — added in the same commit, directly below — exists precisely to quote values containing `,` or `"`. Any row value containing a comma (a free-text field, a formatted number, an address) emits extra columns and silently corrupts the output for every downstream consumer. Wrap the cell in `csv_escape`: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same gap exists in `csv_header`, which joins column names unescaped.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins raw field values without applying csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter functions ship with no tests
findings.body: csv_rows and csv_escape (csv_export.py), dump_streaming and dump_pretty (json_export.py), and margins_for and usable_width (pdf_export.py) are all new public behaviour with no accompanying tests in this diff. The repo already tests the analogous csv_header function, so the same standard should apply here. Edge cases worth covering: csv_escape with embedded quotes/commas, dump_streaming chunk boundaries, and margins_for/usable_width arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one from integer division) are all currently unverified — a regression in any of them would pass CI silently.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote values containing newlines or CR
findings.body: RFC 4180 requires a field to be quoted if it contains a comma, a double quote, CR or LF. `csv_escape` only tests for `,` and `"`, so a value with an embedded newline is emitted verbatim and terminates the record early, shifting every subsequent field. Extend the condition to `any(ch in value for ch in ',"\r\n')`. Separately, the function assumes `value` is a `str` — `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for an int or `None`, so either coerce with `str(value)` or document the precondition.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized sequence and emits nothing for empty input
findings.body: `dump_streaming` is a generator whose name and docstring suggest it can consume a stream, but `len(rows)` and `rows[i : i + chunk_size]` require a materialised sequence — passing a generator or any lazy iterator raises `TypeError`, defeating the point of streaming. Use `itertools.islice` over an iterator if lazy input is intended. Also note that an empty `rows` yields no chunks at all, so a consumer concatenating the output gets an empty body rather than `[]`; if the caller expects at least one array, yield `"[]"` for the empty case.

findings.title: Date comparison is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`token.issued_at.date()` is captured inside `issue_token()` and compared against `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` evaluated a moment later. If the token is issued at 23:59:59.999 UTC and the assertion runs after midnight, the two dates differ and the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The existing test on line 5-6 avoids this by pinning an explicit `issued` instant; do the same here — freeze or inject the clock (e.g. `issue_token(now=fixed)`), or assert a bounded window such as `abs(token.issued_at - before) < timedelta(seconds=5)` where `before` is captured before the call.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test depends on real system clock, not deterministic

findings.title: `is_expired` called without the `now=` injection used elsewhere
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 passes an explicit `now=` so the outcome does not depend on the machine clock. Line 12 drops it, so the assertion depends on the real current time relative to whatever expiry `issue_token()` bakes in. That makes the test both non-deterministic and silently sensitive to a future change in the default token lifetime. Pass an explicit `now=` here too.

findings.title: Possible mismatch in what the first argument to `is_expired` means
findings.body: On line 6 the first argument is `issued + timedelta(hours=2)` while `now` is only `issued + 1h1s`, and the test asserts the token *is* expired — that only makes sense if the first parameter is the *issued* time (expiry derived from a one-hour lifetime), since a token expiring two hours out cannot be expired one hour in. Line 12 instead passes `token.expires_at`. One of the two call sites is using the wrong field; under the line-6 reading, `is_expired(token.expires_at)` would treat the expiry timestamp as an issue time and give a wrong (likely vacuously passing) result. Please confirm the parameter's meaning and make both call sites agree.

findings.title: No test covers coupon expiry rejection
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test in tests/test_coupons.py exercises a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), i.e. the non-expired path. If the comparison direction were reversed, the exception type wrong, or the check removed entirely, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: expires_at of None or naive datetime raises TypeError, not CouponExpired
findings.body:
Line 9 compares `coupon.expires_at` directly against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. Two reachable inputs break this:

- A coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`.
- A coupon whose `expires_at` is a naive datetime (common when loaded from a DB column without timezone) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

In both cases callers see an opaque `TypeError` from the billing path rather than either a successful application or `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but calls `requests.get`, a synchronous blocking API. Awaiting this coroutine will block the entire event loop thread for up to the 5s timeout, stalling every other concurrent request handler — not just this one. The function also contains no `await` at all, so declaring it `async` buys nothing but the false impression that it yields.

Use the same pattern as `fetch_plan` above: take an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or construct one) and `await client.get(...)`, e.g. `response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the sync call genuinely cannot be replaced, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it leaves the event loop thread. The new `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

findings.title: New fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a network call via the synchronous `requests` library (a blocking call inside an async def) and returns parsed JSON. No test file is included in this diff. If this function were changed to silently swallow errors, return the wrong data, or if the blocking call caused event-loop stalls, nothing in the codebase would fail. At minimum a test mocking the request and asserting on the returned value (and ideally verifying it doesn't block the event loop) is needed.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. Nothing in the function validates or percent-encodes `tenant_id`. If that value originates from a request (path segment, query string, JSON body, or a header), a caller can inject `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` and reach a different resource on the internal billing host — e.g. `tenant_id="../../admin/accounts"` becomes `https://billing.internal/limits/../../admin/accounts`, which `requests`/`urllib3` forward largely as written and most servers resolve. The billing service is on an internal network and is very likely reachable only from this service, so it may not enforce its own authorisation on the caller; that is exactly the trust boundary being crossed here.

Fix: coerce and constrain the identifier before it reaches the URL — e.g. validate it against the expected shape (`int(tenant_id)` or a UUID/`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$` check) and/or `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper is worth doing once.

Adversary: any client that can influence the tenant identifier for this handler. Controls: the path segment appended to an internal URL. Gets: arbitrary GETs against other endpoints of `billing.internal` under this service's network identity, and whatever those endpoints return, since the JSON body is handed straight back to the caller on line 12.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are discarded and turned into a normal `None` return. That makes the process un-interruptible during a push and can mask a shutdown signal as a successful-looking call. Additionally, the PR description says failures should be "catch and log", but the handler body contains no logging at all — every failure, including genuine bugs such as a `TypeError` from a malformed payload, becomes invisible.

Use `except Exception as exc:` and emit a log record (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc)`) before returning.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change adds a try/except that catches all exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating. There is no test verifying that push_metrics(payload) returns None (rather than raising) when _client.send raises, so a regression that removes or narrows the except clause would not be caught.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then awaits at line 18, then writes `current + cost` at line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which every other mutation of `_counters` (line 9-11 in `consume`) does hold.

Two concrete defects:

1. **Limit bypass.** Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current` below the threshold at line 15, both pass the check at line 16, and both write — total consumption ends up above `LIMIT`. The `await` at line 18 is a guaranteed yield point, so the interleaving is not merely theoretical; it happens on every pair of concurrent calls.
2. **Lost update.** Line 19 writes an absolute value computed from the stale `current` rather than re-reading or incrementing in place. Any `consume()` or `try_consume()` that completed for the same tenant during the await is overwritten and its cost vanishes from the counter, permanently under-counting the tenant.

Fix by taking the same lock and doing the read, check and write inside it:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

(and drop the `asyncio.sleep(0)`, or move it outside the critical section, since awaiting inside the lock would re-open the same window if it were anything other than a no-op yield).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrency behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point), then writes _counters, all without holding _lock. Under concurrent calls for the same tenant this is a classic check-then-act race that can let combined cost exceed LIMIT. There is no test in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume, so a regression that removes the sleep, changes locking, or breaks the limit check would go undetected.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple it has always returned. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict yields its keys and raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call, so weekly report rendering fails unconditionally. Either update all callers in the same change (`user = lookup_user(id); user["name"], user["email"]`), or keep the tuple contract and add a separate function/parameter for the richer shape.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts return type change
findings.body:
The docstring promises `(name, email)` but the function now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. Callers like the one in reports/weekly.py that unpack a tuple will break. Update the docstring to reflect the new dict return type and document all keys.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: No test catches the tuple→dict contract break for lookup_user
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict {"name":..., "email":..., "tier":...} instead of a (name, email) tuple. The existing caller reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise a ValueError (dict unpacks its keys, not two values) at runtime. There is no test in this diff exercising lookup_user's return shape or render_row against it, so this break would ship silently until it hits production.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding failed inserts
findings.body:
The error returned by `db.Exec` on line 15 is bound to the `if` statement's scope and is only logged on line 16. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` — which is unconditionally nil — and return it. The function's `error` return value therefore can never be non-nil for an insert failure; only the `validate` path on lines 12-14 can ever report an error.

For an end-of-day settlement batch this means a failed INSERT looks like a success to the caller: the row is silently dropped with no retry and no failure count, and any caller that marks the batch settled on a nil return will do so incorrectly. If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs to the batch loop, not to a function that advertises an `error` return — either propagate the error (`if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil { log.Printf(...); return err }`) or change the signature so callers cannot mistake nil for a successful write.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ WriteSettlement swallows insert failure and always returns nil

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement name misleads about error handling

findings.title: WriteSettlement's error-return behavior is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` on line 18 and returns it on line 19, so the function always returns nil regardless of whether the insert on line 15 succeeded or failed — only a log line is emitted on failure. There is no test in this diff exercising the failure path of WriteSettlement (e.g. asserting the returned error when the INSERT fails), so this behavior — intended or not — would not be caught by any test today.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends into it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, and so on for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get an ever-growing, wrong result, and the list is also aliased into every caller's hands so an external mutation corrupts future calls.

Use the standard sentinel form:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
```

Note that the adjacent existing code on line 2 already uses exactly this defensive pattern (`dict(extra_headers or {})`), so the fix matches local practice.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: No test catches the mutable default argument bug in send_with_retries
findings.body: send_with_retries uses `attempted=[]` as a default argument, which is shared across calls and accumulates entries from previous invocations that didn't pass an explicit list. Nothing in this diff tests calling the function twice without an explicit `attempted` list, so this bug (state leaking between calls) would go unnoticed. A test that calls send_with_retries twice with failing dispatches and asserts the second call's returned list only contains recipients from that call would catch this.

findings.title: compute_rounding silently changes half-cent boundary from >= to >
findings.body:
Every other function in this hunk is a pure rename with an identical body. `compute_rounding` is the exception: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0` and the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For a line with `remainder_cents == 0.5` — exactly the half-cent case this function exists to resolve — the result flips from 1 to 0, so those invoices now round down instead of up. On monetary totals this is a real, silently-wrong result that reconciliation will eventually surface.

If the rounding rule was genuinely meant to change, it belongs in its own PR with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rename commit also flips rounding comparison from >= to >

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Module docstring references old function names
findings.body: The module docstring states 'Line-item calculators' but all functions have been renamed from `calc_*` to `compute_*`. The docstring should be updated to reflect the new naming convention so readers know what to expect when importing from this module.

findings.title: page_of_sorted returns fewer items than page_of
findings.body:
The `page_of_sorted` function slices with `[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` (line 12), returning one fewer item than `page_of` does with `[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` (line 6). This breaks the implicit contract that pagination functions should return consistent batch sizes. Callers expecting PAGE_SIZE items per page (except possibly the last page) will receive PAGE_SIZE - 1 items instead, causing off-by-one errors in iteration and batch counting. Fix by removing the `- 1` from line 12.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ page_of_sorted drops the last record of every page

findings.title: AttributeError when purchase_order is None (the common case)
findings.body: `header_lines` now calls `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` unconditionally. The retrieved model declares `purchase_order: "str | None"` and documents that it is "only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty" — so the removed guard was load-bearing, not redundant, and the majority of invoices will now raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` during rendering. Restore the conditional append (or build the list and conditionally extend it) so the PO line is only emitted when `purchase_order is not None`.

findings.title: No test covers header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), but the Invoice model documents purchase_order as optional (str | None) for the majority of customers. Nothing in the repo appears to test header_lines with a None purchase_order, so this regression (AttributeError on None) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: File handle leaked on the header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, `StopIteration`, I/O errors) escapes with the handle open too. Under CPython refcounting this is masked most of the time, but in a bulk importer that rejects many partner files it will exhaust file descriptors, and on PyPy/other runtimes it leaks immediately. Wrap the body in `with open(path) as fh:` the way `read_rows` on line 5 already does, and drop the explicit `close()`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Header-mismatch path leaks the file descriptor (weak DoS vector)

findings.title: read_validated has no tests covering its branches or resource handling
findings.body: The new read_validated function has at least three distinct behaviors: returning None on header mismatch, returning parsed rows on success, and leaving the file handle open if csv.reader/next raises before fh.close() is reached. No test file is included in this diff, so none of these paths — including the early-return leak path where fh.close() is skipped — would be caught by CI if the logic regressed (e.g. if the header check were inverted, or if rows were returned unparsed).

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() — duplicate charges on transient failure
findings.body:
`charge_card` decorates `billing.gateway.charge` with `@retry(attempts=3)`, but `charge()` is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure mode where the POST reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will be retried and bill the customer up to three times. Real money, no compensating action.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge (outside the retried function, e.g. caller-supplied or derived from an order id) and pass it through `charge()` so retries collapse server-side. Until that key is plumbed through, `charge_card` should not retry — only `fetch_charge` (a GET, explicitly "Safe to repeat") is safe under this decorator.

findings.title: Non-idempotent operation wrapped in retry without documented safeguards
findings.body: The `charge_card` function at lines 10-12 wraps `charge()`, which the underlying `billing/gateway.py` documents as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries. The wrapper function has no docstring, so callers cannot see this critical constraint. A caller using `charge_card` with retries enabled will create multiple charges on failure unless they pass an Idempotency-Key — but there is no indication they must do so. Add a docstring that either (1) documents the idempotency requirement and how to provide the key, or (2) explains that the wrapper handles it internally.

findings.title: No test guards against duplicate charges on retry
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is documented as NOT idempotent and requires an Idempotency-Key to be safe under retry. The new @retry(attempts=3) decorator will call charge() multiple times on transient failure, potentially creating multiple real charges for one logical request. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that verifies charge_card either passes an idempotency key or otherwise avoids duplicate side effects on retry — a test asserting call_count on a mock would not catch this, and none exists here.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `datetime.now()` (line 9) returns a naive local datetime, while `invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails for every invite — this function can never return normally. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the types matched, naive `now()` is local wall-clock time, so the comparison would be off by the UTC offset for any non-UTC deployment.

findings.title: Timezone mismatch in expires_within comparison
findings.body: The `expires_within` function compares `invite.expires_at` (a timezone-aware UTC datetime per the Invite class docstring) with `cutoff` (a naive datetime from `datetime.now()`). Python will raise `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` when this comparison is attempted. The fix is to use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` instead of `datetime.now()`, consistent with the pattern established in `is_expired` on line 5.

findings.title: expires_within has no test coverage
findings.body: expires_within is a new function that mixes datetime.now() (naive) with invite.expires_at (tz-aware per the Invite model docstring), which would raise a TypeError at runtime when subtracted. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so this defect (and any future regression in its logic) would go undetected.

findings.title: Public function ignores optional property
findings.body:
The function `contactEmail` accesses `account.billingContact.email` without checking whether `billingContact` exists. The `Account` type defines `billingContact` as optional (line 4 of web/src/types.ts: `billingContact?: { ... }`). A caller passing an account that has not completed onboarding will get a runtime error. Either add a null check and return a fallback (as `bannerFor` does on line 4 above), or update the type hint and add a JSDoc explaining that this function requires onboarding to be complete.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard

findings.title: contactEmail throws on missing billingContact, and nothing tests it
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email directly, unlike bannerFor which uses optional chaining. Since Account.billingContact is documented as optional and 'absent until the customer completes onboarding', this will throw a TypeError for accounts without a billing contact. There is no test in this diff exercising contactEmail with either a present or absent billingContact, so this behavior change (and the crash) would go completely uncaught.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS and that callers wanting seconds must multiply. Passing `timeout=30` gives the slow partner API a 30ms budget, which the PR description ('Timeout set generously since their API is slow') shows is not the intent. Worse, the docstring notes retries share the same budget, and `retries` defaults to 3, so all three attempts must complete within those 30ms. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count × 1000) instead.

findings.title: Timeout value contradicts fetch() contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring explicitly states that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS. This call passes `timeout=30`, which will be interpreted as 30 milliseconds (0.03 seconds) rather than the 30 seconds intended for a slow partner API. Either multiply by 1000 to pass `timeout=30000`, or verify the intention against the documented contract in `clients/http.py`.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering timeout value
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue calls fetch(...) with timeout=30, but clients/http.py documents timeout in milliseconds. Nothing in this change exercises this function or asserts on the timeout value passed to fetch, so a caller-supplied wrong unit (30ms instead of the intended 30s) would silently pass with no failing test.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from 0007
findings.body: `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` is already indexed by `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql and applied 2025-11-02. Because the new index uses a different name, `IF NOT EXISTS` does not suppress it — Postgres will happily build a second, identical index. The result is duplicated storage plus extra write amplification on every insert/update of `invoices`, with no planner benefit. Drop this statement, or if the intent was to rename, do an explicit `ALTER INDEX invoices_tenant_created_idx RENAME TO ...` instead.

findings.title: priority=9 sends reset email to the back of the queue, not the front
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**, and explicitly warns that a job at 9 waits behind every other job on the queue. Passing `priority=9` therefore does the exact opposite of the PR's stated goal: password-reset mail now drains after the nightly digest batch instead of ahead of it, and is strictly worse than the previous default of 5. Use a low value — `priority=0` (or a small number reserved for interactive mail) — to drain reset mail first.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 delays reset email; 0 is drained first, not 9

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ priority=9 queues reset email last, not first

findings.title: Priority value inverted: 9 drains last, not first
findings.body: The diff sets `priority=9` to queue password resets ahead of other jobs, but the queue documentation states that 0 is drained first and 9 is drained last. This means password resets will actually be delayed behind other jobs, opposite to the stated intent. Use `priority=0` to drain password resets first.

findings.title: Upsert contract violated: terms not lower-cased
findings.body: The `search.index.upsert()` function has explicit documentation stating that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated. The indexer will not normalize them, creating unfindable postings if case differs from the query. Line 7 passes `article.title.split()` directly without lowercasing, violating this contract. Either lower-case the terms here, or update the upsert docstring if the contract has changed.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised terms; titles silently unsearchable
findings.body:
`search.index.upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly states it does not normalise them — a term differing only by case creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries can never match. `article.title.split()` yields the title's words verbatim, so any capitalised word (i.e. virtually every title, which are typically title- or sentence-cased) is indexed under a posting key no query will reach. The article appears to index successfully and is silently unfindable by those terms.

Normalise before the call, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {t.lower() for t in article.title.split()})`. Note that `split()` also leaves trailing punctuation attached (`"release."`), which has the same silent-miss effect, so consider stripping non-word characters too.

findings.title: No test covers that published articles become searchable
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()) to index articles for search, but no test in this diff verifies that a published article is actually findable afterward. upsert's documented contract requires terms to be lower-cased and de-duplicated already; article.title.split() satisfies neither, so a title like "Big News" would be indexed under "Big" and "News" (mixed case) while queries lower-case their terms and would never match. A test asserting that publish(article) followed by a search/query for a term in the title returns that article would catch this; without it, the feature can silently fail to make articles searchable and nothing in the test suite would notice.

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token
findings.body:
The previous code special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it; the replacement stores `request.headers[header]` for every header including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, so the browser sends the token inside the Referer on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live auth token into the log, where it is readable by anyone with log access and is typically shipped off-host. Restore the scrubbing branch for `Referer` (and keep passing `extra_param_keys` through) rather than logging the raw value.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Referer scrubbing removed — auth token written to server log

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscubbed despite containing tokens
findings.body: The code at line 5 now logs the Referer header directly without scrubbing, but the docstring in `token_authenticated_url` (in jupyter_server/auth/identity.py) states that "the browser sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request." This means tokens are being logged to error logs, contradicting the apparent intent to protect sensitive authentication material. Either the logging logic should scrub the token from Referer headers (restore the removed `_scrub_uri` call), or the docstring should be updated to reflect that tokens are now logged. If intentional, document why tokens in 5xx logs are acceptable.

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no test guarding against reintroduction/regression
findings.body: The change deletes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously redacted the Referer header before logging (which per jupyter_server/auth/identity.py can carry the auth token as a query parameter). No test file is part of this diff, so nothing would fail if this scrubbing is removed or reintroduced incorrectly in the future. A test asserting that a Referer containing a token/query param is scrubbed in the emitted log output would catch this class of regression.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` is now unused in this function
findings.body: With the `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` call removed, `extra_param_keys` appears to have no remaining consumer in this function. If it is a parameter of the enclosing log helper, callers still pass it and it silently does nothing — a signature that no longer means what callers assume. Either restore the scrubbing (preferred, see the Referer finding) or remove the now-dead parameter and update its callers.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from the URL check allows javascript: in SVG links
findings.body:
The intent stated in the PR is to *drop* a rarely used SVG attribute, but removing `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` from this branch does not remove the attribute from the output — it only removes the `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)` scheme check for it. Execution now falls through past line 7 to whatever the default return is, so `xlinkhref` is treated like an ordinary inert attribute.

`xlink:href` is a live navigation target on SVG `<a>` and is honoured by browsers with `javascript:` URLs, so author markdown containing `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` is no longer blocked. Per the file's own header comment, this markdown includes end-user submitted content and `validateProp` is the only barrier to the DOM.

If the goal really is to stop supporting the attribute, reject it outright (return `false` for `xlinkhref`) rather than removing it from the scheme check. If it should remain supported, restore it to the condition on line 6.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer URL-scheme validated, enabling stored XSS

findings.title: No test guards removal of xlinkhref from validateProp
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed in validateProp. This is a security-relevant behaviour change (per the module's own comment, validateProp is 'the only thing standing between markdown and the DOM'), yet no test in the diff exercises validateProp with attribute='xlinkhref' either before or after this change. If this removal is wrong — e.g. because SVG xlink:href can still be used to inject javascript: URLs — nothing in the test suite would fail to catch it.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller precondition
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, reaches the DAO layer without any identifier check. `internal/api/database/file/file.go` documents the opposite contract: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join` does not scope a path to its first argument — it calls `Clean`, so `filepath.Join(d.Folder, "../../etc", kind)` resolves outside the storage root. The PR description's justification ("the path join already scopes under the folder root") is therefore incorrect.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check, or push an equivalent validation/containment check (e.g. verify the cleaned result still has `d.Folder` as a prefix) into `buildPath` itself before relaxing the caller.

Note also that the equality check on line 4 does not compensate: it only runs when `parameters.Project` is non-empty, and it compares the two values rather than validating either, so a crafted value supplied in both path and query passes it unchanged.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets project query param traverse out of storage root

findings.title: No test covers removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The validation call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) was removed, meaning a projectQueryParameter containing path-traversal characters (e.g. '../') would now flow unchecked into buildPath, which per its own doc comment relies on callers to validate names. There is no test in this diff exercising list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter to confirm the join-based scoping actually prevents traversal, or to catch a future regression where validation is needed again.

findings.title: Part buffer sized from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` is the declared length of an S3 UploadPart request body (the `Content-Length` header / the value the S3 server hands to this helper); it is supplied by the client, not measured from the stream. Feeding it straight into `Reserve()` makes the allocation size a function of an unverified header, so a client that sends `Content-Length: 50000000000` and then zero or a handful of body bytes causes the process to reserve tens of gigabytes up front. Repeating this over a few concurrent connections OOM-kills the serving process; the previous code was self-limiting because the pool-backed RW only grew as real bytes arrived from `io.Copy`.

If the pre-reservation is worth keeping, clamp it: `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize))` with a sane cap (S3 part size limit, e.g. 5 GiB, or preferably a much smaller configured ceiling), reject negative values, and reject requests whose declared length exceeds the configured maximum part size before allocating. Also verify after `io.Copy` that `n == contentLength` so a short body cannot leave an oversized reservation held for the life of the part.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test guards Reserve(contentLength) against bad/large lengths
findings.body: The new call `multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` changes allocation behavior based on the declared Content-Length. If contentLength is attacker-controlled and mismatched with the actual body size (too large, negative, or zero), nothing in this diff or visible surrounding code exercises that path — no test asserts that a mismatched or malicious contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation, a panic, or silent truncation of the buffered data. Since this PR is specifically about avoiding declared-length allocation issues (per the PR title referencing a CVE), the fix itself should be covered by a test that supplies a wrong Content-Length and shows correct/safe behavior.

findings.title: contentLength may be -1 (unknown length) when passed to Reserve
findings.body:
For requests with chunked transfer encoding or an absent Content-Length, Go's `http.Request.ContentLength` is `-1`, and `0` for an empty/unknown body. If that value flows into `contentLength` here, `Reserve(-1)` is handed a negative size. Depending on how `Reserve` is implemented this is either a panic (the `bytes.Buffer.Grow`/`make` convention is to panic on a negative count) or a silently ignored no-op. Neither is obviously intended by this change.

Guard the call: only reserve when `contentLength > 0`, and fall back to the previous grow-as-you-read behaviour otherwise.

findings.title: S3 scheme now defaults to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP on an explicit `is_secure=False`; every other value, including the common case where the key is absent (`.get` returns `None`), produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` as falsy, so any request that does not explicitly set `is_secure` is now sent over plaintext `http://` to `s3.amazonaws.com`, carrying the AWS signature/credentials and the object body in the clear. Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)` if truthiness semantics are wanted.

Secondary effect of the same line: values that are falsy but not `False` (`0`, `""`) also now downgrade, whereas before they did not.

findings.title: S3 requests now default to plaintext HTTP, disabling TLS
findings.body:
The old expression (`"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`) was fail-secure: TLS was used unless the caller explicitly set `is_secure=False`. The new expression is fail-open: when `is_secure` is absent from `request.meta` (or is `None`, `0`, `""`), `request.meta.get("is_secure")` is falsy and the scheme becomes `http`, so the URL built on line 6 is `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`.

S3 downloads carry AWS authentication material (an `Authorization` header with the access key id and the request signature, or query-string presigned parameters). Sending them over cleartext exposes the access key id, the signature, the bucket/object names and the response body to anyone on the network path, and allows response tampering.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: Default scheme flip (https->http) has no test coverage in this diff
findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False. The new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy — meaning requests with no is_secure meta (the common case) now silently downgrade to plaintext http instead of https. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this default-value change breaking or altering security-relevant behavior for the common unset case.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
Previously `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` produced a `ResourceAction{Action: "delete"}`, which the authorization layer checked against the account's delete grant. After this change the only branches are `pull` (GET/HEAD) and `push` (everything else), so a DELETE request is authorized as `push`.

Adversary: any authenticated account (or anonymous, if the repo policy grants anonymous push) that has been granted `push` on a repository but deliberately *not* granted `delete`. They control only the HTTP method of their own request. What they get: the ability to delete existing tags/manifests/blobs — destructive access the operator explicitly withheld. Per `pkg/api/config/config.go`, the three actions are "distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones."

Restore an explicit `http.MethodDelete -> "delete"` branch before the catch-all. If the intent really is to fold delete into push, that is a breaking policy change that needs to be reflected in the config semantics and documented, not an implicit fallthrough.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now maps to "push", erasing the delete action

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods flips from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old switch had an explicit `default: action = "pull"`, so methods outside the enumerated set (notably OPTIONS, and anything else routed here) required only pull access. The new condition treats every method that is not GET/HEAD as push, so OPTIONS/preflight and any other verb now demand push permission and will be rejected for pull-only clients. If the previous permissive default was intentional, keep it by checking explicitly for the write verbs (POST/PATCH/PUT) rather than negating the read verbs.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the distinct 'delete' action and now maps HTTP DELETE requests to 'push'. Per the repository's own documented access model (pkg/api/config/config.go), pull/push/delete are intentionally distinct so an account can be granted push without delete. This diff silently collapses that distinction, but no test file is part of the change, so nothing would fail if this mapping is wrong (e.g., if DELETE should still map to a 'delete' action, or an account with only push permission is now allowed to delete repositories).

findings.title: Size check clears the whole cache, discarding the just-fetched entry
findings.body:
`_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately followed by `if len(_CACHE) > 1000: _CACHE.clear()`. When the threshold is crossed the clear removes every entry *including the one just written*, so a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` and then `get_tenant(x)` gets `None` back even though the fetch succeeded — the documented purpose of the helper ("a live fetch into the shared cache") silently does not hold on that call. It also evicts every other tenant at once, so all concurrent readers fall back to `None`/refetch simultaneously (a stampede) rather than losing one entry.

Suggested fix: evict a bounded number of *other* entries (e.g. pop the oldest via an `OrderedDict`/`lru_cache`-style structure) before or instead of inserting, and never drop the key being refreshed. If a full flush really is intended, re-insert `tenant_id` after the clear.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Full cache flush on overflow allows cheap cache-wipe amplification

findings.title: Misleading function name: `get_*` that mutates cache
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which conventionally implies a read-only operation. However, the implementation mutates the shared cache by writing to it (line 10) and clearing it when size exceeds 1000 (lines 11-12). A caller expecting a simple read operation could use this function without anticipating these side effects, potentially causing unexpected cache eviction. Rename to reflect the mutation: `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or similar.

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: fetching a live value, writing it into the shared _CACHE, and clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the eviction threshold logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, or clearing on every call), or if the cache write were dropped, nothing would fail.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body: The README on line 7 still references `--workers`, but the CLI has been updated to use `--concurrency` (cli.py line 6). Users following the README documentation will use an argument that no longer exists. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Renaming --workers breaks existing invocations and args.workers readers
findings.body:
`p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` became `--concurrency`. Two contracts break at once:

1. Any existing invocation (scripts, CI jobs, systemd units, Dockerfile CMDs) passing `--workers 8` now fails with argparse's "unrecognized arguments" error and exit code 2 — silently at deploy time, not at build time.
2. argparse derives the destination from the option name, so the parsed namespace attribute changes from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Every consumer of `parser()` that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime.

If the rename is intended to be non-breaking, keep the old spelling as an alias and pin the destination explicitly, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="workers", type=int, default=4)` — or, if the new attribute name is wanted, `dest="concurrency"` plus updating every `args.workers` read site in the same PR. The README still documents `--workers` on line 7, which suggests the call sites were not swept.

findings.title: No test covers the renamed --concurrency flag
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency but no test file is included in this diff. If the rename were reverted, incomplete, or the argument name misspelled, nothing would fail — there's no assertion anywhere that parser() accepts --concurrency or rejects --workers.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring promises an integer total, but the function now returns a dictionary with per-day breakdown. Callers relying on the documented contract will break. Update the docstring to describe the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict; docstring still promises an integer
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. The signature is unchanged, so every existing caller that does arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently operate on a dict or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so callers reading the contract get the old behaviour.

Either keep the total available (return both, or add a separate `daily_usage` function) or update the docstring and audit/adjust all call sites in the same change.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day dict return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage's return type changed from an int total to a dict keyed by day. Any caller relying on the old scalar contract would break, but no test in this diff exercises the new shape or verifies the grouping/aggregation logic. If the SQL or dict comprehension is wrong (e.g., wrong key names, missing days, incorrect aggregation), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body:
The docstring describes the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 has renamed it to `limit`. A caller reading the documentation will attempt to pass `page_size=` and receive a TypeError. Update the docstring on line 6 to say `limit:` instead of `page_size:`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter

findings.title: Renaming public parameter page_size breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level (apparently public) function and the second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected, so this failure will only surface at runtime in whichever call sites use the keyword form. Either grep and update all call sites in the same change, or keep backward compatibility (e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias and map it onto `limit`) before removing the old name. No call sites were retrieved for this review, so the blast radius could not be verified here.

findings.title: Absolute import of `adapters` will fail inside the requests package
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so on Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError` unless a top-level module named `adapters` happens to exist. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped — TLS verification no longer applied
findings.body:
The new `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature (lines 148-149) but never assigns them to `req` before `req.prepare()` (lines 151-165), and `send()` (lines 363-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration and calls `adapter.send(request)`. There is therefore no path by which a caller-supplied CA bundle, `verify=True`, or client certificate reaches the transport. Callers that today pass `verify='/path/ca.pem'` or `cert=(...)` will get a connection that ignores both, with no error. The same applies to `timeout` (line 141), so a hostile or merely slow server can hold a connection open indefinitely.

Either thread `verify`/`cert`/`timeout` onto the `PreparedRequest` (or pass them as arguments to `Session.send()` → `adapter.send()`), or raise/fail loudly until the refactor is finished, rather than accepting the arguments and discarding them.

Adversary: anyone in a position to intercept the connection (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream ISP, compromised proxy — note `proxies` is still honoured on line 162). They control the network path and, if the adapter's default is not to verify, they get full plaintext read/write of the session including `auth` credentials set on line 158.

findings.title: `old_request` calls `_send_request`, which this diff deletes
findings.body: `_send_request` is removed in this hunk, but the surviving code path (now `old_request`) still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches that line raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: Per-call HTTPAdapter plus no-op close() leaks pooled connections
findings.body: `send()` constructs a brand new `HTTPAdapter` on every call, so each request gets a fresh connection pool and nothing is reused — the Session no longer pools anything. At the same time `close()` became `pass`, so the pools that are created are never cleared and sockets are left to the garbage collector; `__exit__` (line 129) now does nothing useful either. Hold a single adapter on the Session (created in `__init__`) and have `close()` dispose of it.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch and session state
findings.body: The new `request()` accepts `timeout`, `allow_redirects`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` and `cert` but only copies a subset onto the `Request` and never passes the rest to `send()`. A caller doing `session.get(url, timeout=1, verify=False)` now gets an unbounded, certificate-verifying request with no error — silent misbehaviour is worse than a `TypeError`. `return_response=False` likewise no longer changes the return shape. Equally, none of the session-level state (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.config`) is merged into the request, so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare one. If these are intentionally staged, drop the parameters from the signature or raise `NotImplementedError` rather than accepting and discarding them.

findings.title: Session.send() and close() behavior changes are untested
findings.body: send() previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates. close() previously closed self.poolmanager and is now a bare `pass`, silently dropping connection cleanup. No test file is present in this diff to verify that HTTPAdapter.send() returns an equivalent response object or that resources are still released on close(). If HTTPAdapter.send() is later wrong (e.g. drops headers, doesn't set .request, or leaks connections since close() no longer clears anything), nothing in this change would catch it.

findings.title: Stale docstring: close() no longer closes PoolManager
findings.body: The `close()` method on line 131–132 now contains only `pass`, but the docstring that previously documented its behavior (closing pooled connections via the PoolManager) was removed. If callers rely on the documented behavior of `close()` to clean up resources, they will find the method does nothing. Either restore the cleanup logic or update any remaining documentation that describes what `close()` does.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows module shadowing
findings.body:
Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager` on lines 18-19). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, whose first entry for a script-invoked process is the script's directory (and, in some embedding/interactive cases, the current working directory). Any `adapters.py` a local attacker can place there is loaded in preference to the library's own module, and that module owns the entire HTTP send path — request bodies, `auth` credentials, and responses. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

Adversary: a local user or any process that can write to a directory that ends up on `sys.path` of the consuming application; they control the file contents; they get arbitrary code execution inside every outbound request.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body: When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises (malformed/hostile Cookie header), the property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Every consumer then fails: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError`. The old code kept `_cookies` as a `SimpleCookie` instance (and additionally expired the bad cookies via `clear_all_cookies()`), so a bad header degraded to "no cookies" rather than an exception. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the except branch instead of `None`.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing callers
findings.body:
The entry point is the client-supplied `Cookie` request header (line 518-521). When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises on a malformed value, the new code caches `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Every consumer in this diff treats the return value as a mapping: `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367). `name in None` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 on any handler that reads a cookie — including `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths that go through `get_cookie`.

The adversary is any remote client; what they control is the raw `Cookie` header; what they get is a guaranteed 500 on every cookie-reading endpoint. It is not purely self-inflicted: an attacker who can plant a cookie in a victim's browser (XSS on the site, or a sibling/parent-domain host writing a domain-scoped cookie with an illegal key) persistently breaks every subsequent request that victim makes, since browsers will keep replaying the bad header.

The previous code never returned a non-mapping: on failure it called `clear_all_cookies()` and still returned the (partially loaded) `SimpleCookie`. Preserve that invariant — on exception reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` rather than `None`. If the old side effect of emitting delete headers is wanted, that belongs in `RequestHandler`, not in `HTTPRequest`.

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no delegating shim
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a public, documented attribute; the diff deletes it entirely rather than replacing it with `@property def cookies(self): return self.request.cookies`. Any application subclass, template, or other tornado module that reads `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` now raises `AttributeError`. Keeping a one-line delegating property preserves the old contract at no cost.

findings.title: No test covers behavior change on malformed Cookie header parsing
findings.body: The original RequestHandler.cookies caught parse exceptions and called self.clear_all_cookies() to reset handler-level state, leaving self._cookies as an initialized SimpleCookie. The new HTTPRequest.cookies instead sets self._cookies = None on parse failure. Callers such as RequestHandler.get_cookie ('name in self.request.cookies') and clear_all_cookies ('self.request.cookies.iterkeys()') will now raise a TypeError/AttributeError when a malformed Cookie header is sent, instead of behaving as if no cookies were present. There is no test in this diff exercising a malformed 'Cookie' header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Boundary never matched: split(";") leaves leading whitespace in key
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the conventional space after the semicolon still attached, e.g. `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary"`. `field.partition("=")` then produces `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called for the normal header form and the `for`/`else` falls through to `logging.warning("Invalid multipart/form-data")`. Every standard multipart upload would be parsed as empty. The previous code used a substring test (`'boundary=' in content_type`) and was immune to this. Strip the token before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

findings.title: No test covers multi-parameter Content-Type boundary parsing
findings.body: The new logic iterates over all ';'-separated fields in the Content-Type header to find 'boundary=', fixing a bug where boundary was assumed to be the last field (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8' would previously fail to find the boundary correctly). No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type header with boundary followed by another parameter, so a regression back to the old split-based logic (or a similar bug) would not be caught.

findings.title: Quoted boundary value passed through with quotes intact
findings.body: RFC 2046 permits (and some clients emit) `boundary="----foo"`. The value handed to `_parse_mime_body` still contains the double quotes, so the delimiter used to split the body will not match the actual `------foo` lines. Since the parsing here is being reworked anyway, consider `v.strip('"')` before use. Note this matches the old behaviour, so it is not a regression introduced by this change.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#', allowing host confusion vs. urlparse
findings.body:
`get_host` only cuts the authority at the first `/`. RFC 3986 (and `urllib.parse.urlsplit`) also terminate the authority at `?` and `#`. Because the `@` split happens after the `/` split, a query or fragment containing `@` moves the parsed host:

- `get_host('http://good.com?@evil.com/')` -> after the `/` split the value is `good.com?@evil.com`, the `@` split then yields host `evil.com`.
- `get_host('http://good.com#@evil.com/')` behaves the same way.
- `urlsplit` returns `good.com` for both.

Adversary: anyone who can supply a URL to an application that allow-lists the destination with the stdlib parser (webhook targets, user-supplied image/avatar fetchers, redirect followers). They control the full URL string; they get a connection made to a host they chose while the application's allow-list saw a host it trusted — i.e. an SSRF filter bypass.

Suggested fix: cut the authority at the first occurrence of any of `/`, `?`, `#` before the `@`/`:` handling, and take the *last* `@` rather than the first (matching how the stdlib and browsers resolve `a@b@c`). Also consider rejecting bracketed IPv6 forms explicitly rather than mis-splitting them on `:`.

findings.title: New util.py functions have no accompanying tests in this diff
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped each contain non-trivial branching logic (encoding normalization, URL component splitting with a malformed-port error path, and platform-specific poll/select dispatch), but no test file is included in this change. If any of these were subtly broken during the lift (e.g. the get_host port-parsing error message uses an unformatted '%s' placeholder, or the accept_encoding list/string handling regresses), nothing would fail. Since this is presented as a pure code-motion refactor, at minimum the existing behavior should be pinned with tests for each function's branches.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: The raised message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — there is no `% url` (or `% port`) applied, so every parse failure surfaces the placeholder instead of the offending value. Callers catching this exception and logging `str(e)` get no diagnostic information at all. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode string silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The type dispatch tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)` only. On Python 2 a `unicode` value (very common for callers using `from __future__ import unicode_literals`, or values read from config/JSON) is neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls into the `else` branch and the caller's explicitly requested encoding is silently discarded and overwritten with `'gzip,deflate'` — the opposite of the documented "String will be used as provided" contract. `six` is already imported on line 16; use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)`.

findings.title: 'status' sort column has no test coverage
findings.body: SORTABLE maps three keys (created_at, amount, status) but only created_at (default) and amount are exercised by tests. If the status branch had a typo (e.g. wrong column name) or SQL issue, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Location attribute no longer stores the constructed string
findings.body: The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. However, line 8 now stores a `URL` object instead of the original string. This breaks the documented contract and could cause application code relying on string comparison or `str.startswith()` to fail with an AttributeError.

findings.title: `self.location` now a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location = location` stored exactly the value the caller passed (a string in the common case). After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. `URL` has no `startswith` method (AttributeError at runtime) and `URL("/foo") == "/foo"` is False, so equality checks silently flip to False. Additionally `URL()` normalises/percent-encodes, so even `str(self.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip the original string.

If the intent is only to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original value:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

If changing the attribute type is intentional, it is a breaking public API change and needs a docs update plus a changelog entry.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location changes from str to URL, breaking string-based redirect checks

findings.title: No test guards location's documented string type/behavior
findings.body: The diff changes self.location from the raw string/original location value to a URL object (self.location = URL(location)). This contradicts docs/web_reference.rst, which states location is 'the string it was constructed with' and that application code calls str.startswith on it — a URL object lacks that method and would raise AttributeError. No test in this diff exercises `.location`'s type or verifies startswith/string behavior still works, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer — the docstring explicitly tells callers to "re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on an empty buffer with `_eof` still false, returning `b""`. Callers of `readany` (and iteration helpers built on it) treat empty bytes as end-of-stream, so a chunk boundary can silently truncate a response body. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait lets a peer make readany() return b"" as a false EOF

findings.title: No test covers the case where _wait resolves without new data
findings.body: The docstring for `_wait` explicitly states the waiter can be resolved at the end of a chunk with no new data in the buffer, requiring callers to re-check their condition. The diff changes `readany`'s wait from a `while` loop to a single `if`, meaning that if the waiter resolves without new data being added (buffer still empty, not EOF), the method will now call `_read_nowait(-1)` and return an empty result instead of continuing to wait for real data. There is no test in this change (or referenced) that simulates a spurious wake with an empty buffer to catch this regression.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module load on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Python 3 removed implicit relative imports (PEP 328), so this resolves as a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on `sys.path` — importing `requests.sessions` (and therefore `import requests`) raises `ModuleNotFoundError`. Even under Python 2 this silently breaks as soon as `from __future__ import absolute_import` is in effect, and it can accidentally shadow an unrelated top-level `adapters` package. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or use the absolute form `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`), matching the adjacent relative import on line 6.

findings.title: Unqualified `import adapters` allows module shadowing of the HTTP transport
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` guarantees the adapter comes from the `requests` package directory. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead, so the first `adapters.py` (or `adapters/` package) found anywhere on the path wins — including the empty-string entry (process CWD for `python -c`, `python -m`, the REPL, and many task runners), the invoking script's directory, and any writable `site-packages`/PYTHONPATH entry.

Adversary: anyone able to place a file in a directory that lands earlier on `sys.path` than the `requests` package — a local user on a shared host, a CI job that checks out an untrusted repo and runs tooling from that checkout, or a user-writable app directory. What they control: the contents of `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code executed at import time in the importing process, and control of the `HTTPAdapter` class that performs every outbound request — i.e. they can return an adapter that disables certificate verification, rewrites the target host, or exfiltrates request bodies and Authorization headers, silently, for all traffic through this `Session`.

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. On Python 3 the new form also simply fails to import, so there is no upside to trade against.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The premise of the change ("cookies is always a mapping after construction") is contradicted by the retrieved `HTTPRequest.cookies` property, which returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed and documents that "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 on any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including secure-cookie/XSRF paths that build on it). Restore the guard, e.g. `cookies = self.request.cookies; if cookies and name in cookies:`, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` — but the latter is a contract change for other consumers and must not be done implicitly here.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header now raises TypeError in get_cookie
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully attacker-controlled by any unauthenticated remote client. Sink: the membership test on line 3. What the attacker gets: an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) on every handler that calls `get_cookie` — which in Tornado includes `get_secure_cookie`, session/identity lookup and XSRF token retrieval — simply by sending one junk `Cookie:` header. That is a trivially reproducible availability/error-handling defect, and it turns a normally-succeeding request path into a server error for anyone who can be induced to carry a poisoned cookie (e.g. a cookie set on a sibling subdomain).

Either restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and` guard here, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping on parse failure and update its docstring — but do not drop the check while the property can still yield `None`.

findings.title: Removed None-guard on request.cookies has no regression test
findings.body: The retrieved httpserver.py docstring states cookies is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, contradicting the PR's premise that 'cookies is always a mapping after construction.' No test exercises get_cookie() with a malformed Cookie header (which would make self.request.cookies None), so if this simplification reintroduces a TypeError on 'name in None', nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that retain the whitespace that conventionally follows the semicolon, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz"` → `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=xyz"]`. The removed `.strip()` was what normalised that segment before `partition("=")`; without it `k == " boundary"` and the comparison on line 5 fails, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and all multipart form fields/files are silently discarded for any client that sends the standard `; boundary=` spacing (i.e. nearly all of them).

The PR description says the strip was "redundant on the parameter value", but the strip was applied to the whole field *before* partitioning, so it was load-bearing for the key. If the intent was only to stop stripping the value, keep the key normalisation: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip only the key: `k, sep, v = field.partition("="); k = k.strip()`.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary lookup and creates a parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that keep the leading OWS that RFC 9110 permits (and that essentially every client emits): for `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the second element is `" boundary=abc"`.
